Reference ticket for the Graphify follow-up work delivered on branch EOP-3-graphify-followups.

Context

Graphify was wired up across three earlier changes (PRs #22, #23, #24) but the reasoning lived only in the Blueprint, several onboarding facts were wrong, and the tool namespace was ungoverned. This ticket covers closing those gaps.

Scope

Decision record — a new ADR under docs/adr/ records the Graphify decisions: repo-local 0.17.1 pin over a global install, graphify serve over a hand-rolled plugin, graphify opencode install rejected, repo-relative MCP command path, assistant enrichment mode, English pinned via --description-lang en --label-lang en, community names maintained but node descriptions deliberately not, commit-msg hook installed but Graphify's post-commit hook deliberately not.

Onboarding correctness — docs/devops/local-development.md claimed Node.js was needed "for the planned React front-end only" and that the OpenCode plugins do not need it. False: Graphify's CLI is a separate Node process spawned from mcp.graphify.command, and below Node 20 the MCP server fails silently with no graphify_* tools. Added the missing per-clone bootstrap (cd tools/graphify && npm install --ignore-scripts) and git config core.hooksPath .githooks to both SETUP.md and the local development guide.

Governance — added a graphify_ deny-then-allow-list to .opencode/opencode.json mirroring the existing github_ block, so a mutating tool in a future version is denied until reviewed.

Commit convention enforcement — .githooks/commit-msg machine-enforces the ticket prefix plus a conventional type, activated per clone via core.hooksPath.

Honest consequences recorded — the graph is ~96% git metadata against 21 code edges; a single keyword query returns 91% of the graph; node descriptions are neither durable across a rebuild nor rendered over MCP.

Decisions taken, and work deliberately not done

The `.graphify/scope.json` recommendation is declined. --scope all would ingest 27,989 ignored files, 99.5% of them node_modules. A graphify.yaml inputs.corpus would not help either: documentation is skipped because doc extraction needs a model backend we deliberately do not configure, not because of scope. Revisit only as a cost decision.

Graphify's `post-commit` hook is not installed — its fast path rebuilds topology without labels, silently discarding enrichment.

Notes

Commits on the already-merged PRs #22, #23 and #24 carry the prefix of a since-deleted ticket and were not rewritten; only this branch was reconciled to this ticket.

fields.summary: Make the Graphify knowledge graph operational, documented and governed, and correct false documentation claims

renderedFields.description:
Give the PoC a public URL so the running application can be demonstrated, and provision everything as code so that moving to a different AWS account later is a variable change rather than a rebuild.

Goal. A reachable demo at http://<elastic-ip>:8080/health served by the real packaged artifact, not a development-mode JVM.

Container as the portability boundary. The deployment unit is an OCI image built in CI and published to GitHub Container Registry. The registry deliberately does not live in the AWS account, so it does not have to move when the account does. The same image runs locally under Compose and on the instance, with the same Spring profile, so local behaviour predicts deployed behaviour.

Database. PostgreSQL in a container alongside the application, not Amazon RDS. Its data directory lives on a separate EBS volume so that terminating or replacing the instance does not destroy the data, and so a volume snapshot is a complete migration path.

Infrastructure as code. Terraform, committed to the repository. No hardcoded AMI identifiers — Amazon Linux 2023 is resolved from the public SSM parameter so the same code works in any region. No account identifiers, ARNs or CIDR blocks inlined; all of them are variables. No console clicks, because anything created by hand will not exist in the next account.

Instance. A t3.small in eu-west-2. Two gigabytes of memory rather than one, so that a JVM and PostgreSQL can coexist without memory tuning games and without an out-of-memory kill masquerading as a mysterious crash.

Accepted risks, recorded rather than hidden. The demo is plain HTTP against a bare IP address, so browsers will report it as not secure; public certificate authorities do not issue certificates for bare IP addresses on the normal path. Shell access is by SSH keypair, which means port 22 must be open on a public IP and a private key must be managed; if continuous deployment later drives the instance over SSH, that private key becomes a repository secret and the current zero-secrets property of the pipeline is lost. Both choices are deliberate and are recorded in the accompanying decision record.

Production configuration change. The production profile binds to loopback only. Inside a container that provides no isolation, merely unreachability, so the bind address changes to all interfaces. Isolation comes from the security group and from which ports are published.

Out of scope. TLS, a domain name, autoscaling, load balancing, Amazon RDS, and the front-end scaffold.

fields.summary: Deploy the walking skeleton to a personal AWS account on EC2, provisioned with Terraform

renderedFields.description:
Goal.

A development team can play a full game of Elevation of Privilege threat modelling together in a browser on the same machine, with game state that survives a browser refresh and a server restart. Multiplayer is simulated across three browsers (Chrome, Safari, and Chrome Incognito) to avoid shared cookie state, running the full stack locally via the container runtime delivered in EOP-16.

Why.

Threat modelling works best as a collaborative activity with a shared vocabulary. Microsoft's Elevation of Privilege card game provides that, but requires a physical deck and a shared table. Distributed teams cannot play it. This application is the digital equivalent.

Product decisions taken by the owner.

Multiplayer, as a digital replacement for the around-the-table design review rather than a solo learning tool. Game state persists so a session can be resumed. Card content reproduces the Microsoft deck, subject to licence verification. The front end is a separate container behind a reverse proxy. Accessibility is best effort using GOV.UK Design System defaults, with full WCAG 2.2 AA explicitly not claimed.

Deployment model.

The application runs locally on the developer machine using the container runtime installed in EOP-16. No cloud account is required. A public URL is not a goal of this epic. If a cloud deployment is wanted later, the Terraform code under infra/ is a valid starting point and requires no changes to the application artifacts.

Requirements document.

docs/requirements/PRD-eop-card-game.md in the repository is the source of truth for scope, journeys, domain concepts, assumptions and risks.

Starting point.

The build-and-verify half of the walking skeleton already exists and is proven in CI: the application compiles and tests on every push, is packaged as a container image, boots under the production profile against real PostgreSQL with Liquibase enabled, has its health endpoint asserted, and is published to the GitHub container registry. The local container runtime (EOP-16) is installed and the whole stack runs on the developer machine. This epic does not recreate any of that.

Known blocker resolved.

The card deck licence terms and card count were previously unverified. That is now resolved: the deck is copyright 2009 Microsoft Corporation, licensed under Creative Commons Attribution 3.0 United States, and the full 78-card machine-readable deck is committed. EOP-13 is Done.

Architectural decisions this epic will force.

Real-time transport for multiplayer, player identity within an anonymous session, concurrency control when two players act at once, and reverse-proxy topology for serving the front end. Each needs a recorded decision before the story that depends on it starts. Decisions 014, 015, 016 and 019 are already recorded.

fields.summary: EoP threat modelling card game: playable multiplayer session

renderedFields.description:
Epic: EOP-5. Order: first. Size: M. Blocked by: nothing.

As a developer building the game, I want the threat cards stored in the database and served from the API, so that every later story has a real domain model and a real endpoint to build on.

Why this goes first. It is the thinnest slice that proves the whole stack end to end, and it needs no deployment to verify. CI already boots the application under the production profile against real PostgreSQL with Liquibase enabled and asserts the health endpoint, so a new entity, a migration and an endpoint are fully provable in the pipeline. This deliberately does not wait on the AWS account.

Deck content. Six placeholder cards, one per STRIDE category, with prompts written by us. The real Microsoft deck lands later as a data-only change once its licence and card count are verified. That keeps a legal question off the engineering critical path.

Acceptance criteria

Deployed behind flag. The endpoints are merged and running in the pipeline with the feature flag off, and while off they are not advertised and return 404. The application still starts, the health endpoint still returns exactly OK, and the existing smoke test still passes.

Released to users, flag on. A request to GET /api/v1/cards returns 200 and a paged body of exactly six cards. Each card carries an identifier, a STRIDE category drawn from the existing six-constant enum, a card number, and a non-empty threat prompt. A request to GET /api/v1/cards/

{id}

with a known identifier returns 200 and that single card. With an unknown identifier it returns 404 carrying an RFC 9457 problem detail body.

Hard constraints this story must satisfy

Migration first, or the application will not start. There are zero entity classes today, and that is the only reason startup succeeds against a validate-only schema with an empty changelog. The first Liquibase changeset creating the card table must be written and applied as part of this story. A change that adds an entity without a changeset must be rejected.

Contract before code. The OpenAPI 3.1 specification is hand authored at docs/api/openapi.yml and committed before any controller exists. That file does not exist yet, so this story creates it. URLs follow /api/v1/

{resource}

. Lists are paged. Note the API schema and Swagger UI are disabled in the production profile by an earlier decision, so the committed specification is the only contract on the deployed instance.

First error handler. This story introduces RFC 9457 problem details for the first time. Every 4xx and 5xx response from this point forward uses that format.

Clean architecture. The card type in the domain has zero Spring and zero Jakarta imports. A separate data transfer object crosses the boundary. Retrieval logic lives in a use case. The controller is an adapter only.

renderedFields.description:
Epic: EOP-5. Order: second. Size: S engineering, but blocked on owner tasks. Blocked by: no AWS account exists.

As the product owner, I want the application running at a public IP address, so that I can send someone a URL and have them see it working.

Why this is second and not first. It is the only story that cannot be completed by engineering alone, so it must not gate anything else. It is independent of every other story in this epic: the card catalogue, the transport spike and the UI scaffold can all proceed and be verified in CI while this waits.

What already exists. The build-and-verify half of the walking skeleton is complete and proven. Terraform under infra/ describes a t3.small in a dedicated VPC with an Elastic IP and a separate encrypted volume for database data, and it passes validation. A deployable image for the correct architecture is already published to the GitHub container registry. Nothing here is being designed; it is being applied for the first time.

Owner pre-conditions, not engineering work

A personal AWS account on a non-corporate email address, with multi-factor authentication enabled on the root user and no root access keys ever created. The malformed credentials file on the development machine repaired or deleted, because in its current state it breaks every AWS command. A bootstrap identity with keys in a named profile, referenced per command, never exported globally and never placed in the repository environment file, because that file holds the model-provider bearer token and populating the standard AWS key variables risks breaking model access. A spending alarm created before the first resource. The container registry package made public, so the instance can pull the image without credentials; note this cannot be automated because the available token lacks the packages scope. Confirmation of the region and the profile name.

Acceptance criteria

Infrastructure provisioned. A plan runs clean, an apply succeeds, and the instance is running in the provisioned network with the Elastic IP associated and the encrypted data volume attached and mounted at the expected path.

Reachable and verified. A request from the public internet to the health endpoint on the Elastic IP returns 200 with a body of exactly OK.

Data survives instance replacement. The database data directory is confirmed to be on the separate volume and not on the root volume. This is the single most important check in the story: the mount uses a no-fail option, so a failed mount would silently let the database initialise an empty directory on the root volume, which looks exactly like data loss and is destroyed on termination.

Note on scope. No reverse proxy in this story and no change to the exposed port. The health endpoint is verified on its current port. Serving on port 80 arrives with the front end, where it belongs.

Note on the health endpoint. It must continue to return exactly OK. The smoke test and the load test both assert that literal value, so changing it would remove the only automated proof that the artifact starts.

Deployment remains manual. Rolling a new image is a pull and restart over SSH. An earlier decision deliberately rejected pipeline-driven SSH deployment rather than place a private key into repository secrets, which would destroy the current property that the pipeline holds no secrets at all. If automated deployment is wanted later, that is a separate decision with a real cost.

comments.body:
Postponed, not withdrawn. This story is still wanted and still correct. It is being left in To Do rather than closed, because unlike EOP-12 — which described the wrong game and was retired — nothing here is wrong. Only the timing has changed.

What changed. The owner has decided to run the proof of concept on the developer machine for now rather than in the cloud. That work is EOP-16 and is complete: a container runtime is installed, the whole stack runs locally, and the verification gates that had only ever run in the pipeline now run on a real host.

Why this story survives intact. The pivot to local required no change to a single artifact this story depends on. Same container image definition, same compose file, same active profile, same environment variable contract. That is the strongest available evidence that the portability argument in the deployment decision record was sound, and it is why that record has been amended with a dated note rather than superseded.

What is still unproven. The infrastructure code is untouched and has still never been applied. It parses and validates, and that is all it proves. Every claim about how the instance behaves remains unverified against a real cloud API: the machine image resolving from the public parameter store in the chosen region, the bootstrap script running to completion, the volume discovery by device serial, an anonymous pull of the published image, and the database coming up before the application. The mount hazard called out in this story's third acceptance criterion — where a failed mount silently lets the database initialise an empty directory on the ephemeral disk, which looks exactly like data loss — is the single most important thing this story checks and it has never been checked.

The five owner pre-conditions remain outstanding. None have been started. They are unchanged from the original description: a personal cloud account on a non-corporate address with multi-factor authentication on the root identity; the malformed credentials file on the developer machine repaired or deleted, because in its current state it breaks every command against that cloud provider; a bootstrap identity with keys in a named profile referenced per command, never exported globally and never placed in the repository environment file, because that file holds the model provider bearer token and populating the standard key variables risks breaking model access; a spending alarm created before the first resource exists; and the container registry package made public so the instance can pull without credentials, which cannot be automated because the available token lacks the packages scope.

One correction to the original scope note. The owner also asked to destroy and recreate the instance on every demo rather than leave it running. If that model is adopted, three things in the infrastructure code change: the guard preventing destruction of the data volume blocks the destroy outright and must be removed or made conditional; the separate data volume loses its entire justification, and removing it also removes the mount hazard described above; and the static address buys nothing, at the cost of the address changing every session so no link can be shared in advance. That is a decision to take when this story starts, not now.

What unblocks it. Only the owner pre-conditions. No engineering work is waiting on anything.

Delivery attempted 2026-08-10; still blocked on owner pre-conditions. Two corrections to the previous comment, and one decision now needed.

Verified on the developer machine just now, not assumed.

Engineering half: still green, still unproven. terraform fmt -check -recursive is clean and terraform validate returns "Success! The configuration is valid." A terraform plan against the example variables gets as far as resolving the random-suffix resource and then stops at the provider: Error: No valid credential sources found — followed by failed to refresh cached credentials, no EC2 IMDS role found. So the configuration parses, and that remains all it proves. Nothing has been applied and no claim about instance behaviour has been checked.

Pre-condition 2 is confirmed outstanding and is the immediate hard stop. ~/.aws/credentials exists (21 bytes, last modified 21 May) and is unparseable. Both aws configure list-profiles and aws sts get-caller-identity fail identically with aws: [ERROR]: Unable to parse config file: /Users/…/.aws/credentials. Until that file is repaired or deleted, no command against this cloud provider can run at all, with or without an account.

Correction one: pre-condition 5 is already satisfied. The container registry packages are public. An anonymous manifest fetch — a token request with no credentials, then a manifest GET — returns HTTP 200 for both eop-threat-medeling and eop-threat-medeling-ui. The instance will be able to pull without credentials. Four owner pre-conditions remain, not five: the account itself with multi-factor authentication on the root identity, the malformed credentials file, a bootstrap identity with keys in a named profile, and a spending alarm before the first resource. Region and profile name still need confirming; the configuration defaults to eu-west-2 with the profile variable commented out.

Correction two: this story now has two images, not one. infra/variables.tf carries both app_image and ui_image, because the front end and its reverse proxy landed after this story was written. The scope note here — "no reverse proxy in this story and no change to the exposed port" — is therefore stale, and what the first deployment actually serves needs restating before it is applied.

The deferred decision is now due. The previous comment recorded that destroying and recreating the instance per demo "is a decision to take when this story starts, not now." The story has started, so it is needed before any apply. Choosing destroy-and-recreate removes the guard on the data volume, removes the separate volume and with it the mount hazard that is this story's third and most important acceptance criterion, and makes the static address pointless — no link can be shared in advance. Choosing to leave the instance running keeps all three, keeps the mount check meaningful, and costs money continuously.

Unrelated finding, raised because it changes what a first deployment would actually deploy. The branch EOP-10-session-lifecycle is 26 commits ahead of main with no open pull request, and it carries the whole of EOP-10 — which is marked Done here — plus five engineering-system commits. main currently ends at the EOP-13 deck merge. The published :latest image therefore predates the session lifecycle, so deploying today would put a demonstrably older artifact on the instance. That branch wants merging before the first live deployment is worth doing.

Withdrawn 2026-08-10. The deployment goal has changed; this story is superseded by EOP-16.

The product owner has decided not to deploy to AWS. The application will be demonstrated locally on the developer machine, with multiplayer simulated across three browsers (Chrome, Safari, and Chrome Incognito) to avoid shared cookie state. This is the same model EOP-16 already anticipated and delivered: its description explicitly states "Multiplayer is simulated with several browser tabs, which works because the player credential is held per tab."

EOP-16 is Done and satisfies the walking skeleton's deployment half in the new model. There is no remaining engineering work in this story.

The Terraform code under infra/ is retained in the repository as a valid, validated artefact. It has never been applied and makes no claims about runtime behaviour. If a cloud deployment is wanted in the future, it remains the starting point and the decisions it embodies — portability boundary, no hardcoded AMIs, no account identifiers in code — are still sound. The mount hazard called out in this story's third acceptance criterion (a failed no-fail mount silently initialising an empty directory on the ephemeral disk) is the one thing that has never been checked and would need to be verified if the Terraform path is ever resumed.

Closing as Done — superseded, not delivered. No code was written against this story.

renderedFields.description:
Epic: EOP-5. Order: third. Size: S, time-boxed to two days. Blocked by: nothing.

As the engineering team, I want a time-boxed spike that proves how state reaches every connected player, so that the multiplayer stories are not built on an unvalidated assumption.

Why this exists. Multiplayer is the largest decision in this epic and it introduces a class of problem the application has never had. There is currently no push mechanism of any kind, no websocket dependency on the dependency list, and no notion of player identity. Guessing at all three inside a feature story would surface the surprises mid-implementation. This spike surfaces them first, cheaply, and its output is decisions rather than production code.

Goal. Demonstrate that two browser tabs receive a server-pushed state change within half a second, running against the real application under the container stack.

What must come out of it

A recorded decision on transport, number 014. Websocket with a message broker, versus server-sent events, versus periodic polling. Server-sent events deserve serious consideration: the game is overwhelmingly server-to-client, they need no new protocol, they reconnect automatically by specification, and they pass through a reverse proxy with less configuration. Websockets are the reflex answer and may still win, but the reflex should be challenged. Any new dependency must be justified in the decision.

A recorded decision on player identity, number 015. Anonymous does not mean identity-free. Something must answer whose turn it is and whether this browser is that player, and it must survive a refresh. Options include a signed cookie, a value in browser storage, or a server-issued opaque token. Note the security consequence: whatever this is becomes the only thing standing between a stranger with a session code and the ability to act as another player.

A throwaway branch demonstrating the chosen transport, deleted once the decisions are merged. No production code graduates from this spike.

The constraint that shapes everything downstream

The application runs as a single instance with no load balancer and no session affinity, and every deployment is a container restart. Every connected client therefore loses its connection on every deploy. Reconnection is not a refinement to add later; it is a functional requirement, and the spike must demonstrate it rather than assume it.

the multiplayer stories are not built on an unvalidated assumption.

Multiplayer is the largest decision in this epic and it introduces a class of problem the application has never had. There is currently no push mechanism of any kind, no websocket dependency on the dependency list, and no notion of player identity. Guessing at all three inside a feature story would surface the surprises mid-implementation. This spike surfaces them first, cheaply, and its output is decisions rather than production code.
Demonstrate that two browser tabs receive a server-pushed state change within half a second, running against the real application under the container stack.
What must come out of it
A recorded decision on transport, number 014.

Websocket with a message broker, versus server-sent events, versus periodic polling. Server-sent events deserve serious consideration: the game is overwhelmingly server-to-client, they need no new protocol, they reconnect automatically by specification, and they pass through a reverse proxy with less configuration. Websockets are the reflex answer and may still win, but the reflex should be challenged. Any new dependency must be justified in the decision.
A recorded decision on player identity, number 015.

Anonymous does not mean identity-free. Something must answer whose turn it is and whether this browser is that player, and it must survive a refresh. Options include a signed cookie, a value in browser storage, or a server-issued opaque token. Note the security consequence: whatever this is becomes the only thing standing between a stranger with a session code and the ability to act as another player.
demonstrating the chosen transport, deleted once the decisions are merged. No production code graduates from this spike.
The constraint that shapes everything downstream

The application runs as a single instance with no load balancer and no session affinity, and every deployment is a container restart. Every connected client therefore loses its connection on every deploy. Reconnection is not a refinement to add later; it is a functional requirement, and the spike must demonstrate it rather than assume it.

Epic: EOP-5. Order: fourth, and can run in parallel with the spike. Size: M. Blocked by: a decision on delivery topology, number 016.

As a player, I want to open a browser and see a real page, so that I know I am in the right place and can start or join a game.

Why now. This is the first slice that makes the project look like a product rather than a health endpoint. It contains no game logic deliberately: it is the shell every later screen builds on. It can be developed and verified in the pipeline without any deployment.

Delivery topology, chosen by the owner. A separate container behind a reverse proxy, rather than folding the built assets into the application jar. The proxy also gives a place for the eventual TLS termination. Recommendation is Caddy over nginx, purely because it obtains and renews certificates automatically once a domain exists, turning the accepted no-TLS limitation into a one-line change rather than a project. Nothing in any existing decision record selects a proxy, so this needs recording as decision 016 before work starts.

Acceptance criteria

Deployed behind flag. The proxy and front-end containers are added to the container stack and start cleanly. With the flag off, the proxy serves a holding page and no application route changes. The health endpoint still returns exactly OK through the proxy, and the existing load-test threshold still passes.

Released to users, flag on. A browser request to the site root returns 200 and renders a page using GOV.UK Design System markup, with a heading identifying the application and two calls to action for creating and joining a game. Neither button needs to work yet.

API reachable through the proxy. A request to a card-catalogue path from the browser is proxied to the application and returns without a cross-origin error. Same-origin through a single proxy is the point: it removes cross-origin configuration entirely rather than working around it.

Port surface reduced. The application port is no longer reachable from the public internet; only the proxy is. Note this is a change to the network rules in the infrastructure code as well as the container stack, not a container-only change.

Hard constraints

React with TypeScript built by Vite under a top-level ui directory, using GOV.UK Design System CSS, per the existing front-end decision. Accessibility is best effort using Design System defaults; full WCAG 2.2 AA is explicitly not claimed, and the gap is recorded rather than hidden. The pipeline must build the front-end artefact, which means the container build and the workflow both gain a step. Note there is no container runtime on the development machine, so the pipeline is the verifier for anything container-shaped.

Epic: EOP-5. Order: fifth. Size: L, the most complex story in the epic. Blocked by: decisions 014 and 015 from the spike.

As a facilitator, I want to create a game session and share a code with my team, so that we can all gather in the same lobby before play begins.

Why it is large. Two new persistent aggregates, two migrations, the first push events, and identity issuance and validation. It is the core multiplayer primitive and everything after it depends on it.

Acceptance criteria

Deployed behind flag. Session endpoints are merged and running with the flag off, returning 404 while off. Existing behaviour is untouched.

Creating a session, flag on. A create request with a display name returns 201, a session identifier, a short join code and a player identity credential. The creator becomes the facilitator and the session state is lobby.

Joining a session. A join request against a valid code with a display name returns 200, adds the player as a participant, and pushes a player-joined event to everyone already connected.

Unknown code. Returns 404 with an RFC 9457 problem detail. The response must not distinguish between a code that never existed and one that has expired, because that difference is an enumeration aid.

Joining a game already in progress. Returns 409 with a problem detail.

Rejoining after a refresh. A player holding a valid identity credential returns to the session URL, is recognised as the same player, and sees current lobby state without re-entering a display name.

Reconnecting after a server restart. State is read from the database rather than memory, so a container restart loses connections but not the game. The client re-establishes its stream and resynchronises. This is a functional requirement, not a refinement: every deployment restarts the container.

Hard constraints

Migrations for the session and player tables, written before the entities. Name the table game_session rather than session, to avoid ambiguity with HTTP sessions and any reserved-word trouble. The specification at docs/api/openapi.yml is updated before the controllers. Problem details for all errors. Clean architecture, with domain types free of framework imports and data transfer objects at the boundary. Tests as before.

Security requirements, called out because this is the first externally reachable write path

Join codes come from a cryptographically secure generator, never a general-purpose random. Codes must be long enough that guessing is impractical, and consider a rate limit on join attempts, because a short code plus unlimited guesses is an open door. Display names are validated and length-bounded on input and escaped on output. The identity credential is the only thing preventing a stranger from acting as another player, so its integrity matters more than its convenience. There is no authentication in this application by design, which makes each of these the entire control rather than one layer of several.

comments.body:
Amendment to this story's scope, from the corrected game rules.

The product requirements document was corrected after the real Elevation of Privilege rules were established from primary sources. One consequence lands here.

Assign a stable seat order when a player joins. Elevation of Privilege is a trick-taking game. Play proceeds clockwise, and the winner of each trick leads the next one. That means "who plays next" is derived by walking round the table from the current player, so the table itself must be an ordered structure. A Player therefore needs a seatOrder integer, assigned at the moment of joining and stable for the life of the session. This is load-bearing domain data, not bookkeeping - without it the turn sequence in EOP-14 cannot be computed at all.

Two constraints follow. Seat order must not be re-derived from a database sort or from join timestamps at read time, because a disconnect and reconnect must not move a player around the table. And it must survive the session being reloaded from PostgreSQL, since resuming mid-trick is a hard requirement.

Dealing the deck is not in this story. It belongs to EOP-14, which covers dealing the whole deck evenly into per-player hands at game start. Note there is no draw pile in this game - the deck is exhausted by the deal - so nothing in this story should model a remaining-deck or draw-pile concept.

Section 5 of docs/requirements/PRD-eop-card-game.md carries the corrected domain model and is the source of truth over this ticket.

Session lifecycle is complete and open for review as PR #35. Behind eop.features.session-lifecycle, which stays off in the deployed stack — merging this releases nothing.

Edited to repair formatting. Jira reads a bare ADR-NNN token as an issue key and links it to an issue that does not exist, which also broke the emphasis around each one. Monospace suppresses it, so the ADR references below are in backticks — worth knowing for the next comment that cites one.

Decisions this ticket turned from accepted into implemented (ADR index updated with the evidence for each):

  • ADR-013 — feature flags via configuration properties. The flag withholds the controller bean through @ConditionalOnProperty rather than branching inside a request. A test asserts the bean is absent and all five routes 404, so the mechanism is pinned and not just the symptom.
  • ADR-014 — real-time transport via SSE. One endpoint publishes state; the stream announces that something changed and never what. A reconnecting client therefore takes the same path it took on first load, and there is exactly one producer of state to keep correct.
  • ADR-015 — server-issued opaque token. Issued once on admission, 43 characters, stored only as a SHA-256 digest. Sent in a header, never in a URL, because a query parameter would land in every proxy log. IdentityTokenHash.toString() is a constant so a careless log line cannot print one, and no response shape has a field for the digest.
  • ADR-018 — UUID v7 through an application port. Identifiers are minted in the use case, not at flush, so the aggregate knows its own identity before it is stored. A test pins the version nibble, the variant bits and time ordering across 2,000 draws, so a Hibernate upgrade that quietly reverted to version 4 fails the build.
  • ADR-019 — session lifecycle, join codes, header-only stream auth. Crockford base32, seat contention settled by a unique index rather than a lock.

The entropy and throttling tradeoff, recorded because it constrains anything built on top. A six-character Crockford base32 code is about thirty bits. That is short enough to read aloud over a video call, which is the whole point of it, and short enough to enumerate if the endpoint answers honestly. So it does not: a malformed code, a well-formed code nobody holds, and a code belonging to a session that has moved on all produce one indistinguishable refusal, identical in status, title and detail. JoinCode.parse returns an empty optional rather than throwing precisely so that "that is not a code" cannot be told apart from "no session has that code".

Guessing is then throttled per client address and per normalised code — ten and thirty failures a minute. Two consequences worth stating plainly:

  • Only failures are counted. A popular lobby cannot throttle its own players, and a successful join is never charged. The limiter is a guess-rate limit, not a request-rate limit.
  • The limiter is in-memory, so it is per instance. Correct at one instance, which is what ADR-012 deploys. It is the first thing to revisit if a second instance ever appears, because the effective allowance multiplies by the instance count. Recorded here rather than left as a surprise.

Normalisation feeds the throttle too: the code bucket is the parsed code, so abc230, ABC23O and " abc23o " share one counter and an attacker gains nothing by varying spelling.

Two defects the tests exposed, both fixed on this branch.

  1. The seventh player got 400 "Invalid request" leaking an internal invariant instead of 409 "Session is full" — nextSeatOrder() returned the player count regardless of capacity, so the seat-range guard fired before the capacity check, and the handler for SessionFullException was mapping an exception the API could not actually emit. Fixed in the domain: a full table has no next seat.
  2. SessionStateDto shared the caller's mutable player list. SpotBugs failed the build on it; the constructor now copies. It surfaced only at close-out because the feature commits were checked with test rather than verify — worth remembering as a habit, not just a fact.

A production Javadoc claim was also corrected rather than believed: handleUnknownJoinCode said every failed lookup returns a byte-identical response, and it does not, because Spring populates instance with the request URI. The security property is intact — instance echoes only the caller's own input — and the test now pins what is load-bearing instead of what was merely written down.

Verification. ./mvnw verify green: 298 tests, 0 failures, instruction coverage 97.34% against the 0.80 floor, checkstyle/spotbugs/enforcer clean.

Also run against the real stack — PostgreSQL 17 behind Caddy — because a green suite on H2 is not the same claim. Migration 003 applied cleanly to PostgreSQL with ddl-auto: validate accepting the mappings, so the schema is now proven on both engines. A live curl -N stream through the proxy carried retry:3000, :subscribed, repeated :heartbeat comments, two player-joined events and a game-started. It survives a browser's Accept-Encoding: gzip as well, since Caddy excludes text/event-stream from compression — worth knowing, because a proxy that buffered it would break the feature without breaking a single test.

Not done here, deliberately. No front end consumes these endpoints yet, so the flag flip belongs to the lobby UI ticket — the one that can actually verify it end to end. ADR-012 stays Partly implemented; Terraform has still never been applied.

Epic: EOP-5. Order: sixth. Size: M. Blocked by: the session endpoints story and the UI scaffold story.

As a facilitator or player, I want to create or join a session from the browser, so that my team and I can gather in a lobby without anyone touching an API client.

Why it is separate from the scaffold. The scaffold proves the delivery topology; this proves the round trip. Splitting them means a proxy or build problem cannot masquerade as a game problem.

Acceptance criteria

Deployed behind flag. The lobby screens ship with the flag off, and while off the two calls to action on the home page are visibly disabled rather than broken.

Creating, flag on. The facilitator enters a display name, creates a session, and lands on a lobby screen showing the join code prominently and copyable, along with their own name.

Joining, flag on. A second player enters the code and a display name and arrives in the same lobby. The facilitator's screen updates to show the new player without a manual refresh. This is the first end-to-end proof that push actually works for a real user.

Returning after a refresh. A player who refreshes is returned to the lobby as themselves, without re-entering anything.

Failure is legible. An unknown or expired code produces a clear, human-readable message rather than a raw status code or a silent failure. Error text is derived from the problem detail response, not invented in the client.

Hard constraints

GOV.UK Design System components for every form control, with no custom CSS overriding Design System colour tokens, since that is the fastest way to widen the accessibility gap. Form fields validated client side for usability and server side for correctness, never client side only. Display names escaped on render.

This story is superseded. Do not work it. It is closed as superseded, not as delivered. No code was written against it.

Why it was retired. This story described the wrong game. It modelled a shared deck from which the active player drew a card blind, then played it against a component. Elevation of Privilege is not that game. It is a trick-taking card game, closest in mechanics to Spades: the whole deck is dealt evenly to the players, there is no draw pile, play proceeds in tricks, players must follow the led suit if they hold it, and Elevation of Privilege is the trump suit. This was established by reading the primary sources - the shipped instruction card, the Microsoft score card and Adam Shostack's whitepaper - all of which are now committed under docs/EoP_Microsoft_Docs/ with their licence recorded.

Replaced by two stories. The corrected mechanic is materially larger than what this story described, so it was split rather than rewritten in place. EOP-14 covers the trick mechanics: dealing the deck into hands, deriving the opening lead, enforcing follow-suit server-side, resolving the trump, awarding the trick and passing the lead. EOP-15 covers scoring and end of game: one point for a threat linked to the system, one more for taking the trick, computed server-side, with the winner declared when the hands are exhausted.

Where the rules now live. docs/requirements/PRD-eop-card-game.md is the source of truth and wins over any Jira story that disagrees with it. Its section 3 carries the sourced mechanic, section 5 the corrected domain model and section 11 a sources appendix citing each claim to a file and page.

_Epic:_ [EOP-5|https://maglez.atlassian.net/browse/EOP-5]. _Order:_ seventh. _Size:_ XL, the largest story. _Blocked by:_ the session story, the lobby UI story, and a decision on concurrency control, number 017.

*As the* active player, *I want* to draw a card and play it against a component of our system, *so that* the team discusses the threat it describes.

*This is the story that makes it a game.* Everything before it is infrastructure with a health check.

_Assumptions that must be confirmed before this starts_

The round mechanic and the treatment of the system being modelled were never answered. Working assumptions: the active player draws, names a component as free text, the group discusses, the card is marked discussed, and the turn passes round-robin in join order with the facilitator first. The game ends when the deck is exhausted or the facilitator ends it. There is no scoring. The system being threat-modelled is not represented in the application at all; players refer to their own diagram, and the only thing stored is the component name typed when a card is played. If any of that is wrong, this story changes shape, so confirm before starting rather than after.

_Acceptance criteria_

*Starting.* With at least two players in the lobby, the facilitator starts the game. The state becomes in-progress, the deck is shuffled and bound to the session, every player is notified, and the first turn begins.

*Drawing.* On their turn the active player draws. The card leaves the remaining deck, every player sees its category and prompt, and the active player is offered a field for the component name.

*Playing.* The active player submits a component name. The play is persisted and shown to everyone.

*Passing.* Marking the card discussed passes the turn and notifies everyone.

*Acting out of turn is refused.* A player who is not the active player cannot draw or play. This must be enforced on the server against the identity credential, not merely hidden in the interface.

*Finishing.* When the last card is played the session completes and everyone sees a summary of what was played against what.

*Ending early.* The facilitator can end the session at any point, and only the facilitator can.

_Hard constraints_

Migrations for the played-card table and the game-state columns, written first. Specification updated before controllers. Problem details for errors. Clean architecture, with the turn rules living in the domain and not in a controller, because they are business rules and putting them in an adapter is precisely the mistake the architecture exists to prevent.

_The test that matters most._ Two simultaneous draw requests must never deal the same card twice. This needs a real concurrent test, not a sequential one that assumes interleaving cannot happen. Optimistic locking with a version column is the likely mechanism, but the conflict semantics, meaning what the losing request is told and what the interface does about it, are a decision to record rather than an implementation detail to improvise.

renderedFields.description:
Replace the six placeholder cards seeded by EOP-6 with the full Elevation of Privilege deck, and show the attribution the licence requires.

This story is no longer blocked. It previously carried a blocked-on-owner label because the deck's licence was unverified. That is now resolved. The deck is copyright 2009 Microsoft Corporation, licensed under Creative Commons Attribution 3.0 United States. This is attested independently in three places: the copyright page of the shipped instruction card, footnote 6 of Adam Shostack's whitepaper, and the README of the adamshostack/eop repository. All three sources are committed under docs/EoP_Microsoft_Docs/, alongside LICENCE-eop-deck.md which records the terms. The whitepaper explicitly invites derivative work.

Seed 78 cards, not 74. The printed deck contained 74 playing cards because, in Shostack's words, the Elevation of Privilege suit starts at 5 and Tampering starts at 3 - Microsoft did not have enough distinct hints to fill those two suits and wanted to avoid repetition. The whitepaper's Future Work section names filling the deck out to 13 threats per suit as the intended direction, and the machine-readable cards.yaml in the adamshostack/eop repository is that completed deck: six suits of thirteen ranks, uniform. Seed from cards.yaml. Doing so removes two suit-specific minimum-rank special cases from the domain, which is a real simplification and not merely a larger number.

Fetch the content at implementation time. Get cards.yaml from the raw content URL of the adamshostack/eop repository on the master branch. It carries a rank_order list and a ranks map that the seeding code should follow rather than reinvent.

Acceptance criteria.

One Liquibase changeset, data only, adds the full deck. It introduces no schema change - EOP-6 already established that a card carries a suit, a rank and a threat text and nothing else. The changeset is additive and idempotent under Liquibase's own checksum rules, and it must not rewrite or delete the EOP-6 changeset, which is immutable once merged.

After the changeset applies, the card endpoint returns 78 cards: thirteen in each of the six STRIDE suits, with no gaps and no duplicates. A test asserts the count per suit rather than only the total, because a total of 78 can be reached with an uneven distribution.

Every Ace reads as an open-threat card in the form Microsoft used - an invitation to name a new attack of that suit - because EOP-14 gives Aces distinct behaviour and the seeded text must match it.

Attribution is visible in the running application, not only in the repository. This is the single obligation the licence imposes and it is not discharged by a file in docs/. Until the front end exists the attribution can live in the API response or a dedicated endpoint, but the acceptance criterion is that a person using the deployed application can see that the card content is Microsoft's and is licensed under CC-BY-3.0 US, with a link to the licence.

The placeholder cards from EOP-6 are removed or superseded, so the deck a player is dealt contains no invented filler.

Sizing. Small in engineering terms - one data changeset, one attribution surface, tests that count. The bulk of the work is transcription accuracy, which is why the content is taken from a machine-readable file rather than retyped from the card images.

items.fromString:
_Epic:_ [EOP-5|https://maglez.atlassian.net/browse/EOP-5]. _Order:_ eighth, and can land any time after the card catalogue. _Size:_ S engineering, but blocked on a question only the owner can answer. _Blocked by:_ unverified licence terms.

*As a* player, *I want* the real threat prompts, *so that* the game covers the full range of STRIDE scenarios rather than six samples.

*Data only.* No new endpoint, no new screen, no schema change if the assumptions in the card catalogue story hold. One migration inserting rows, plus attribution.

_The blocker, stated plainly_

The deck's licence terms and card count are unverified. A figure of 74 cards under a Creative Commons attribution licence has been repeated during planning, but it has not been checked against the publisher's own material, and it should not be trusted on the strength of having been said confidently. Committing third-party content to a public repository under an assumed licence is a real problem, not a cosmetic one. Before this story starts the owner must confirm the actual licence, the attribution wording it requires, and the real card count and field set.

*If the answer is inconvenient, nothing else stalls.* The placeholder deck was chosen precisely so that every other story could proceed. This can sit blocked indefinitely without holding anything up.

_Acceptance criteria_

*Deployed behind flag.* The migration is applied and the rows exist, but with the flag off the catalogue endpoint continues to return only the placeholder cards, so the change is inert until released.

*Released, flag on.* The catalogue returns the full verified deck. Every card has the correct category, number and prompt, matching the source. The count matches the confirmed figure.

*Attribution is visible.* The required attribution appears in the application interface, not only in a repository file, and its wording matches what the licence actually demands.

_Watch for a field set wider than assumed._ If real cards carry a score value, a difficulty, or suggested mitigations, this stops being data-only and needs a schema change. That is why the field set must be confirmed before the card catalogue story fixes the table shape.

renderedFields.description:
Replaces EOP-12, which described a shared deck with blind draws. Elevation of Privilege is a trick-taking game, closest to Spades. EOP-12 is retired rather than edited because the mechanic it specified was not the game. See the requirements document at docs/requirements/PRD-eop-card-game.md sections 3.3 and 5, which are sourced from the shipped instruction card and the author's whitepaper, both committed under docs/EoP_Microsoft_Docs/.

Goal. A group in a started session can play tricks: cards are dealt, the correct player leads, follow-suit is enforced, and the trick winner is resolved and leads the next trick. Scoring is deliberately NOT in this story - it is EOP-15.

Size: XL. This is the core game mechanic and the largest story in the backlog.

Dealing. On game start the entire deck is dealt evenly between players. There is no draw pile. Cards live in a Hand, one per player per session. Any remainder when the deck does not divide evenly must be handled explicitly and the same way every time.

The opening lead must be derived, never hardcoded. The rule is: the holder of the lowest-ranked Tampering card present in the deck leads the first trick. The shipped instructions say the 3 of Tampering and the whitepaper says the 2, and both are correct for their own deck - the printed 74-card deck has no 2 of Tampering, the 78-card source file does. A literal 2 or 3 in the code is a defect and will be rejected in review.

Follow suit. A player holding any card of the led suit must play one. A player holding none may play any card. This must be enforced server-side against the player's actual hand, not merely offered or hidden in the UI.

Elevation of Privilege is the trump suit. The highest card of the led suit takes the trick, unless one or more Elevation of Privilege cards were played, in which case the highest Elevation of Privilege card takes it. Only the led suit or Elevation of Privilege can take a trick. The winner leads the next trick.

A card may be played with no valid threat. The rule is explicit: if the player cannot link the threat to the system, play proceeds. Such a play is legal, scores nothing, and does not block the trick. TrickPlay.threatLinked carries this. Do not model an unlinked play as an error or as a skipped turn.

Turn order. Play is clockwise from the leader, using the stable seat order assigned on join. Out-of-turn plays must be rejected server-side against the player identity credential, not merely prevented in the UI.

Where the rules live. Turn order, legality and trick resolution belong in the domain layer with no framework imports, not in the controller. The controller is an interface adapter.

Aces are Open Threat cards. The player must name a threat not printed on any other card. The application cannot adjudicate that, so it captures the text; the group decides. A searchable list of all threats helps here and is a cheap win worth including.

Constraints. Liquibase changesets for hand, trick and trick_play before the entities, or startup fails against validate. The OpenAPI document updated before any controller code. RFC 9457 for all error responses. Clean Architecture boundaries. A genuinely concurrent test proving two simultaneous plays cannot both be accepted for the same seat, and that a card cannot be played twice.

Blocked by EOP-10 (session and players must exist to be dealt to) and by the real-time transport and player identity decisions from EOP-8. Also needs the concurrency-control decision, number 017.

comments.body:
Tech Lead — delivery plan and three decisions confirmed before implementation.

Correction to this ticket's text. The description closes with "Also needs the concurrency-control decision, number 017." That reference is wrong: ADR-017 is Frontend Delivery Topology. The concurrency-control decision is [ADR-020](docs/adr/ADR-020-session-concurrency-control.md) — Concurrency Control by Compare-and-Set on `status`, Not by Optimistic Locking. This matters more than a typo, because ADR-020 exists specifically to warn that the @Version column on GameSessionJpaEntity is bookkeeping and not the enforcement mechanism. Implementation of this story must use status-guarded conditional UPDATE with rows-affected checks plus unique constraints — not JPA optimistic locking.

Decision 1 — the deal remainder. 78 cards divides evenly for 3 players (26 each) and 6 players (13 each), but leaves a remainder for 4 players (19 each, remainder 2) and 5 players (15 each, remainder 3). Neither the PRD nor this ticket specified the rule.

Resolved: every card is dealt; the extras go to seats in ascending order. The alternative — setting the remainder aside undealt — carries a latent defect: the lowest-ranked Tampering card can land in the discard, at which point "the holder of the lowest-ranked Tampering card leads the first trick" has no holder, and the opening lead silently requires a fallback branch. Dealing every card makes the opening-lead rule always resolve, matches how the physical deck is dealt, and keeps maximum threat coverage in play, which is the purpose of the deck.

Accepted consequence: hands are unequal, so the final trick is short. This is already sanctioned by PRD §3.3, whose end condition is players running out of "time, cards, or ways to connect their threats to the system." The domain will therefore define a trick as one card from each player who still holds cards, not as a fixed card count.

Decision 2 — where the current leader lives. PRD §5 lists a GameState block (currentLeader, currentTrick) with no corresponding entity, and GameSession is an immutable aggregate root. Resolved: the current leader's seat is stored on `game_session`. It gives the turn-order guard a single row to compare-and-set against, which is what makes the concurrency requirement in this ticket provable rather than asserted; and the opening leader has to be persisted somewhere regardless.

Decision 3 — this XL story ships as five PRs, not one. A single XL pull request breaks trunk-based development. Five short-lived branches off main, each merged and deployed on its own, all behind a new eop.features.trick-play flag defaulting to false (ADR-013):

Slice Content
A Pure domain: Hand, Trick, TrickPlay, follow-suit legality, trump resolution, derived opening lead. No framework imports, no schema.
B Liquibase changeset 004 for hand/trick/trick_play before the JPA entities, plus ports and adapters. Additive, no behaviour change.
C Dealing wired into session start behind the flag; endpoint returning the caller's own hand.
D OpenAPI document updated before any controller code; play-a-card endpoint; follow-suit and out-of-turn rejected server-side against the identity credential; RFC 9457 errors; the genuinely concurrent double-play test.
E Trick resolution wired, winner leads next trick, SSE events, flag default flipped under review.

Every slice takes all five Definition-of-Done gate approvals. Scoring remains out of scope — that is EOP-15.

The opening lead will be derived at runtime from the cards actually dealt. A literal 2 or 3 anywhere in the implementation is a defect, per this ticket and PRD §3.3.

Decisions 1 and 2 are being recorded as ADR-023. Slice A is in progress on branch EOP-14-trick-domain.

Second defect in this ticket's description, found during Slice A review.

The description still says the deck "is dealt evenly between players". That contradicts the very next requirement in the same paragraph, which says any remainder must be handled explicitly — if the deal were even there would be no remainder to handle. 78 cards divide evenly only at three players (26 each) and six (13 each); at four it is 20/20/19/19 and at five 16/16/16/15/15.

The confirmed decision, recorded in ADR-023 and now implemented, is that the whole deck is dealt out with the remainder going to the lowest seat numbers. "Whole deck" is the load-bearing half of the source sentence — it is what makes "there is no shared draw pile" true — and "evenly" is the incidental descriptor that cannot hold at four or five players. PRD §3.3 has been amended accordingly; this ticket has not, so anyone reading only the ticket would conclude the implementation is wrong.

Consequences already accepted: hands are unequal, the final trick is short, and a trick is therefore one card from each seat that still holds cards rather than a fixed count.

Together with the ADR-017 → ADR-020 correction in my earlier comment, that is two stale statements in this description. Both are recorded here rather than silently edited.

Third stale statement in this description — recorded, not edited.

The description says, in the trump paragraph, that "The winner leads the next trick." That is the third statement in this ticket that the implemented rules contradict, and it is the one this story's central remediation was about.

It is only true while every seat still holds a card. Because every card is dealt and the remainder goes to the lowest seats (ADR-023, decision 1), hands are unequal at four and five players — at four players seats 0 and 1 hold twenty cards and seats 2 and 3 hold nineteen. So a seat can play its last card and win the trick it played it into. After trick nineteen, a win by seat 2 or 3 leaves the winner holding nothing while two seats each still hold one card.

Handing the lead back to that winner opens a trick nobody can ever play into: no seat can legally play, the trick is not complete because it has no plays, and the game stops with no exception, no error and nothing to log. That is not a hypothetical — it is a certain configuration at four and five players whenever a short-handed seat takes the penultimate trick.

The implemented rule is: the lead passes to the winner if the winner still holds a card, and otherwise to the next seat clockwise from the winner that does. Trick.nextLeaderSeat(seatsHoldingCards) answers it, and returns empty when no seat holds a card — one of the three end conditions in PRD §3.3. The method that answers "who took this trick" is deliberately called winningSeat() rather than nextLeaderSeat(), so that reaching for the winner is no longer the path of least resistance.

This was caught by @architecture-guardian reviewing its own ADR against the code, one section away from where the ADR had named the same class of defect.

Both the ADR and PRD §3.3 now carry dated deviation notes. Slice E, which wires lead passing, must implement the rule above rather than the sentence in this description.

For the record, the three corrections now tracked against this description are:

  • ADR-017 → ADR-020 for the concurrency-control decision (comment 10204). ADR-017 is Frontend Delivery Topology.
  • "dealt evenly between players" contradicting the same paragraph's own requirement that a remainder be handled explicitly (comment 10237).
  • "The winner leads the next trick" — this comment.

The description is left as written; the code, ADR-023 and PRD §3.3 are the authorities.

Slice C1 complete — EOP-14 remains In Progress

PR #46 is open for Slice C1 (persistence), all five DoD gates approved on 7c7208e. This does not close EOP-14. Three of the five slices remain: C2 (use cases), D (endpoints + OpenAPI), E (resolution, SSE, flag flip).

What Slice C1 ships

Ports HandRepository/TrickRepository, TrickPlayRepositoryAdapter implementing both, JPA mappings for all five trick-play tables, changeset 005 range bounds, eight domain exception types with RFC 9457 mappings, and three compare-and-set session updates. 27 commits, 45 files, +6555/-66.

./mvnw verify — 722 tests, 0 failures, exit 0. Checkstyle 0, SpotBugs 0, JaCoCo gate met.

Containment has changed and this matters for planning. All five tables are now mapped and reachable by any bean that injects either port. The old containment — "no entity, adapter or route" — is false as of this slice. What remains is no use case and no route, which is why eop.features.trick-play becomes a genuine merge precondition for C2 rather than a formality.

Two defects review found that the build did not

  1. A replayed trick resolution answered 500. Reachable on an ordinary hand, not an exotic one: advanceLeaderSeat sets current_leader_seat where it already equals the seat it compared against, so whenever the seat that led a trick also wins it the guard is idempotent and a replay passes it. The winner update's winner_play_id IS NULL predicate is what actually refuses. Now 409. This means trick resolution serialises on the `trick` row, not the session row — the one place in the design where the contended row is not game_session. Recorded in ADR-020.
  1. The port `@throws` contracts were wrong in both directions — declaring an exception a path cannot raise, and omitting two the test suite proved it does. All three write methods now declare everything their shared zero-rows helper can return.

New decision record

ADR-024 — one adapter implements both ports, and neither port authorises anybody. No method takes an acting player, so none can. The seat check is a check on the row, not the requester. This is the correction of an earlier comment that claimed otherwise.

Slice C2 obligations, carried explicitly

These are the ones where nothing in C1 fails if C2 forgets them:

  • Authorise the requester in every use case, deriving the acting player from the authenticated identity and refusing a caller-supplied seat. assertSeated looks exactly like an authorisation gate and is not one.
  • Cross-session scoping on the play, deal and delete paths, for cards as well as seats — the composite keys prove a player holds that seat somewhere, not at this table.
  • `trick.leader_seat` has no CHECK constraint — refused only by the domain on read. The other three seat columns got theirs in changeset 005.
  • `fk_trick_winner_play ON DELETE SET NULL` silently unresolves a trick if a winning play is deleted directly; only a comment prevents it today.
  • `eop.features.trick-play` in front of the new route, defaulted false.
  • `mentions` matches a constraint name by substring, not equality — a future name containing an existing one would be answered as the existing domain exception instead of failing loudly.

Description corrections

The three stale statements flagged earlier still stand as corrections and are now implemented as described: the concurrency decision is ADR-020, not 017; the whole deck is dealt with the remainder to the lowest seats, so hands are unequal and a trick is one card from each seat still holding cards; and the lead passes to the winner only if the winner still holds a card, otherwise to the next seat clockwise that does.

C1's four obligations are discharged

  1. Authorise the requester first, in every use case — done, and each has a test asserting a stranger is refused before any hand is read, asserted on the repository double's read log. This is the ADR-024 obligation that no port could enforce and no C1 test failed for.
  2. Cross-session scoping — closed by construction rather than validation: one sessionId scopes every read and write, and the trickId handed to appendPlay can only come from a session-scoped read.
  3. `eop.features.trick-play` — added, default false, gating the beans rather than a route, with tests in both positions.
  4. trick.leader_seat still has no CHECK constraint. Reassigned off C2 in ADR-023 with the reason recorded: C2 ships no changeset, and adding one here would put a migration in a PR whose claim is that it changes no schema.

One correction to the record, worth reading

ADR-025's original central claim was false and is retracted. It had argued the seam between starting a session and dealing was forced, because the two writes could not share a transaction without putting org.springframework.transaction into the use-case layer. An architecture review refuted it: a @Transactional composer in the outer ring joins two already-transactional adapter methods through REQUIRED propagation with no import inside usecase. The seam is chosen, not forced. The real reason for two calls is that StartSessionUseCase publishes GAME_STARTED over in-process SSE, and no transaction rolls back a delivered frame — so a composed transaction would trade a recoverable inconsistency (started but undealt, and idempotently retryable) for an unrecoverable one (every subscriber told a game started that was never dealt).

That claim was then hunted across the whole repository and found in eight places, including production javadoc in TrickRepository and TrickPlayRepositoryAdapter. All are now retracted in place rather than deleted, because a changelog and an ADR are records of what was believed at the time.

A group in a started session can play tricks: cards are dealt, the correct player leads, follow-suit is enforced, and the trick winner is resolved and leads the next trick. Scoring is deliberately NOT in this story - it is
This is the core game mechanic and the largest story in the backlog.

On game start the entire deck is dealt evenly between players. There is no draw pile. Cards live in a Hand, one per player per session. Any remainder when the deck does not divide evenly must be handled explicitly and the same way every time.
The opening lead must be derived, never hardcoded.

The rule is: the holder of the lowest-ranked Tampering card present in the deck leads the first trick. The shipped instructions say the 3 of Tampering and the whitepaper says the 2, and both are correct for their own deck - the printed 74-card deck has no 2 of Tampering, the 78-card source file does. A literal 2 or 3 in the code is a defect and will be rejected in review.

A player holding any card of the led suit must play one. A player holding none may play any card. This must be enforced server-side against the player's actual hand, not merely offered or hidden in the UI.
Elevation of Privilege is the trump suit.

The highest card of the led suit takes the trick, unless one or more Elevation of Privilege cards were played, in which case the highest Elevation of Privilege card takes it. Only the led suit or Elevation of Privilege can take a trick. The winner leads the next trick.
A card may be played with no valid threat.
The rule is explicit: if the player cannot link the threat to the system, play proceeds. Such a play is legal, scores nothing, and does not block the trick.
carries this. Do not model an unlinked play as an error or as a skipped turn.
Play is clockwise from the leader, using the stable seat order assigned on join. Out-of-turn plays must be rejected server-side against the player identity credential, not merely prevented in the UI.
Turn order, legality and trick resolution belong in the domain layer with no framework imports, not in the controller. The controller is an interface adapter.

The player must name a threat not printed on any other card. The application cannot adjudicate that, so it captures the text; the group decides. A searchable list of all threats helps here and is a cheap win worth including.
