renderedFields.description:
The second half of the retired EOP-12. Split out from the trick mechanics because trick-taking is provable without any score, and bundling them made one story that could not be reviewed in a sitting. See docs/requirements/PRD-eop-card-game.md section 3.4.

Goal. The server keeps score, players can see it, and the game reaches an end with a winner.

Size: M.

The scoring rule is deliberately simple. One point for a threat on your card, plus one point for taking the trick. That is the whole shipped rule and it must not be embellished.

Why the simplicity matters, and must be preserved. A richer system was designed and then abandoned during playtesting - four points for a threat on your own card, three then two then one for threats on other people's, a point for the trick, two for a face card, three for an ace. It was scrapped because, in the author's words, players "even the dedicated repeat playtesters, were looking to me at the end of every round to ascertain who scored". The complexity was removed because humans could not compute it at the table, not because it was thought to be a worse game.

This is where the digital form earns something real. The constraint that forced the simplification does not apply to a server. Richer scoring becomes cheap once the machine keeps score. That is worth recording as an option, and is explicitly NOT in this story - ship the shipped rule first.

Only threats that were actually linked score. A card played with threatLinked false scores nothing for the threat, though its player can still take the trick with it. The written rule counts only the highest card actually connected to the system; the whitepaper notes this is sometimes relaxed in practice to involve beginners. Implement the written rule, and note the variant as a possible future toggle rather than building both.

The score sheet is a real artefact and its shape is known. The shipped sheet has these columns: Name, Points, Card, Component(s), Notes on Threat. Component(s) is plural in the original - one card's threat may apply to several components. A players view of the running game should be reconstructible into that shape.

End of game. Play continues until players run out of time, cards, or ways to connect threats to the system. When play ends the highest score wins, and ties should be shown as ties rather than broken arbitrarily. The facilitator can end the game early.

Constraints. Scores are computed and stored server-side; a client must never assert its own score. Scoring belongs in the domain layer, not the controller. Liquibase changeset before any entity change. The OpenAPI document updated before controller code. RFC 9457 for error responses. Unit tests must cover the awkward cases: an unlinked play, a trick won by a trump, and a tie.

Blocked by EOP-14. There is nothing to score until tricks resolve.

comments.body:
Delivery plan — three slices off main, all behind eop.features.trick-play

EOP-14 is now Done (all five slices merged, PR #49 landed as 4a99387), so this story is unblocked. Moving to In Progress.

Interpretation decisions taken before any code

These are the reading choices this story rests on. They are written down first so the review gates can challenge the interpretation rather than only the implementation.

  1. Threat point iff `threatLinked`; the trick point goes to the winner regardless of linkage. The ticket says so outright, and it matches shipped behaviour — Trick.winningPlay() ignores threatLinked entirely. The whitepaper's "only count the highest card which was actually connected" is therefore read as a restriction on scoring, not on winning a trick. The beginner-relaxation variant is noted as a possible future toggle, not built, per the ticket.
  1. A linked threat that names no component still scores. TrickPlay's javadoc explicitly hands this open decision to EOP-15, so here is the answer and the reasoning: the shipped rule keys on the threat being linked, not on naming a component; PRD line 146 records that the application holds no model of the system, so it cannot validate a component name; making a score hinge on unvalidated client free text sits badly with "a client must never assert its own score"; and the Score Card's Component(s) column may legitimately be blank.
  1. The running score is derived from resolved tricks; only the final outcome is stored. The score is a pure function of the trick_play rows plus each trick's winner_play_id, so deriving it cannot drift from the play that produced it. What gets persisted at completion is the terminal status and the standings, because SessionStatus.COMPLETED already means "every trick has been played and the score is final". This reads the ticket's "computed and stored server-side" as a statement about authority — the server computes, never the client — rather than a requirement for a running-score table. Flagging it explicitly because it is the one decision here that reinterprets the ticket's wording; it is reversible, since a stored projection would be purely additive.
  1. The facilitator's early end is `COMPLETED`, not `ABANDONED`. The ticket says the highest score wins when play ends, so an early end is a finish. ABANDONED stays reserved for expiry and abandonment (EOP-22).
  1. Ties are shown as ties, never broken. Trick-level ties cannot occur — the deck holds no duplicate suit+rank — but score ties are ordinary, and the ticket requires them displayed as ties.
  1. No `ScoreRepository`. Names come from SessionRepository.findById → GameSession.players(); the tricks come from one new read method on TrickRepository, because reading tricks is that port's job. A port that only re-read tricks would be a port for nothing. Any new method keeps ADR-024's rule: no acting player in any signature — authorising the requester stays the use case's job.
  1. Richer scoring stays out. The abandoned v0.21 system (4 for a threat on your own card, 3/2/1 on others', +2 face, +3 ace) was dropped because players could not compute it at the table, not because it played worse — and a server removes that constraint. Worth recording as an option; explicitly not built here.

Slices

Slice A — the scoring rule, pure domain. New entity types computing points from resolved tricks. Zero framework imports, no routes, no schema, purely additive. Unit tests cover the three awkward cases the ticket names: an unlinked play, a trick won by a trump, and a tie.

Slice B — read the running score. docs/api/openapi.yml first, then the new TrickRepository read method, a GetScoreUseCase, {{GET /api/v1/sessions/

{sessionId}

/score}}, and a DTO reconstructible into the Score Card's five columns (Name | Points | Card | Component(s) | Notes on Threat). Membership required — a score is not information a stranger is owed.

Slice C — end of game. Changeset 006-*.xml, SessionRepository.recordCompleted in the existing compare-and-swap style, the automatic COMPLETED transition keyed off nextLeaderSeat already being empty at resolution, the facilitator's early end, winner and ties in the read model, the ADR, and a documentation sweep.

Two things noted now so they are not forgotten at the end

  • This story makes several existing documents false in the present tense — exactly what got three EOP-14 slices rejected repeatedly. The known list: SessionStatus's class javadoc ("nothing here advances a session out of IN_PROGRESS"), the eop.features.trick-play comment block in application.yml which names EOP-15 as an outstanding blocker, and TrickState.handComplete's "says nothing about the score". Every cardinal count of use cases, ports and routes gets re-derived from source rather than read for plausibility.
  • Flipping `eop.features.trick-play` is not this story's job (ADR-028). The flag ships false; flag-on remains its own story, and this story discharges one of its predecessors.

All five DoD gates run on every slice.

Slice A of 3 is merged to main as 2fec0a0 (PR #54, squashed). The scoring rule now exists in the domain layer. Nothing is reachable over HTTP yet and eop.features.trick-play stays false.

WHAT SHIPPED

Three pure domain types with zero framework imports: ScoredPlay (one Score Card row, carrying all five columns - Name, Points, Card, Component(s), Notes on Threat), Standing (one player's place, competition ranking) and ScoreSheet (derives both from the seated players and the tricks). Decisions are recorded in ADR-030.

The shipped rule is unembellished: one point for a threat connected to your card, plus one point for taking the trick. The richer v0.21 system is recorded in ADR-030 as a future option and deliberately not built.

Build at merge: 962 tests, 0 failures, 0 errors. SpotBugs 0. JaCoCo met over 112 production classes; the three new types are individually at 100% instruction and 100% branch coverage (ScoredPlay 145/145 and 12/12, Standing 57/57 and 8/8, ScoreSheet 470/470 and 48/48). Checkstyle 0 violations.

INTERPRETATION DECISIONS TAKEN, for the record

  1. Threat point if and only if threatLinked; the trick point goes to the winner regardless of linkage. Trick.winningPlay() ignores threatLinked entirely, so the whitepaper's "only count the highest card actually connected" is a scoring restriction, not a trick-winning one. The beginner relaxation is noted, not built.
  2. A linked threat that names no component still scores. This was the open decision TrickPlay's javadoc handed to this story; that javadoc now records the answer in the past tense and cites ADR-030.
  3. The score is derived from resolved tricks, never accumulated. "Computed and stored server-side" is read as being about authority - the server computes, the client never asserts - rather than as mandating a running-score table.
  4. The facilitator's early end will be COMPLETED, not ABANDONED. ABANDONED stays reserved for expiry (EOP-22).
  5. Ties are shown as ties and never broken. A trick-level tie is impossible (no duplicate suit and rank in the deck); a score tie is ordinary.
  6. Deciding the game has ended stays the session's job, following the precedent GameSession.start() set. That transition is slice C.

DEFINITION OF DONE - all five gates approved

@tester-unit-and-quality approved on re-review, having first rejected: Standing sat at 68.4% instruction coverage and ScoredPlay at 86.2%, because every guard in both is unreachable through ScoreSheetTest. New StandingTest and ScoredPlayTest fixed that.

@tester-api approved, having proved the HTTP surface untouched.

@security-auditor approved. Confirmed ScoreSheet.of never touches a Hand, so the one confidential fact - a player's association with a card they have not played - is structurally unreachable, and confirmed no identity token digest is copied into any scoring type.

@code-reviewer approved with one warning, carried below.

@architecture-guardian approved on the third review, having rejected twice. Both rejections were documentation accuracy, not code: a false per-class coverage claim in ADR-030 (the JaCoCo gate is a bundle measurement, per ADR-006, not a per-class one), and a staleness inventory that omitted the one javadoc this slice's own decision falsified.

The seven refusal tests that asserted on exception message substrings now assert the property instead: the malformed input is refused, and correcting only the single defect makes the same input accepted. That pins which guard fired without coupling a test to prose - six guards throw the same exception type, so asserting the type alone would have proved nothing.

CONDITIONS CARRIED INTO SLICE B, from the gates

  1. Convert all eight route-reachable IllegalArgumentException throws to named domain exceptions with typed fields, starting with ScoreSheet.pointsOf - it is the only one a reading route calls with a client-supplied identifier, so it is the first that could echo one into a Problem Details body. Do ScoredPlay's and Standing's four in the same pass.
  2. Bound components and notes at ScoredPlay's canonical constructor. Today the guarantee rests on ScoredPlay.of being the only caller, which is a comment rather than a constraint.
  3. Add a redacted toString to nothing further - ScoredPlay got one in this slice, since the generated record version would reproduce up to 2000 characters of player note and twenty component names per row, and ScoreSheet.rows() cascades into it.
  4. The new TrickRepository read method carries no acting player (ADR-024). The use case authenticates the token, confirms the player is seated in that session, and scopes the trick query to one session id.
  5. ADR-027 is cited for its prohibition, not its naming rule: a score sheet is by construction every player's rows, so slice B must argue in writing why that is not the forbidden collection. The argument available is that a score names only cards already face up.
  6. Contract first (ADR-004): docs/api/openapi.yml before the controller. Gate on eop.features.trick-play with havingValue true, and test the OFF position by asserting the beans are absent as well as the routes returning 404.
  7. runtime-view.md gains a sequence diagram for the score read; C4-Diagrams.md gains the use case, the DTO and the port method with caller counts updated.
  8. Fix ADR-030's identifier enumeration to include trickId and the two throws that name no identifier.
  9. Consider restoring ADR-006's reserved 70% branch limit in pom.xml: the bundle now measures 90.11% branch coverage, so it would pass with twenty points of headroom.

CONDITION CARRIED INTO SLICE C

Persisting final standings stays conditional, not planned. It must be justified by a purpose derivation cannot serve - and the PRD excludes any ranking that outlives a single session, which is the main thing such a table would buy - and a persisted standing must never be read back to answer the score, not even for a COMPLETED game. If neither condition can be met, slice C persists nothing.

Slice B is next: read the running score. Slice C: end of game, the COMPLETED transition, the facilitator's early end, and the documentation un-staling sweep.

EOP-15 Slice B — Merged to main as deb95e4 (PR #55)

*`GET /api/v1/sessions/

{sessionId}

/score`* is now deployed behind eop.features.trick-play (still false).

What shipped

Seven new production types, all at 100% instruction coverage, zero branches:

  • ScoreNotDerivableException + nested Reason enum — one exception type for eight refusals, mapped to 500 with a body that names no identifier (RFC 9457 §3.2: one type per client-actionable condition, and there is exactly one here — none)
  • GetScoreUseCase — two collaborators: ResolvePlayerUseCase (which yields the session and its players, so no second SessionRepository read) and TrickRepository
  • ScoreController — one route, the sixth behind the flag, separate from TrickController because a score is not a move
  • ScoredPlayDto, StandingDto, ScoreSheetDto — the Score Card's five columns over HTTP

TrickRepository gained findTricks(UUID sessionId) — four batched reads for the whole session instead of seventy-nine at three players. ScoreNotDerivableException replaces eight IllegalArgumentException throws that would have echoed player/trick identifiers into a 400 Problem Details body.

Build at merge

  • 989 tests, 0 failures, SpotBugs 0, Checkstyle 0
  • JaCoCo: 80% instruction + 70% branch (both bundle-level), met over 119 classes
  • All five DoD gates approved (7 architecture gate rounds — all on documentation arithmetic, never on code)

Conditions carried to Slice C

  1. Keep eop.features.trick-play: false on merge; flipping the flag is its own story
  2. Close the COMPLETED transition so a client watching {{GET /sessions/ {id}

    }} sees a session finish

  3. Persisted standings stay conditional — justify by a purpose derivation cannot serve; never read back as authority
  4. Rewrite SessionStatus's class javadoc
  5. Resolve the 13-use-cases-none-logging ADR-026 gap before flag-on
  6. Re-derive every cardinal in the same commit that prints it

Security conditions carried to Slice C (from @security-auditor)

  • MEDIUM: before flag goes true — add ETag/short-TTL or per-caller rate limit (worst case ~468 KB recomputed from 4 queries per GET, pollable by any seated player)
  • MEDIUM: pointsOf must never receive a caller-supplied UUID
  • LOW: bound components/notes on ScoredPlay the moment any path builds one from something other than a revalidated TrickPlay
  • LOW: add sessionId to the handleScoreNotDerivable log line

Goal. Run the application, its database and the load-test tooling on the developer machine, so that the game can be developed and played end to end without an AWS account. Multiplayer is simulated with several browser tabs, which works because the player credential is held per tab.

Why now. Deployment to a cloud account is deferred (see EOP-7, which stays open and unstarted). Until then nothing could be run outside continuous integration, because no container engine was installed. Four verification gates defined earlier in the project had never been executed on a developer machine.

Constraint that shaped the choice. The developer machine is centrally managed and the user cannot install software that requires administrator rights. Docker Desktop is distributed as an application bundle needing a privileged helper, and its licence requires a paid subscription for commercial use in organisations above a size threshold. Both rule it out. The runtime must therefore be installable from Homebrew formulae with no elevated privileges.

What is delivered. A documented local runtime, a new architecture decision record explaining the choice and its honest limits, an amendment to the deployment decision record recording that its decisions still stand and only the timing changed, and correction of every place in the documentation that names a prerequisite which is not in fact installable.

Acceptance criteria.

One, the runtime installs without elevated privileges. Given a machine with no container engine, when the documented installation commands are run, then no password is requested and a container daemon is reachable from the existing command line client.

Two, the application image builds locally. The image must build from source on the developer machine's own processor architecture. This had only ever been built in continuous integration, on a different architecture.

Three, the whole stack runs and answers. The application and its database must start with the same single command used by continuous integration and by the cloud bootstrap script, the database must be reported healthy before the application starts, and a request to the health endpoint must return exactly the two characters that the smoke test and load test both assert.

Four, the card catalogue serves real data from the real database. The endpoint delivered earlier must return seeded rows from the containerised database rather than the in-memory one, exercising the migration, the persistence adapter and the error handler together outside continuous integration for the first time.

Five, the load test runs against the container. The load test must execute against the running container rather than a development-mode process, and its thresholds must pass. This is the first time the ninety-fifth percentile figure quoted in the documentation will have been measured against the real artefact.

Six, no documentation names an uninstallable prerequisite. Three files currently instruct the reader to install a tool that cannot be installed on this machine. Each must be corrected, in the style already used elsewhere in the same files: what the tool is for, how to install it, and how it fails if absent.

Seven, every step that cannot be committed is written down. Setting up this stack requires local actions that version control cannot carry and that fail silently when skipped. They must be listed with a verification command each, alongside the existing entries of the same kind.

Out of scope. Public access for people other than the developer. The reverse proxy and the front end, which are separate stories. Any cloud resource. Repair of the metrics visualisation pipeline, which this work found to be broken for three independent reasons and which needs its own story.

renderedFields.description:
User Story

As a player joining a lobby

I want to receive a meaningful HTTP status code when a seat is contested or no join code can be generated

So that my client can react correctly instead of treating a normal race condition as a server crash

Context & Business Value

  • Epic: EOP-5 — Session Lifecycle
  • Defect class: Escaped defect — code is merged to main behind feature flag eop.features.session-lifecycle (currently OFF). Not yet exploitable in production, but the flag must not be enabled until this is resolved.
  • Value Proposition: Two reachable exception types have no mapping in GlobalExceptionHandler, causing HTTP 500 with a full stack trace on every occurrence. This is a log-flooding amplifier and a misleading signal to callers.

Root Cause

JoinSessionUseCase.execute() retries a contested seat up to 8 times (MAXIMUM_SEAT_ATTEMPTS) then rethrows the last SeatAlreadyTakenException. GlobalExceptionHandler has no handler for this type, so it falls through to handleUnexpected(Exception) → HTTP 500. The class Javadoc and @throws declaration on execute() both document this path explicitly — the claim that "the exception is always absorbed" is false.

Same shape for JoinCodeUnavailableException: CreateSessionUseCase rethrows after 5 consecutive join-code collisions, also unmapped, also 500.

A caller holding a valid join code can force the SeatAlreadyTakenException path by firing ~20 concurrent joins at one lobby, making it a log-flooding amplifier.

Deployment & Feature Flag Strategy

  • Feature Flag Name: eop.features.session-lifecycle
  • Deployment Behavior: Fix is merged to main with flag remaining OFF.
  • Release Condition: This ticket is a gate on enabling the feature flag. Do not enable eop.features.session-lifecycle until this story is Done.

Acceptance Criteria

Scenario 1: Seat contention exhausts retries

  • Given a lobby exists and all seats are contested on every attempt
  • When JoinSessionUseCase exhausts MAXIMUM_SEAT_ATTEMPTS retries
  • Then the API returns HTTP 409 with a JSON error body containing a human-readable message (e.g. "The lobby filled while you were joining")
  • And no stack trace is logged at ERROR level

Scenario 2: Join-code collision exhausts retries

  • Given the join-code generator returns a collision on every attempt
  • When CreateSessionUseCase exhausts its 5-attempt retry loop
  • Then the API returns HTTP 503 with a Retry-After header
  • And no stack trace is logged at ERROR level

Scenario 3: Existing mappings are unaffected

  • Given any other exception type handled by GlobalExceptionHandler
  • Then its existing status code and response shape are unchanged

Implementation Notes

Add two @ExceptionHandler methods to GlobalExceptionHandler (adapter layer — org.maglez.eop.adapter.web):

  • SeatAlreadyTakenException → 409
  • JoinCodeUnavailableException → 503 with Retry-After: 5

Add matching test cases to GlobalExceptionHandlerTest (which currently covers the other eight mappings but neither of these).

Add an integration-level assertion that concurrent joins to a full lobby yield 409, not 500.

Suggested commit: [EOP-NNN] fix: map SeatAlreadyTakenException to 409 and JoinCodeUnavailableException to 503

Definition of Done

  • GlobalExceptionHandler has handlers for both exception types with correct status codes.
  • GlobalExceptionHandlerTest covers both new mappings.
  • Integration test confirms concurrent-join contention returns 409.
  • No stack traces logged for either exception type.
  • ./mvnw verify passes (checkstyle, SpotBugs, JaCoCo ≥ 0.80).
  • All child Bug Sub-tasks resolved and verified green.

comments.body:
Delivered — merged to main as be2d0ef via PR #53

https://github.com/maglez/eop-threat-medeling/pull/53

What changed

GlobalExceptionHandler (org.maglez.eop.adapter.web) gained the two missing mappings. Both escape paths — JoinSessionUseCase:160 rethrowing the last SeatAlreadyTakenException after MAXIMUM_SEAT_ATTEMPTS, and CreateSessionUseCase:110 rethrowing JoinCodeUnavailableException after its 5-attempt budget — previously fell through to handleUnexpected(Exception) and answered 500 with a full stack trace at ERROR.

Exception Status Body Logging
SeatAlreadyTakenException 409 "The lobby filled while you were joining" fixed detail, ProblemDetail DEBUG, no throwable
JoinCodeUnavailableException 503 "No lobby could be opened" + Retry-After: 5 fixed detail, ResponseEntity<ProblemDetail> WARN, with throwable

Acceptance criteria

  • Scenario 1 — seat contention exhausts retries. 409 with a human-readable body, no stack trace at ERROR. SessionContentionIntegrationTest.shouldAnswerSeatContentionWith409 proves it over HTTP; GlobalExceptionHandlerTest.shouldLogSeatContentionAtDebugWithoutATrace pins Level.DEBUG and getThrowableProxy() null.
  • Scenario 2 — join-code collision exhausts retries. 503 with Retry-After, no stack trace at ERROR. shouldAnswerJoinCodeExhaustionWith503 asserts header().string("Retry-After", "5"); shouldLogJoinCodeExhaustionAtWarnRatherThanError pins Level.WARN.
  • Scenario 3 — existing mappings unaffected. shouldLeaveTheUncontestedPathUntouched drives create-then-join with both stub switches closed (201 then 200); the pre-existing 49-test handler suite is unchanged and green.

Four decisions worth recording

  1. Neither response echoes its exception's message. SeatAlreadyTakenException.getMessage() names the internal session UUID and seat order, and a joining caller supplied only a join code — so it never held either. JoinCodeUnavailableException's message describes our own generator colliding with itself. Both details are compile-time literals.
  2. The log-level asymmetry is derived from provokability, not severity. DEBUG-without-throwable for the 409 because a WARN-plus-stack-trace would merely relocate the log-flooding amplifier this ticket exists to remove; WARN-with-throwable for the 503 because that path is not caller-provokable and each occurrence is genuine evidence the live-lobby count is approaching what a ~30-bit code space bears. Neither logs at ERROR.
  3. The 503 is a capacity statement, not a fault. Five seconds is documented in the constant's own Javadoc as a guess that only has to be defensible — there is no queue draining at a known rate to derive a figure from.
  4. A unit test could not have caught this defect. What escaped was an absent handler, and an absent @ExceptionHandler is invisible to a test that names the handler it expects. Hence SessionContentionIntegrationTest, which drives the full web adapter through a @Primary SessionRepository decorator (hand-written, no Mockito, per house convention) and so proves Spring dispatches to the new methods.

Verification

./mvnw -o verify — BUILD SUCCESS, Tests run: 915, Failures: 0, Errors: 0, Skipped: 0; SpotBugs BugInstance size is 0; JaCoCo All coverage checks have been met over 109 classes; checkstyle clean. GlobalExceptionHandler is at 100% instruction (438), line (133) and method (32) coverage. CI on PR #53: build, ui, image all pass.

Definition of Done — five of five gates approved

Gate Verdict Commit reviewed
@tester-unit-and-quality APPROVE 270dacf
@tester-api APPROVE 4cad0df
@security-auditor APPROVE f06e5ea
@code-reviewer APPROVE f06e5ea
@architecture-guardian APPROVE f06e5ea

@tester-api initially REJECTED 270dacf over Retry-After being declared without required: true on both ServiceUnavailable and the pre-existing TooManyRequests, while the implementation sets the header unconditionally. That rejection was actioned, not downgraded — 4cad0df fixed both declarations and the gate was re-dispatched and converted to APPROVE.

@architecture-guardian declined to write a new ADR and justified it: ADR-005 enumerates no status codes, so choosing one cannot depart from it — and its Mitigation clause ("unit tests cover every known domain exception → HTTP status mapping") means the missing handlers were a violation this change restores. It instead amended ADR-019, which already records the sibling 429-with-Retry-After inline beside the retry design, and added terminal HTTP exits to both retry loops in docs/architecture/runtime-view.md. No C4 change: the handler is a responsibility box that lists no statuses.

docs/api/openapi.yml gained the new shared ServiceUnavailable response, '503' on POST /api/v1/sessions, and a correction of the Conflict prose from thirteen 409 cases to fourteen — a count three separate reviewers verified independently against the source.

Flag position unchanged

eop.features.session-lifecycle remains OFF. This ticket was a gate on EOP-25, not the flip.

Five follow-up tickets filed for pre-existing findings

Reviewers surfaced nine findings, none introduced by this change:

  • EOP-54 — handleSessionFull echoes the internal session UUID and capacity via exception.getMessage(). A sibling 409 on this very endpoint already leaks exactly what this ticket set out to protect. Blocks EOP-25.
  • EOP-55 — handleSessionNotJoinable echoes the session UUID and lifecycle status. Blocks EOP-25.
  • EOP-56 — POST /api/v1/sessions is entirely unthrottled. Blocks EOP-25.
  • EOP-57 — the logback-spring.xml that observability.md mandates does not exist; production runs at default INFO plain-text, which is what makes the new DEBUG line safe incidentally rather than by design.
  • EOP-58 — docs/NITs, including runtime-view.md:357 claiming the join returns 201 when it returns 200.

One correction to this ticket's own premise. @security-auditor established that SeatAlreadyTakenException is effectively unreachable over HTTP: MAXIMUM_SEAT_ATTEMPTS = 8 exceeds GameSession.MAXIMUM_PLAYERS = 6 and SessionRepository exposes no seat-vacating method, so a joiner loses at most five races before its own re-read yields the already-mapped SessionFullException. The claim that ~20 concurrent joins force the path at will does not hold. The escaped 500 was a real code defect and the mapping is correct defence-in-depth, but the log-flooding amplifier it was credited with removing was largely theoretical — and that unwritten attempts > capacity invariant is captured in EOP-58.

User Story

As a system operator

I want the join-attempt rate limiter to enforce its limit even when its key map is saturated

So that an attacker cannot disable the limiter by exhausting tracked-key capacity from a large address pool

Context & Business Value

  • Epic: EOP-5 — Session Lifecycle
  • Target Persona: Security / Operations
  • Value Proposition: InMemoryJoinAttemptLimiter currently fails open when its MAX_TRACKED_KEYS = 10_000 map is full. An attacker keeping 10,000 distinct source addresses warm inside the 1-minute window leaves nothing reclaimable, at which point failures from every previously-unseen address are silently discarded and the limiter is globally off. A single IPv6 /64 prefix provides 1.8 × 10^19 addresses. This directly violates the project security rule: "fail securely — default-denied access".

Deployment & Feature Flag Strategy

  • Feature Flag Name: eop.features.session-lifecycle
  • Deployment Behavior: Fix is merged to main with flag remaining OFF.
  • Release Condition: This ticket is a gate on enabling the feature flag. Do not enable eop.features.session-lifecycle until this story is Done.

Acceptance Criteria

Scenario 1: Saturation causes refusal, not silent pass-through

  • Given the limiter's key map is at capacity (MAX_TRACKED_KEYS distinct addresses all active)
  • When a request arrives from a new, previously-unseen address
  • Then the limiter throws TooManyJoinAttemptsException (or equivalent refusal)
  • And the request is not silently allowed through

Scenario 2: Check-and-record is atomic under concurrency

  • Given a single address is at limit - 1 recorded failures
  • When two threads call checkAllowed() and recordFailure() concurrently
  • Then at most one thread proceeds; the second is refused
  • And the recorded failure count does not exceed the limit

Scenario 3: Normal operation is unaffected

  • Given the map is below capacity
  • When a new address makes its first join attempt
  • Then the attempt is allowed and recorded normally

Implementation Notes

Two independent fixes, both in InMemoryJoinAttemptLimiter (adapter layer — org.maglez.eop.adapter.security or equivalent):

Fix A — Fail-closed on saturation:

Invert the saturation branch: when the map is full and the incoming key is new, throw TooManyJoinAttemptsException rather than returning silently.

Preferred alternative: replace the unbounded-key map with a fixed-size sharded counter array (hash the key into N buckets). This bounds memory by construction, removes the saturation branch entirely, and eliminates the need for eviction logic.

Fix B — Atomic check-and-record:

checkAllowed() and recordFailure() are currently separate non-atomic operations. For a single-instance deployment, synchronise the check-and-record pair (e.g. synchronized block or ReentrantLock per address bucket) so the per-address limit is hard, not soft.

Suggested commit: [EOP-NNN] fix: fail-closed on limiter saturation and make check-and-record atomic

Definition of Done

  • Saturation path throws a refusal exception (or is eliminated by fixed-size sharding).
  • Check-and-record is atomic; concurrent threads from one address cannot both observe "under limit".
  • Unit tests cover: saturation refusal, concurrent check-and-record, normal allow path.
  • ./mvnw verify passes (checkstyle, SpotBugs, JaCoCo ≥ 0.80).
  • No regression to existing limiter tests.

comments.body:
Severity re-assessment from the EOP-10 review (PR #36) — @security-auditor

This story is more severe than it was filed, because of a defect found during the review and now filed as EOP-26.

As filed, the fail-open on saturation reads as an accidental degradation: if enough distinct addresses appear organically, the tracking map fills and the limiter stops protecting. That framing assumes an attacker has to wait for that condition.

They do not. ClientAddresses.of(HttpServletRequest) honours X-Forwarded-For with no trusted-proxy check anywhere in the codebase, so when the application is reached without Caddy in front — the normal ./mvnw spring-boot:run mode — a caller supplies the value the limiter keys on. That means an attacker can deliberately fill all 10,000 address keys on demand and switch the limiter off wholesale, in seconds, rather than waiting for organic load.

A fail-open an attacker can trigger at will is a different class of defect from one that only manifests under load. Two consequences for planning:

  • EOP-26 should land before this story, or at least alongside it. Making the check-and-record atomic and fail-closed is the right fix, but it protects a bucket the attacker can currently sidestep entirely.
  • The fail-closed behaviour this story adds becomes considerably more valuable once EOP-26 lands, because saturation stops being attacker-controlled.

No change to this story's acceptance criteria is required — the work described is still exactly right. This is a priority and sequencing note.

User Story

As a system operator

I want lobby creation to be rate-limited per source address and request bodies to be capped at the network edge

So that an unauthenticated caller cannot flood the database with permanent rows or terminate the container with an oversized payload

Context & Business Value

  • Epic: EOP-5 — Session Lifecycle
  • Target Persona: Security / Operations
  • Value Proposition: POST /api/v1/sessions requires no credential, is not rate-limited, and inserts permanent rows that are never deleted. At 500 req/s that is ~43 million lobbies/day (~8–9 GB/day), irreversible without manual database surgery. As the table fills toward the 1.07 × 10^9 join-code keyspace, the 5-attempt collision retry exhausts and legitimate facilitators receive opaque 503s. There is also no request-body size cap: Jackson's default StreamReadConstraints allows a single string of 20,000,000 characters (~40 MB transient heap per request); with Tomcat's default 200 threads and -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError, a few dozen concurrent oversized bodies terminate the container.

Deployment & Feature Flag Strategy

  • Feature Flag Name: eop.features.session-lifecycle
  • Deployment Behavior: Fix is merged to main with flag remaining OFF.
  • Release Condition: This ticket is a gate on enabling the feature flag. Do not enable eop.features.session-lifecycle until this story is Done.

Acceptance Criteria

Scenario 1: Rate limit on lobby creation

  • Given a source address has created 5 lobbies within the last 60 seconds
  • When it sends a 6th POST /api/v1/sessions
  • Then the API returns HTTP 429 (or equivalent refusal from the limiter)
  • And no new row is inserted

Scenario 2: Oversized body rejected at the edge

  • Given a request body larger than 16 KB is sent to any /api/* endpoint
  • When it reaches Caddy
  • Then Caddy returns a 4xx response before the body reaches the application
  • And the application's Tomcat connector also enforces the cap as belt-and-braces

Scenario 3: Normal lobby creation is unaffected

  • Given a source address is below the creation rate limit
  • When it sends a well-formed POST /api/v1/sessions with a body under 16 KB
  • Then the lobby is created normally and a 201 is returned

Implementation Notes

Rate limiting: Apply the existing JoinAttemptLimiter (or a sibling instance configured for creation) to POST /api/v1/sessions, keyed on ClientAddresses.of(request). Suggested limit: 5 creations per address per minute.

Body cap — Caddy: Add {{request_body

{ max_size 16KB }

}} inside the handle /api/* block in ui/Caddyfile.

Body cap — Tomcat (belt-and-braces): Add server.tomcat.max-swallow-size: 16384 (16 KB) to application.yml.

Note: @Size(max = 40) on displayName is enforced by bean validation only after Jackson has materialised the string — it does not prevent the heap spike.

Suggested commit: [EOP-NNN] feat: rate-limit session creation and cap request body size at 16KB

Definition of Done

  • POST /api/v1/sessions is rate-limited per source address using the existing limiter infrastructure.
  • ui/Caddyfile rejects bodies > 16 KB on /api/*.
  • application.yml sets server.tomcat.max-swallow-size: 16384.
  • Unit test covers: creation rate-limit refusal, normal creation allowed.
  • ./mvnw verify passes (checkstyle, SpotBugs, JaCoCo ≥ 0.80).

renderedFields.description:
User Story

As a player in an active session

I want SSE connections to be bounded per session and globally, with finite timeouts

So that a single attacker cannot exhaust Tomcat's connector capacity and deny service to all users

Context & Business Value

  • Epic: EOP-5 — Session Lifecycle
  • Target Persona: Security / Operations
  • Value Proposition: SseSessionEventPublisher keeps subscribers in an unbounded ConcurrentHashMap, creates emitters as new SseEmitter(0L) (no timeout, ever), and there is no per-session cap, no global cap, and no spring.mvc.async.request-timeout. One valid token authorises unlimited concurrent {{GET /api/v1/sessions/ {id}

    /events}} subscriptions. Tomcat's NIO maxConnections defaults to 8192; one attacker holding ~8k sockets stops the connector accepting all traffic including /health. Additionally, beat() iterates every emitter on the single sse-heartbeat thread; one deliberately slow reader blocks the sweep and starves every legitimate client of the keep-alive that stops proxies reaping the connection.

Deployment & Feature Flag Strategy

  • Feature Flag Name: eop.features.session-lifecycle
  • Deployment Behavior: Fix is merged to main with flag remaining OFF.
  • Release Condition: This ticket is a gate on enabling the feature flag. Do not enable eop.features.session-lifecycle until this story is Done.

Acceptance Criteria

Scenario 1: Per-session subscriber cap enforced

  • Given a session already has 12 active SSE subscribers
  • When a 13th subscriber attempts to connect
  • Then the API returns a 4xx response (e.g. 429 or 503)
  • And no new emitter is registered

Scenario 2: Emitter timeout is finite

  • Given an SSE emitter is created
  • When 10 minutes elapse with no activity
  • Then the emitter is completed and the connection is closed

Scenario 3: Slow reader does not stall the heartbeat sweep

  • Given one subscriber's kernel buffer is full (slow reader)
  • When the heartbeat sweep runs
  • Then other subscribers continue to receive heartbeats without delay

Scenario 4: Clean shutdown

  • Given the application is shutting down
  • When destroy() is called on SseSessionEventPublisher
  • Then the method waits up to 5 seconds for the heartbeat thread to finish before returning

Implementation Notes

  • Cap subscribers per session at 12 (2× MAXIMUM_PLAYERS = 6, to allow reconnect churn). Refuse beyond that with a 429.
  • Add a global emitter ceiling (e.g. 500) as a secondary guard.
  • Change new SseEmitter(0L) to new SseEmitter(TimeUnit.MINUTES.toMillis(10)).
  • Add spring.mvc.async.request-timeout: 600000 to application.yml.
  • For the heartbeat stall: move sends to a small bounded thread pool or use non-blocking writes per emitter.
  • In destroy(): add heartbeats.awaitTermination(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS) after shutdownNow(). DisposableBean.destroy() declares throws Exception, so this is legal.

Suggested commit: [EOP-NNN] fix: cap SSE subscribers per session, add emitter timeout, and fix heartbeat stall

Definition of Done

  • Per-session subscriber cap (12) is enforced; excess connections receive 4xx.
  • SseEmitter is created with a 10-minute timeout.
  • spring.mvc.async.request-timeout is set in application.yml.
  • Heartbeat sweep does not block on a slow reader.
  • destroy() calls awaitTermination(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS).
  • Unit tests cover: cap enforcement, timeout creation, shutdown sequence.
  • ./mvnw verify passes (checkstyle, SpotBugs, JaCoCo ≥ 0.80).

renderedFields.description:
User Story

As a player whose identity is a bearer token

I want all traffic to the application to be encrypted in transit and protected by standard security response headers

So that my token cannot be captured by passive network observation and the application is protected against content-injection attacks

Context & Business Value

  • Epic: EOP-5 — Session Lifecycle
  • Target Persona: Players, Security / Operations
  • Value Proposition: The entire identity model is a bearer token that traverses plaintext HTTP. ui/Caddyfile sets auto_https off and serves a bare :8080 site block. The 43-character token is returned in a 201 body and replayed in X-EoP-Player-Token on every request. Passive capture on any shared network is enough to become that player permanently — there is no expiry, rotation or revocation. EOP-10 is what made this load-bearing: before this story the only traffic was public reference card data and there was no credential to steal. Additionally, DisplayName deliberately does not escape HTML (delegating to React), and a display name is broadcast to every other player — the textbook stored-XSS shape. There is no Content-Security-Policy to catch the day a consumer stops being React.

Deployment & Feature Flag Strategy

  • Feature Flag Name: eop.features.session-lifecycle
  • Deployment Behavior: Infrastructure changes are deployed continuously; no application flag governs this ticket.
  • Release Condition: This ticket is a gate on enabling the feature flag. Do not enable eop.features.session-lifecycle until this story is Done.

Acceptance Criteria

Scenario 1: TLS is active

  • Given the application is running
  • When a client connects to the Caddy endpoint
  • Then the connection is TLS-encrypted (via tls internal for a closed demo, or a real certificate for a public hostname)

Scenario 2: Security response headers are present on all API responses

  • Given any request to /api/*
  • When the response is returned
  • Then the response includes all of the following headers:
  • Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none'
  • X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff
  • Referrer-Policy: no-referrer
  • Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains (once TLS is live)

Scenario 3: Existing traffic is unaffected

  • Given TLS and headers are configured
  • When the application serves normal API and SSE traffic
  • Then all existing integration tests pass

Implementation Notes

This is infrastructure work — route to @team-member-devops-engineer.

TLS options (choose one):

  • tls internal in ui/Caddyfile for a closed demo (self-signed, trusted within the compose network).
  • Real hostname + auto_https if a domain is available.
  • Bind to loopback and reach via SSH tunnel / Tailscale (no Caddyfile change needed).

Security headers: Add a header block in ui/Caddyfile applying the headers listed above to all responses. Add Strict-Transport-Security only after TLS is confirmed live.

Note on credential transport: The header-over-cookie choice (X-EoP-Player-Token) is defensible and worth keeping — no cookie means no CSRF surface. The consequence is that the browser must hold the token in a JavaScript module-scope variable or React state only, never localStorage or sessionStorage, accepting that a page refresh loses the seat in exchange for not persisting a non-expiring credential where any injected script can read it. Document this constraint in docs/ or an ADR.

Suggested commit: [EOP-NNN] chore: enable TLS and add security response headers in Caddyfile

Definition of Done

  • Caddy serves traffic over TLS (internal or real certificate).
  • All five security headers are present on API responses.
  • Strict-Transport-Security is added once TLS is confirmed live.
  • Token-storage constraint (React state only, not localStorage) is documented.
  • Existing integration tests pass against the TLS endpoint.
  • ./mvnw verify passes.

renderedFields.description:
User Story

As a facilitator or player

I want sessions and credentials to expire automatically

So that a captured token or a forgotten lobby cannot be used indefinitely, and the database does not grow without bound

Context & Business Value

  • Epic: EOP-5 — Session Lifecycle
  • Target Persona: Facilitators, Players, Security / Operations
  • Value Proposition: A token minted once is valid forever for that session, and a session never ends. There is no expiry, rotation, revocation list, logout route, or way for a facilitator to eject a player. identity_token_hash carries a global unique constraint (uq_player_identity_token_hash), so the credential table grows monotonically. Consequences: a token captured in transit, leaked via browser history, or read out of web storage grants permanent access; a griefer who joins cannot be removed; every row lives forever, compounding the lobby-flooding risk in EOP-19. The SessionStatus.COMPLETED / ABANDONED enum constants are unreachable today — their Javadoc says they exist so expiry "has somewhere to live when it is implemented". This is that implementation.

Deployment & Feature Flag Strategy

  • Feature Flag Name: eop.features.session-lifecycle
  • Deployment Behavior: Code is merged to main with flag remaining OFF.
  • Release Condition: This ticket is a gate on enabling the feature flag. Do not enable eop.features.session-lifecycle until this story is Done.

Acceptance Criteria

Scenario 1: Session expires after 24 hours

  • Given a session was created more than 24 hours ago
  • When ResolvePlayerUseCase is invoked with a token belonging to that session
  • Then the use case refuses the request (e.g. throws SessionExpiredException → 401 or 403)
  • And the session is not accessible

Scenario 2: Expired sessions are swept to ABANDONED and deleted

  • Given one or more sessions have passed their expires_at timestamp
  • When the scheduled sweep runs
  • Then those sessions are transitioned to ABANDONED status
  • And they are deleted (cascading to their player rows via fk_player_game_session ON DELETE CASCADE)

Scenario 3: Active sessions are unaffected by the sweep

  • Given a session was created less than 24 hours ago
  • When the scheduled sweep runs
  • Then the session remains in its current status and is not deleted

Scenario 4: Normal join and play within the expiry window

  • Given a session is within its 24-hour window
  • When a player joins or the facilitator starts the game
  • Then all existing behaviour is unchanged

Implementation Notes

Route the migration to @team-member-db-designer. Route the scheduled sweep to @team-member-devops-engineer or @team-member-tech-lead.

Migration (new Liquibase changelog — `004-session-expiry.xml`):

  • Add expires_at TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE NOT NULL DEFAULT (NOW() + INTERVAL '24 hours') to game_session.
  • Must be valid on both H2 and PostgreSQL 17 (use CURRENT_TIMESTAMP + INTERVAL '24' HOUR for H2 compatibility, or use a dbms condition in the changelog).

Domain guard:

  • In ResolvePlayerUseCase (the single authorisation chokepoint), add a two-line guard: if session.expiresAt().isBefore(Instant.now()) throw SessionExpiredException.
  • This is a pure domain check — zero framework imports in the use case layer.

Scheduled sweep:

  • A Spring @Scheduled method (adapter layer) that queries for sessions where expires_at < NOW() and status != ABANDONED, transitions them to ABANDONED, then deletes them.
  • fk_player_game_session is already ON DELETE CASCADE, so players are deleted automatically.

Suggested commits:

  • [EOP-NNN] feat: add expires_at to game_session and guard in ResolvePlayerUseCase
  • [EOP-NNN] feat: scheduled sweep to transition and delete expired sessions

Definition of Done

  • Liquibase changelog 004-session-expiry.xml adds expires_at and is valid on H2 and PostgreSQL 17.
  • ResolvePlayerUseCase refuses requests against expired sessions.
  • Scheduled sweep transitions expired sessions to ABANDONED and deletes them.
  • Unit tests cover: expiry guard refusal, sweep transitions, active sessions unaffected.
  • ./mvnw verify passes (checkstyle, SpotBugs, JaCoCo ≥ 0.80).

Task

Document the load-bearing guard order in GameSession.start() and flip the spring.h2.console.enabled default to false in the base profile.

These are two independent micro-fixes bundled because both are one-line changes with real regression risk if left undone.

Fix A — Guard-order comment in GameSession.start()

GameSession.start() checks identity before state: unknown player → 403, non-facilitator → 403, wrong status → 409, too few players → 409. This ordering is a deliberate security choice — an unrecognised caller must not be able to infer session state from the error code. It is documented nowhere. A future maintainer reordering the guards "to short-circuit faster" would silently turn a 403 into a 409 information leak.

Fix: Add a comment above the guard sequence stating the order is load-bearing for security reasons and must not be changed without a security review. Example:

// SECURITY: identity checks MUST precede state checks.
// An unrecognised caller must not be able to infer session state from the error code.
// Do not reorder these guards without a security review.

Fix B — Flip spring.h2.console.enabled default to false

spring.h2.console.enabled: true is set in the base application.yml profile. Production overrides it to false, so the console is not exposed in production today. However, the base profile now governs a database that holds player credentials (identity_token_hash). The fail-secure default is false; any environment that genuinely needs the console (e.g. local development) should opt in explicitly.

Fix: Change the base application.yml to spring.h2.console.enabled: false. Add spring.h2.console.enabled: true to application-dev.yml (or equivalent local-dev profile) if one exists.

Acceptance Criteria

  • GameSession.start() has a comment above its guard sequence explaining the load-bearing order.
  • spring.h2.console.enabled defaults to false in the base profile.
  • Any local-dev profile that needs the console opts in explicitly.
  • ./mvnw verify passes.

Suggested commit: [EOP-NNN] chore: document load-bearing guard order and fail-close H2 console default

Scope reduced — the H2 console item has been split out into EOP-27

Raised by @security-auditor during the EOP-10 review (PR #36). This story bundled two items of quite different size:

  1. documenting the load-bearing guard order in GameSession.start(), and
  2. making the H2 console default fail closed.

Item 2 has moved to EOP-27 for two reasons the auditor gave. First, it is the single change in the session-lifecycle work that is not behind the feature flag — every session endpoint is gated by eop.features.session-lifecycle and so does not exist on merge, whereas the H2 console is live the moment the PR merges. Second, a fail-closed default plus a test is a materially larger change than a documentation comment, and bundling them hid that.

This story is now documentation only: record why the guard sequence inside GameSession.start() is load-bearing, so a future reader does not reorder or remove a guard on the assumption that the order is incidental.

Related: ADR-020 was written during this review and already documents the adjacent concurrency-control mechanism — the status-guarded conditional UPDATE, the row lock it holds to end of transaction, and why the @Version field is not the control. Read it before writing the guard-order note; some of the context you need is already there.

renderedFields.description:
Task

Increase the join code from 6 to 8 Crockford base32 characters and amend ADR-019 to record the entropy rationale.

Background

Six Crockford characters is 32^6 ≈ 30.0 bits of entropy. The per-code failure counter (MAX_FAILURES_PER_CODE = 30) does not bind during enumeration because every guess is a different canonical code landing in its own fresh bucket — the only live control is 10 failures/minute/address. Against a commodity proxy pool of ~1,000 addresses and 10–50 live lobbies, a real lobby is found in roughly 1.5–7.5 days, not the "centuries" the class Javadoc claims (that arithmetic assumes a single attacker IP).

Eight Crockford characters is 32^8 ≈ 40 bits — 1,024× harder — costs one constant change plus a VARCHAR(8) migration, and remains typeable aloud. This moves the join code from "defended by a fragile in-memory limiter" to "defended by arithmetic".

Note: the attack model above assumes 10–50 concurrent lobbies. For a demo with near-zero traffic the timelines are 10–50× longer, so the direction is right but the urgency is lower than the raw numbers suggest.

Scope

  1. Change JOIN_CODE_LENGTH (or equivalent constant) from 6 to 8 in the join-code generator.
  2. Add a Liquibase changelog entry to widen join_code VARCHAR(6) to VARCHAR(8) on game_session. Must be valid on both H2 and PostgreSQL 17.
  3. Update the class Javadoc on the join-code generator to reflect the corrected entropy arithmetic (proxy pool model, not single-IP model).
  4. Amend ADR-019 (or create ADR-019 if it does not yet exist as a file) to record: the entropy calculation, the proxy-pool attack model, and the rationale for choosing 8 characters.

Acceptance Criteria

  • Join codes generated are 8 characters long.
  • The VARCHAR column is widened in a valid Liquibase migration.
  • Javadoc reflects the corrected entropy model.
  • ADR-019 records the rationale.
  • All existing join-code tests pass with the new length.
  • ./mvnw verify passes.

Suggested commits:

  • [EOP-NNN] chore: widen join code to 8 Crockford characters for 40-bit entropy
  • [EOP-NNN] docs: amend ADR-019 with corrected entropy model and proxy-pool rationale

comments.body:
*PR opened: https://github.com/maglez/eop-threat-medeling/pull/112* — branch EOP-24-widen-join-code-to-8-chars, three commits.

Scope items, all four delivered

  1. `JoinCode.LENGTH` 6 → 8. This is the only production switch — SecureRandomJoinCodeGenerator, GameSessionJpaEntity's @Column(length = JoinCode.LENGTH) and three test helpers all derive from the constant and widened for free.
  2. `2026-08-22--widen-join-code-to-8-characters.xml` widens join_code to VARCHAR(8) behind a columnExists precondition, valid on H2 and PostgreSQL 17 (modifyDataType emits ALTER TABLE … ALTER COLUMN on both; LENGTH() and || are ANSI). Both changesets carry <rollback>.
  3. Generator Javadoc corrected to the proxy-pool model. The "centuries" claim is gone from InMemoryJoinAttemptLimiter — it says explicitly that the earlier arithmetic assumed the attacker owned one address.
  4. ADR-019 amended with the entropy calculation, the attack model and the rationale for eight.

A correction worth recording on the ticket

The ticket's own framing was right and the ADR's was wrong in a way worth naming: ADR-019's Consequences section had said "Eight characters would have made the limiter a courtesy. Six makes it a control. Anyone tempted to remove or weaken it must lengthen the code first." The amendment quotes that verbatim and explains it did not survive the arithmetic — the per-code window never fires against enumeration at any length, because each guess lands in its own fresh bucket. So the limiter was not downgraded: length bounds how much of the keyspace a blind search must cover, the limiter bounds how fast any one address covers it. ADR-021 is untouched, since header rotation defeats the rate bound at any code length.

Three related ADRs were corrected by amendment rather than rewriting: ADR-021 keeps its verbatim quotation of the old "primary security control" wording and marks it historical; ADR-033's claim that a flood would consume "every six-character join code" is now false at 40 bits (43M rows/day needs ~70 years to exhaust 1.1e12), so its decision is restated on the harm that was always larger — unbounded game_session growth by an unauthenticated caller; ADR-023's aside is now length-neutral so it cannot go stale again.

One design decision the ticket did not anticipate

GameSessionJpaEntity.toDomain() calls the strict JoinCode constructor, so a stored six-character row would throw IllegalArgumentException and 500 the reconnect path {{GET /api/v1/sessions/

{sessionId}

}} for already-seated players. The changeset therefore pads legacy rows (join_code || '00') rather than deleting them: padding keeps every foreign key intact, cannot collide with uq_game_session_join_code, and preserves reconnect. Codes already read aloud stop parsing and 404 indistinguishably, bounded by ADR-036's 24-hour TTL.

Two defects found and fixed in passing

  • DeckTrimMigrationRoundTripTest hardcoded rollback(1)/rollback(2), counting backwards from the end of the changelog — which a new dated changelog breaks, since <includeAll> orders changes/ alphabetically. All six call sites now use a dynamic changesetsAppliedFrom(connection, filename, floor) helper, the idiom SessionExpiryMigrationTest and TrickPlaySchemaRoundTripTest already used, parameterised rather than duplicated a third time.
  • MigrationTestFixtures derived its code with a hardcoded substring(0, 6); it now uses JoinCode.LENGTH.

Acceptance criteria

Criterion Status
Codes are 8 characters Met — JoinCode.LENGTH = 8, pinned by a new shouldCarryFortyBitsOfEntropy test computing log2(ALPHABET.length()) * LENGTH
VARCHAR widened in a valid migration Met — H2 and PostgreSQL 17, with rollback
Javadoc corrected Met — 9 production files; "centuries" removed
ADR-019 records the rationale Met — plus ADR-021/023/033 amendments and the ADR index
Existing join-code tests pass Met — JoinCodeTest rewritten, plus 2 new tests
./mvnw verify passes Met — Tests run: 1274, Failures: 0, Errors: 0, Skipped: 0, BUILD SUCCESS; JaCoCo 96.9% instruction / 88.7% branch against 80/70 gates

npm run verify in ui/ also passes (223 tests). No functional front-end change was required — JoinSessionForm.tsx validates only for non-emptiness and there is no maxLength or pattern anywhere in ui/src.

Definition of Done — all five gates approved

@tester-unit-and-quality, @tester-api, @security-auditor and @architecture-guardian approved on the first pass. @code-reviewer rejected on the substring(0, 8) literal, three stale rollback-depth comments and a JoinCode Javadoc example that illustrated nothing; all were fixed in 3a362c7 and it re-approved.

One recorded non-finding: @security-auditor recalculated the exposure window as 0.1–0.7 days and suggested the documented 1.5–7.5 days was over-conservative. That recalculation inverted the division. Expected guesses = keyspace ÷ live lobbies = 1.07e8 down to 2.14e7; at 1.44e7 guesses/day that is 7.4 down to 1.5 days. @code-reviewer independently confirmed the range is exact, so every documented figure is unchanged.

Honest limits, carried into the ADR

The ticket's own caveat is preserved rather than dropped: the 10–50 concurrent-lobby assumption is load-bearing, so a near-empty demo is 10–50× slower to attack. The prize is a seat in a card game and there is no authentication anywhere (ADR-015). Padded legacy rows still carry 30 bits, though they were already circulating and expire within 24 hours. Changeset 002's rollback would also truncate a genuinely generated code ending 00, so the two rollbacks are documented to run together (rollbackCount=2) or not at all. The direction is right and the change was cheap, which is why it was made — it was not an incident.

Awaiting human approval on the PR.

Merged and closed. PR #112 was merged to main at 2026-08-22 13:59 UTC as merge commit bc21e91, and this ticket has been transitioned To Do → In Progress → Done to match.

All four CI checks passed on the merged head under Actions run 32576849119: build, image, supply-chain and ui. The five Definition of Done gate verdicts recorded in the previous comment stand unchanged — the tree merged is byte-identical to the tree they reviewed at 3a362c7, with no post-review commits.

Two notes for whoever picks up the next session:

  • Legacy six-character rows in game_session were padded rather than deleted, so any row that predates the migration still carries 30 bits until it expires under the 24-hour TTL in ADR-036. Nothing further to do — this drains on its own.
  • The two changesets in 2026-08-22--widen-join-code-to-8-characters.xml roll back together or not at all, because changeset 002's rollback would also truncate a genuinely generated code ending in the digits zero-zero. Use a rollback count of two if it is ever needed.

renderedFields.description:
User Story

As a product owner

I want to enable the eop.features.session-lifecycle feature flag for the deployed container

So that the session lifecycle feature is live for real users

Context & Business Value

  • Epic: EOP-5 — Session Lifecycle
  • Target Persona: Product Owner / Operations
  • Value Proposition: EOP-10 shipped the session lifecycle feature dark (flag OFF). This story is the gate-flip: it may only be done once all blocking stories are Done and verified.

Deployment & Feature Flag Strategy

  • Feature Flag Name: eop.features.session-lifecycle
  • Deployment Behavior: This story IS the flag flip.
  • Release Condition: All blocking stories (EOP-17, EOP-18, EOP-19, EOP-20, EOP-21, EOP-22) must be Done before this story is started.

Blocking Stories (must all be Done before this story starts)

  • EOP-17 — Fix: map SeatAlreadyTakenException → 409 and JoinCodeUnavailableException → 503
  • EOP-18 — Harden InMemoryJoinAttemptLimiter: fail-closed on saturation and atomic check-and-record
  • EOP-19 — Rate-limit POST /api/v1/sessions and cap request body size
  • EOP-20 — Cap SSE subscribers per session, add emitter timeout, and fix heartbeat stall
  • EOP-21 — Enable TLS at Caddy and add security response headers
  • EOP-22 — Add session expiry and scheduled sweep

Acceptance Criteria

Scenario 1: Flag is enabled

  • Given all blocking stories are Done
  • When the flag is set to the literal true and the application restarts
  • Then SessionController is registered as a Spring bean
  • And the four session use-case beans are registered — see amendment (a) below
  • And {{GET /api/v1/sessions/ {id}

    /events}} and POST /api/v1/sessions respond normally

Scenario 2: Smoke test passes

  • Given the flag is enabled
  • When a facilitator creates a lobby and a player joins
  • Then the full join flow completes end-to-end without errors

Scenario 3: Health endpoint is unaffected

  • Given the flag is enabled
  • When GET /health is called
  • Then it returns 200

Definition of Done

  • The flag is set to true for the deployed container — see amendment (b) for what that change actually is.
  • ADR-013's flag register and the comment in src/main/resources/application.yml reflect that the flag is now ON — see amendment (c).
  • End-to-end smoke test passes.
  • ./mvnw verify passes.

Suggested commit: EOP-25 Done feat: enable eop.features.session-lifecycle flag

Amended 2026-08-14 (EOP-48)

EOP-48 closed a fail-open defect in this flag's @ConditionalOnProperty (merged as 34d30d7 and 50850d1, PR #52). It changed what flipping this flag involves, on four points. The original text above has been corrected in place where it was actively misleading; the substance of each correction is recorded here so the change is visible rather than silent.

(a) Only the literal true now enables the feature — on, yes and 1 are silent no-ops

This is the most important of the four and the one most likely to waste an afternoon.

Before EOP-48, SessionController's condition omitted havingValue, which under Spring means the condition matches any present value except the literal `false`. So on, yes and 1 would all have enabled the routes — as would off, no, 0, disabled and the empty string, which is what made it a security defect worth its own ticket.

After EOP-48 the condition is havingValue = "true", so exactly one value enables the feature: case-insensitive true. Everything else — including every truthy-looking spelling an operator might reach for — leaves the feature off. An operator who flips this flag with on gets a silent no-op: the application boots cleanly and the five session routes return 404 exactly as they did before.

That inversion is the deliberate price of failing closed, and @security-auditor argued during EOP-48 against adding startup validation to catch it — the failure is loud enough in practice (the feature is visibly absent within seconds of the restart the flag requires anyway) and a validator would turn an operability annoyance into a boot crash. So the safeguard for this story is this paragraph, not a mechanism.

Use the exact string `EOP_FEATURES_SESSION_LIFECYCLE=true`.

(b) Four use-case beans now register with the flag, not just the controller

Scenario 1 originally asserted only that SessionController becomes a bean. As of EOP-48 the flag also gates createSessionUseCase, joinSessionUseCase, getSessionStateUseCase and startSessionUseCase in UseCaseConfiguration (:101, :124, :167, :182). This is what makes the off position a property of the Spring context rather than of the URL space alone.

resolvePlayerUseCase is deliberately ungated and always present: it is a pure read, and it is shared with all five trick-play use cases, so gating it on this flag would make lobby-off/trick-play-on an unsatisfiable context. Do not "tidy" that asymmetry while flipping the flag — the reason is in its javadoc and in ADR-013.

The smoke test in Scenario 2 is unaffected; but if the context fails to start after the flip, the four newly-gated beans are the place to look first.

(c) The flip is an addition to compose.app.yml, not a one-line edit

The original text called this "a one-line change in compose.app.yml". That file has no `EOP_FEATURES_` entry at all* — its only environment entry is SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE: prod at :76. So the flip means adding EOP_FEATURES_SESSION_LIFECYCLE: "true" to the service's environment block, then docker compose -f compose.app.yml up -d.

Worth deciding deliberately rather than by habit: ADR-013 and .opencode/rules/feature-flags.md both say that flipping a flag anywhere other than your own machine is a reviewed change, and that the default should move in application.yml under review rather than leaving an environment override in place. An environment override has no audit trail beyond the shell history of whoever set it. For a permanent rollout, moving session-lifecycle: false → true in src/main/resources/application.yml (currently :79) is the reviewable form; the compose entry is the right shape only if this is a staged or reversible rollout. Say which one this story is doing, and why.

(d) docs/feature-flags.md does not exist and deliberately never will

The original Definition of Done required updating docs/feature-flags.md. That file has never existed, and .opencode/rules/feature-flags.md states there is deliberately no separate flag catalogue — each flag is recorded next to its default in src/main/resources/application.yml and in ADR-013. The DoD above now points at those two instead.

Also worth fixing while in here (pre-existing, not caused by EOP-48)

The Context section says "all five blocking stories" but the list names six (EOP-17 through EOP-22). Reconcile the count before starting.

Status of EOP-48 as a predecessor

Discharged. EOP-48 is Done. Note that neither ticket ever linked the other as a blocker, so there is no Jira link to clear — the relationship was asserted in prose only, which is why this amendment exists.

comments.body:
The gate on this story has widened — EOP-26 and EOP-27 join the list

From the EOP-10 review (PR #36), where all five reviewers signed off on the code but three new defects were accepted as follow-ups.

This story was gated on EOP-17 through EOP-22. Two additions:

  • EOP-26 — `X-Forwarded-For` trusted-proxy bypass. This is now the most important prerequisite. ADR-019 explicitly designates the join-attempt limiter "a primary security control, not defence in depth" at thirty bits of join-code entropy. EOP-26 establishes that the control is currently bypassable by rotating a caller-supplied header, so enabling this flag without it would put the session endpoints live with their primary protection inert. It must precede this story, and it should also precede EOP-24 — widening the code to forty bits reduces the impact of enumeration but does not restore the control.
  • EOP-27 — H2 console fail-closed. Strictly speaking this is not gated on the flag at all, since the console is live on merge regardless. Listed here only so the pre-release checklist is complete in one place.

So the current gate is: EOP-17, EOP-18, EOP-19, EOP-20, EOP-21, EOP-22, EOP-26, with EOP-27 alongside.

The other review follow-ups — EOP-28 (handleIllegalArgument), EOP-29 (contract polish), EOP-30 (correlation id), EOP-31 (documentation sweep) — are deliberately not gates on this flag. None of them affects whether the session lifecycle is safe to expose.

h2. Amended 2026-08-14 ([EOP-48|https://maglez.atlassian.net/browse/EOP-48])

[EOP-48|https://maglez.atlassian.net/browse/EOP-48] closed a fail-open defect in this flag's {{@ConditionalOnProperty}} (merged as {{34d30d7}} and {{50850d1}}, PR #52). It changed what flipping this flag involves, on four points. The original text above has been corrected in place where it was actively misleading; the substance of each correction is recorded here so the change is visible rather than silent.

h3. (a) Only the literal {{true}} now enables the feature — {{on}}, {{yes}} and {{1}} are silent no-ops

*This is the most important of the four and the one most likely to waste an afternoon.*

Before [EOP-48|https://maglez.atlassian.net/browse/EOP-48], {{SessionController}}'s condition omitted {{havingValue}}, which under Spring means the condition matches _any present value except the literal `false`_. So {{on}}, {{yes}} and {{1}} would all have enabled the routes — as would {{off}}, {{no}}, {{0}}, {{disabled}} and the empty string, which is what made it a security defect worth its own ticket.

After [EOP-48|https://maglez.atlassian.net/browse/EOP-48] the condition is {{havingValue = "true"}}, so exactly one value enables the feature: case-insensitive {{true}}. *Everything else — including every truthy-looking spelling an operator might reach for — leaves the feature off.* An operator who flips this flag with {{on}} gets a silent no-op: the application boots cleanly and the five session routes return 404 exactly as they did before.

That inversion is the deliberate price of failing closed, and @security-auditor argued during [EOP-48|https://maglez.atlassian.net/browse/EOP-48] _against_ adding startup validation to catch it — the failure is loud enough in practice (the feature is visibly absent within seconds of the restart the flag requires anyway) and a validator would turn an operability annoyance into a boot crash. So the safeguard for this story is this paragraph, not a mechanism.

*Use the exact string `EOP_FEATURES_SESSION_LIFECYCLE=true`.*

h3. (b) Four use-case beans now register with the flag, not just the controller

Scenario 1 originally asserted only that {{SessionController}} becomes a bean. As of [EOP-48|https://maglez.atlassian.net/browse/EOP-48] the flag also gates {{createSessionUseCase}}, {{joinSessionUseCase}}, {{getSessionStateUseCase}} and {{startSessionUseCase}} in {{UseCaseConfiguration}} ({{:101}}, {{:124}}, {{:167}}, {{:182}}). This is what makes the off position a property of the Spring context rather than of the URL space alone.

{{resolvePlayerUseCase}} is deliberately *ungated* and always present: it is a pure read, and it is shared with all five trick-play use cases, so gating it on this flag would make lobby-off/trick-play-on an unsatisfiable context. Do not "tidy" that asymmetry while flipping the flag — the reason is in its javadoc and in [ADR-013|https://maglez.atlassian.net/browse/ADR-013].

The smoke test in Scenario 2 is unaffected; but if the context fails to start after the flip, the four newly-gated beans are the place to look first.

h3. (c) The flip is an _addition_ to {{compose.app.yml}}, not a one-line edit

The original text called this "a one-line change in {{compose.app.yml}}". That file has *no `EOP_FEATURES_*` entry at all* — its only environment entry is {{SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE: prod}} at {{:76}}. So the flip means adding {{EOP_FEATURES_SESSION_LIFECYCLE: "true"}} to the service's environment block, then {{docker compose -f compose.app.yml up -d}}.

Worth deciding deliberately rather than by habit: [ADR-013|https://maglez.atlassian.net/browse/ADR-013] and {{.opencode/rules/feature-flags.md}} both say that flipping a flag anywhere other than your own machine is a reviewed change, and that the _default_ should move in {{application.yml}} under review rather than leaving an environment override in place. An environment override has no audit trail beyond the shell history of whoever set it. For a permanent rollout, moving {{session-lifecycle: false}} → {{true}} in {{src/main/resources/application.yml}} (currently {{:79}}) is the reviewable form; the compose entry is the right shape only if this is a staged or reversible rollout. Say which one this story is doing, and why.

h3. (d) {{docs/feature-flags.md}} does not exist and deliberately never will

The original Definition of Done required updating {{docs/feature-flags.md}}. That file has never existed, and {{.opencode/rules/feature-flags.md}} states there is deliberately *no separate flag catalogue* — each flag is recorded next to its default in {{src/main/resources/application.yml}} and in [ADR-013|https://maglez.atlassian.net/browse/ADR-013]. The DoD above now points at those two instead.

h3. Also worth fixing while in here (pre-existing, not caused by [EOP-48|https://maglez.atlassian.net/browse/EOP-48])

The Context section says "all five blocking stories" but the list names *six* ([EOP-17|https://maglez.atlassian.net/browse/EOP-17] through [EOP-22|https://maglez.atlassian.net/browse/EOP-22]). Reconcile the count before starting.

h3. Status of [EOP-48|https://maglez.atlassian.net/browse/EOP-48] as a predecessor

Discharged. [EOP-48|https://maglez.atlassian.net/browse/EOP-48] is *Done*. Note that neither ticket ever linked the other as a blocker, so there is no Jira link to clear — the relationship was asserted in prose only, which is why this amendment exists.
