renderedFields.description:
Raised by @security-auditor during the EOP-10 review (PR #36). Not covered by EOP-18 or EOP-24.

The defect

ClientAddresses.of(HttpServletRequest) reads X-Forwarded-For, splits on comma and takes the last entry, falling back to getRemoteAddr(). The reasoning behind taking the last entry is sound as far as it goes — Caddy appends, so the last hop is proxy-written while the first is caller-controlled. But the code then assumes that if no forwarding header is present the connection did not come through the proxy, and never verifies the converse.

There is no trusted-proxy check anywhere in the codebase. server.forward-headers-strategy is set in no configuration file, and ui/Caddyfile relies on Caddy's default append rather than configuring the header explicitly.

Why it matters

Whenever the application is reached without Caddy in front — which is the normal local development mode, ./mvnw spring-boot:run on 8080, and also any peer inside the container network — a caller that sends its own X-Forwarded-For supplies the exact value the rate limiter keys on. Rotate it per request and every request lands in a fresh, empty bucket: MAX_FAILURES_PER_ADDRESS = 10 never fires.

The per-code window cannot compensate, by construction. An attacker enumerating the keyspace tries a different code on each guess, so each code bucket holds one failure and never approaches its threshold. Worse, once MAX_TRACKED_KEYS (10,000) distinct codes have been seen, the code map stops recording at all.

This matters more than it first appears because ADR-019 explicitly designates this limiter a primary security control, not defence in depth: "at thirty bits the rate limiter is a primary security control". This defect removes precisely that control.

Ordering

  • Must land before EOP-25 enables eop.features.session-lifecycle, because until the flag is on, SessionController is not registered and no path consults the limiter.
  • Should land before EOP-24. Widening the join code to 40 bits reduces the impact of enumeration but does not fix the bypass; restoring the control is the stronger fix.
  • Related to EOP-18, but distinct: EOP-18 concerns a single bucket saturating and a non-atomic check-and-record. A fresh bucket per request never saturates and never races.

Acceptance criteria

Scenario 1 — the header is ignored when the peer is not a trusted proxy

Given the application is reached directly, not through Caddy

When a caller sends X-Forwarded-For: 10.0.0.1 and then X-Forwarded-For: 10.0.0.2

Then both requests are throttled against the same bucket, keyed on the real peer address

Scenario 2 — the header is honoured from a configured proxy

Given the peer address is on the configured trusted-proxy allow-list

When a request arrives carrying a forwarded chain

Then the proxy-written entry is used as the client address

Scenario 3 — the allow-list is explicit and default-denied

Given no trusted proxy is configured

Then X-Forwarded-For is ignored entirely and getRemoteAddr() is used

Scenario 4 — a test proves the rotation attack no longer yields a fresh bucket.

Notes

Remediation is either server.forward-headers-strategy with a trusted-proxy allow-list, or an explicit check in ClientAddresses against a configured allow-list. Either way the rule to apply is the project's own: explicit allow-list, fail securely.

comments.body:
PR #40 opened from EOP-26-trusted-proxy-forwarded-for. ./mvnw verify green: exit 0, 386 tests, 0 failures, SpotBugs 0, Checkstyle 0, JaCoCo met.

All four acceptance scenarios covered. Scenario 1 and 3 by ClientAddressResolverTest and TrustedProxiesTest; Scenario 2 by HeaderHonouredFromTrustedProxy; Scenario 4 by RotationAttackBlocked, which drives ten failing joins with a distinct join code each time so only the per-address counter can produce the refusal. Remediation was the explicit allow-list option from the ticket notes, not server.forward-headers-strategy — though that property is now pinned to none as a fence, because RemoteIpValve's default internalProxies covers 172.16.0.0/12, which contains this project's own Compose subnet.

The strongest evidence that this defect was real came out of the work rather than the analysis: the integration suite's freshAddress() helper had been getting its per-test throttle isolation from the vulnerability itself — a test choosing its own rate-limiter key from outside the process, which is precisely the attack. Closing the hole broke sixteen previously-passing tests. A green build had been evidence the bug was still present.

Review gates: 4 of 5 approved. @security-auditor (who raised this on PR #36), @code-reviewer, @tester-unit-and-quality and @architecture-guardian all approved with evidence. The auditor built an InetAddressResolverProvider spy proving zero DNS lookups leak, with a negative control confirming the guard is load-bearing, and verified from bytecode that RemoteIpValve is not installed.

⚠️ @tester-api did not produce a usable sign-off across four dispatches — no file:line findings, no build exit code, no order-independence runs. I am not recording that gate as passed. Filed separately as an agent-configuration issue; the substantive API-boundary questions were answered with evidence by @security-auditor, so this is not believed to be a code risk. PR should not merge until that is resolved.

Two findings worth noting for the record, both caught by @architecture-guardian rejecting twice — correctly:

  1. IpLiteralsTest hard-coded %lo0, green on macOS and red on `ubuntu-latest` where the loopback is lo. It would have broken the build on merge while passing every local review.
  2. My own replacement fix was also wrong: selecting the first network interface passed only because a VPN utun4 sorted first. The platform needs a scope id, which exists only on an interface carrying an IPv6 link-local address.

ADR-021 records the decision plus eight known limitations. An earlier revision of it claimed DNS-free parsing "by construction"; that claim was measured false (a cold colon-bearing hostname lookup blocked a request thread for 5020 ms) and is now explicitly retracted rather than quietly deleted.

Fifth Definition-of-Done gate obtained — @tester-api: VERDICT: APPROVE

All five mandatory gates have now signed off. This one was obtained retrospectively, against the code as it stands on main — see the caveat at the end.

Evidence returned

Build, independently reproduced. ./mvnw verify → exit code 0, Tests run: 905, Failures: 0, Errors: 0, Skipped: 0, SpotBugs BugInstance size is 0, All coverage checks have been met., BUILD SUCCESS in 23.5 s. Matches the numbers I had gathered separately.

The decisive question — is `HeaderHonouredFromTrustedProxy` vacuous? No. The gate confirmed from bytecode (javap -verbose on spring-test-7.0.8.jar) that MockHttpServletRequest.DEFAULT_REMOTE_ADDR is the constant 127.0.0.1, and that no setRemoteAddr() call appears anywhere in the test file — so every request in both nested classes presents getRemoteAddr() == 127.0.0.1. The mirror-pair claim therefore holds: the two nested classes drive identical traffic (11 requests, rotating X-Forwarded-For) and differ only in whether 127.0.0.1 is allow-listed, and the outcome flips — 429 on the 11th request when it is not (ForwardedForThrottleBypassIntegrationTest.java:91), 404 when it is (:138, allow-list set at :133). The pair is evidence about the allow-list, not merely about the header going unread.

All four acceptance criteria covered by genuine — not nominal — tests. AC1 at ClientAddressResolverTest.java:56 and :69 plus end-to-end at ForwardedForThrottleBypassIntegrationTest.java:98; AC2 at ClientAddressResolverTest.java:90 and :103 plus :145; AC3 at ClientAddressResolverTest.java:151 and TrustedProxiesTest.java:49/:57/:66, with the trusted-proxies: [] default confirmed at application.yml:68; AC4 at ForwardedForThrottleBypassIntegrationTest.java:98, which uses a distinct code per attempt (line 104) so the per-code counter cannot be what fires the 429 — only the per-address counter can. That last detail is what makes AC4 a real proof of the fix rather than a restatement of it.

Order-independence: four runs, all green. The three named classes in isolation (3, 14 and 12 tests) and the full suite (905). No order-dependent failures. renderedFields.description:
Split out of EOP-23 at the request of @security-auditor during the EOP-10 review (PR #36). EOP-23 remains the documentation-only task; this is the code change.

The defect

application.yml enables /h2-console in the default profile, and there is no Spring Security dependency anywhere in the project. The console is therefore unauthenticated arbitrary SQL, and it also accepts an arbitrary JDBC URL — the CVE-2021-42392 JNDI/RCE class of exposure.

Why it is worth its own ticket

Two reasons the auditor gave for separating it from EOP-23:

  1. It is the one thing in the session-lifecycle change set that is not behind a feature flag. Every session endpoint is gated by eop.features.session-lifecycle, which defaults off, so those endpoints do not exist on merge. The H2 console is live the moment the PR merges.
  2. A fail-closed default is a materially larger change than the guard-order comment EOP-23 asks for, and bundling the two hides that.

Mitigating context, and why this was not treated as blocking the EOP-10 merge: application-prod.yml disables the console and hardens server.error.*, and the deployment is local-only with no internet exposure following the withdrawal of EOP-7.

Acceptance criteria

Scenario 1 — the default is off

Given no profile explicitly enables it

When the application starts

Then /h2-console returns 404 and no console servlet is registered

Scenario 2 — enabling it is deliberate and local

Given a developer sets the explicit opt-in property

When the application starts

Then the console is reachable, and the property name makes clear it is a local-development affordance

Scenario 3 — a test asserts the console is absent under the default profile, so a future default flip is caught by the build rather than by a reviewer.

comments.body:
Premise correction before this lands — the console was never actually served, and AC2 cannot be met without adding the attack surface this ticket exists to remove.

What I found. I wrote the acceptance tests first, including the AC2 "console is reachable" test, and it failed: with the opt-in set, /h2-console was still 404 and no console servlet bean existed. Investigation was conclusive:

  • The full test classpath contains h2-2.4.240.jar and 33 spring-boot 4.1.0 modules, and `spring-boot-h2console` is not among them.
  • No class named H2Console exists on any jar on the classpath, and no AutoConfiguration.imports file on the classpath mentions the console.
  • Maven Central confirms org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-h2console exists for 4.0.0–4.1.0. Spring Boot 4 modularised the console's autoconfiguration out of spring-boot-autoconfigure into that separate module. Inspecting the jar: it registers ServletRegistrationBean<JakartaWebServlet> h2Console() from org.springframework.boot.h2console.autoconfigure.H2ConsoleAutoConfiguration.

So spring.h2.console.enabled: true was inert — no class on the classpath ever read it. There was no live unauthenticated-SQL endpoint at any point. This is the same failure mode as the Liquibase defect already recorded in the changelog: Boot 4 modularisation leaving configuration that reads as active but is never consulted.

Why the ticket is still worth doing, and what I changed instead. The defect is not a live endpoint but security-sensitive configuration that says yes. One transitive dependency, or one developer adding the module for local convenience, and the exposure arrives silently with consent already granted and nothing prompting a review. So:

  • application.yml now pins enabled: false with the reasoning attached — the exposure it would be, that the module is absent today, and why the line stays rather than being deleted: whoever adds the module has to change a line that says why it is off, instead of inheriting a default. The dead path: /h2-console is removed.
  • application-prod.yml keeps its own redundant false as a second independent guard, now commented as deliberate.
  • src/test/resources/application.properties no longer pins spring.h2.console.enabled=false. That override would have made any "console is absent" assertion pass because of the test's own configuration rather than the shipped default — defeating AC3. The suite now reads what ships.
  • H2ConsoleAbsentIntegrationTest (real port, JDK HttpClient, since MockMvc returns 404 for a servlet registration whether or not it is registered) asserts 404 on both /h2-console and /h2-console/, that the h2Console bean is absent, that the resolved property is false, and — the load-bearing one — that H2ConsoleAutoConfiguration is not on the classpath. That last assertion is the tripwire: it is the only one that can fail today, and it fires the day somebody adds the module, so the decision happens at review time rather than in an incident.

AC2 is not satisfiable as written and I have not faked it. "Given a developer sets the explicit opt-in property, the console is reachable" requires adding spring-boot-h2console to pom.xml. Adding an unauthenticated-SQL servlet in order to demonstrate that we have turned it off would be an own-goal, and it is a dependency decision that deserves its own ticket rather than arriving as a side effect of a hardening story. I propose AC2 be re-read as: enabling the console is a deliberate act that requires adding a dependency, and the build refuses until somebody revisits the guard. That is stronger than a property opt-in — it cannot be done by accident.

Honest limitation, flagged for the reviewers. While the module is absent, the 404, absent-bean and property assertions cannot fail — they are vacuous by construction. They are kept because the tripwire converts them: the day it fires and the module is added deliberately, they become the assertions that the guard actually holds, and they are already in place. The test's Javadoc says this in those terms rather than claiming three independent guards.

Also fixed, because they promised something that does not exist: docs/devops/local-development.md advertised a console at http://localhost:8080/h2-console with sa and no password; ADR-008 recorded "H2 console available at /h2-console in dev profile" — and there has never been a dev profile either (ADR-012 fixes the set at {{

{default, prod}

}}). Both are corrected, ADR-008 by in-place amendment per the ADR README convention, with the index row updated.

Out of scope, deliberately left for EOP-31: local-development.md and ADR-008 name DATASOURCE_URL/DATASOURCE_USER/DATASOURCE_PASSWORD for the default profile while application.yml and .env.example use DB_URL/DB_USERNAME/DB_PASSWORD. The console opt-in was also deliberately not added to .env.example, which is copied to /opt/eop/.env on the deployment target — a security-sensitive toggle does not belong in a file that ships to the host.

Review complete — PR #37 approved by all five reviewers, follow-ups filed

PR: https://github.com/maglez/eop-threat-medeling/pull/37 (2 commits: 904259a, 6a4fb71). ./mvnw verify green — 304 tests, checkstyle, SpotBugs, JaCoCo 80%.

All five mandatory sign-offs obtained: @tester-unit-and-quality, @tester-api, @security-auditor, @code-reviewer, @architecture-guardian.

The security auditor recanted its own finding

The CRITICAL raised during the EOP-10 / PR #36 review was factually wrong, and the auditor said so plainly after re-verifying the premise correction three independent ways: it scanned all 129 jars on the test classpath for H2Console (0 hits), grepped every jar's AutoConfiguration.imports for h2 (0 lines), and decompiled spring-boot-h2console-4.1.0.jar from Maven Central to confirm the FQCN, the h2Console bean name and the spring.h2.console.enabled property key all match what the tripwire asserts.

Two findings that strengthen the ticket rather than weaken it:

  • `h2-2.4.240.jar` already ships all 13 `org.h2.server.web` classes, including JakartaWebServlet, inside the production artifact. So the autoconfiguration's @ConditionalOnClass gate is already satisfied — only the autoconfig module was missing. The "one dependency away" framing in the fix comment is understated, not overstated.
  • A negative control I had not run. The auditor mutated application.yml line 38 back to enabled: true and re-ran: Tests run: 4, Failures: 1, shouldResolveTheShippedDefaultToFalse FAILED, BUILD FAILURE. So deleting the `spring.h2.console.enabled=false` override from `src/test/resources/application.properties` was the single most valuable line in this PR — without it the mutation would have passed silently. My original Javadoc undersold this by claiming only the tripwire could fail; commit 6a4fb71 corrects that account.

AC2 — accepted as deliberately unsatisfied

The security auditor endorsed the re-reading rather than requiring the dependency: adding spring-boot-h2console to make a checkbox green would put the exact artifact this ticket exists to keep off the classpath onto it, in the production dependency graph, guarded only by a property — trading a documented latent risk for a live one. Enabling the console now requires a dependency change plus editing a guard that explains why it is off, which is a stronger consent mechanism than a property toggle.

It also declined to require a maven-enforcer ban in this PR, reasoning that a prohibition with no sanctioned escape hatch trains people to run -Denforcer.skip=true or hand-roll Server.createWebServer(). Deferred to EOP-34 as an addition alongside the tripwire, never a swap.

Follow-up tickets filed

  • EOP-32 — Correct the dev/test profile fiction at its source in .opencode/rules/ and re-sync the ADR index. This is where ADR-008's false consequence almost certainly originated: .opencode/rules/configuration.md:5 names three profiles, two of which have never existed, and that file is injected into every agent's context every session. Also covers .opencode/rules/caching.md:7, SETUP.md:138 (the same fiction sitting inside the accepted-risks register), the feature-flag naming drift, and two stale ADR index rows.
  • EOP-33 — Record the Spring Boot 4 autoconfiguration modularisation trap where it will actually be read. Second occurrence after spring-boot-liquibase; all four existing mentions are incident write-ups nobody consults before adding a property.
  • EOP-34 — Harden the H2 dependency surface: h2 to test scope once prod is Postgres-only, optionally ban the console autoconfiguration module. Closes the hand-registration path that no control in EOP-27 covers.

Ready for human approval and merge.

renderedFields.description:
Raised by @security-auditor during the EOP-10 review (PR #36).

The defect

GlobalExceptionHandler.handleIllegalArgument catches every IllegalArgumentException and returns exception.getMessage() in the 400 body. The javadoc justifies this on the grounds that such exceptions come only from "our own guard clauses with text written for a caller" — but that is an assumption, not an enforced invariant. IllegalArgumentException is thrown pervasively by the JDK, Hibernate, Jackson and Spring, and NumberFormatException extends it.

Two consequences:

  1. Information disclosure. Any library-internal message is echoed verbatim to the caller, potentially including internal identifiers or paths.
  2. A monitoring blind spot, which is the more interesting half. Because this handler is more specific than handleUnexpected(Exception), a fault of this kind bypasses the only LOG.error in the application. An internal defect is reported to the caller as a client-side 400 and is never logged at all.

Note this is the inverse of EOP-17. EOP-17 is two unmapped exceptions falling through to a 500 with a stack trace; this is a mapped exception producing no record whatsoever.

Latent rather than live today: the reachable {{IllegalArgumentException}}s are our own guards, and Jackson and path-variable failures surface as different types handled by the parent class. It is the absence of an invariant that is the defect.

Acceptance criteria

Scenario 1 — only our own guard failures produce a 400 with a message

Given a domain guard clause rejects caller input

When the request is handled

Then a 400 RFC 9457 problem detail carries the guard's message

Scenario 2 — a library-thrown IllegalArgumentException is not echoed

Given an IllegalArgumentException originates outside our own code

When the request is handled

Then the response carries the generic unexpected-error text, not the library message

Scenario 3 — nothing reaches the caller unlogged

Given any exception that is not a deliberate caller-input rejection

When the request is handled

Then it is logged at ERROR

Notes

Remediation is to narrow the catch to a domain-specific exception type or marker interface rather than the JDK type, and to add a LOG.warn on the branch so even legitimate rejections leave a trace.

comments.body:
*PR open and awaiting human approval: https://github.com/maglez/eop-threat-medeling/pull/111*

Branch EOP-28-narrow-illegal-argument-handler, two commits (fbef32c, 0128493).

What changed

A new org.maglez.eop.entity.InvalidInputException now marks the rejections that are genuinely a caller's to fix, and GlobalExceptionHandler maps only that type — keeping 400 and the "Invalid request" title, and adding a LOG.warn so even a legitimate rejection leaves a trace. The old @ExceptionHandler(IllegalArgumentException.class) is gone, so a library-thrown IAE (including NumberFormatException) now falls through to handleUnexpected for a generic 500 and the LOG.error it was previously denied.

It extends `IllegalArgumentException` rather than `RuntimeException`, inverting the house pattern of all 35 existing domain exceptions deliberately. The persistence adapters are @Repository beans, so Spring's translation rewrites an IAE raised while reconstituting an entity from a row into a DataAccessException — the logged 500 a corrupt row deserves. A value object cannot tell whether it is being built from a request or a row, so leaning on that already-tested mechanism is what stops a DB-derived message being echoed as a 400. Extending RuntimeException would have escaped translation and merely relocated this defect.

Scope, from a reachability audit of all 60 throw sites

Only three types had a caller-reachable guard: PageQuery (all 3 converted), DisplayName (all 3), TrickPlay (6 text guards; seatOrder left alone as an internal invariant on a credential-resolved value). Everything else stays on the bare JDK type and so correctly becomes a logged 500 rather than today's silent 400.

Worth recording: the reconstitution guards were never producing 400s — @Repository translation already caught them, pinned by three existing integration tests. The real holes were the use-case and web-layer paths.

Acceptance criteria

  • Scenario 1 — our guards → 400 with the guard's own message, now with a WARN. ✅
  • Scenario 2 — a library-thrown IAE matches no handler, falls to handleUnexpected, gets the generic text. ✅
  • Scenario 3 — rejections at WARN, faults at ERROR; nothing reaches a caller unlogged. ✅

Tests

IllegalArgumentDispatchIntegrationTest drives real Spring dispatch and asserts the contrast — a bare IAE → 500 with no message echo, an InvalidInputException → 400 with it. Only the contrast is evidence; either assertion alone would pass on the broken code. A reflection guard, shouldMapNoForeignExceptionTypeApartFromTheCatchAll, encodes the invariant whose absence was the actual defect, failing if any handler maps a type this project does not own. And 19 assertions were repointed to assertThatExceptionOfType(InvalidInputException.class) so a silent revert of a guard conversion can no longer pass.

./mvnw clean verify → BUILD SUCCESS, 1272 tests, 0 failures, SpotBugs 0, JaCoCo all checks met.

Documentation

ADR-048 records the decision and states the cost plainly: the layer a throw passes through now decides the outcome. CHANGELOG.md updated under [Unreleased] → Fixed.

Definition of Done — 5 of 5 approved

Gate Verdict
@tester-unit-and-quality APPROVE — after one REJECT, remediated in 0128493
@tester-api APPROVE
@security-auditor APPROVE — 4 LOW findings; both halves of the original EOP-10 finding confirmed closed
@code-reviewer APPROVE — 2 warnings, both since remediated
@architecture-guardian APPROVE — authored ADR-048

The rejection is worth recording rather than glossing: @tester-unit-and-quality found that the first attempt's scenario-2 and scenario-3 tests were tautological — they called handleUnexpected directly, which has always returned a generic 500, so they passed on the old code too. It also found that because the new type IS-A IllegalArgumentException, every existing assertThatIllegalArgumentException() passed whether a guard threw the new type or the bare one. @code-reviewer raised that second point independently. Both are now closed.

Known limits

  • Nothing detects the opposite mistake — a new caller-input guard written with a bare IllegalArgumentException. Enforced by review.
  • TrickPlayRepositoryAdapter.seatToWrite stays on the JDK type for an unrelated reason: converting it to an org.maglez.eop.entity type would add an eleventh origin to the set TrickPlayExceptionOriginTest derives, and its numberWord helper stops at ten.
  • No test exercises the TrickPlay seatOrder guard through HTTP dispatch to confirm it reaches the 500 branch — pre-existing, out of scope here.
  • @security-auditor's four LOW findings are not addressed here and may deserve their own ticket: a position-index oracle in TrickPlay's unsafe-text message, input-length reflection in DisplayName's over-long message, no @Min/@Max on CardController's page/size params, and unauthenticated WARN-log amplification via GET /api/v1/cards.

Leaving this In Progress until the PR is merged.

Raised by @code-reviewer and @architecture-guardian during the EOP-10 review (PR #36). Two related contract items.

Item 1 — the join endpoint returns 200 where it should return 201

SessionController.joinSession returns SessionAdmissionDto directly rather than a ResponseEntity, so Spring defaults to 200. The endpoint creates a Player resource. createSession gets this right, returning ResponseEntity.created(location).

The player has no independent URL of its own, so the appropriate Location is the session resource, {{/api/v1/sessions/

{sessionId}

}}.

Note that docs/api/openapi.yml is the authoritative contract, so check which of the two is wrong before changing the code — if the contract documents 200, decide deliberately which to change rather than assuming the code is at fault.

Item 2 — settle the @ApiResponse question, in one direction or the other

.opencode/rules/api-design.md requires @Operation and @ApiResponse on all controller methods. CardController has both. All five SessionController handlers carry @Operation and none carries @ApiResponse.

This is a genuine disagreement rather than an oversight. The SessionController class javadoc argues the case for omitting them: the contract lives in docs/api/openapi.yml, and "duplicating prose in two places is how the two come to disagree". That is a defensible position, and the hand-authored contract does specify the 403, 409 and 429 responses.

So this ticket is not "add the annotations". It is: decide, and make the codebase and the rule agree. Either

  • add @ApiResponse to the five handlers and keep the rule as it stands, or
  • amend .opencode/rules/api-design.md to record that the hand-authored contract is authoritative and @ApiResponse is not required, and then remove the annotations from CardController for consistency.

The second option is probably the better one given a hand-authored openapi.yml already exists, but it is a decision for the reviewer to take deliberately, not a default.

Acceptance criteria

Scenario 1 — creating a player returns the status code the contract specifies, with a Location header pointing at the session, and a test asserts it.

Scenario 2 — .opencode/rules/api-design.md and every controller in the codebase agree on whether @ApiResponse is required, with the reasoning recorded wherever the decision landed.

Raised by @code-reviewer during the EOP-10 review (PR #36).

The gap

.opencode/rules/observability.md requires an X-Correlation-Id request header to be placed on the MDC and to appear on every log line. Neither half exists:

  • there is no logback-spring.xml anywhere in the project, so logging is Spring Boot's default console pattern rather than structured output;
  • no Filter or HandlerInterceptor calls MDC.put.

Why it matters now rather than later

The session lifecycle is the first feature in the project where several clients act concurrently against the same server-side aggregate — three browsers joining one lobby, plus an open SSE stream per browser. Log lines from concurrent requests are currently not correlatable, which is precisely the situation where a correlation id earns its keep. Diagnosing a seat-contention retry or a heartbeat stall from interleaved unstructured lines is materially harder than it needs to be.

Note also that the application currently has only three log statements in src/main/java, so there is very little to correlate yet. Getting the plumbing in before the trick-mechanics work (EOP-14) adds more is the cheap moment.

Acceptance criteria

Scenario 1 — an inbound correlation id is honoured

Given a request arrives carrying X-Correlation-Id

When it is handled

Then every log line emitted during that request carries that value

Scenario 2 — a missing correlation id is generated

Given a request arrives with no X-Correlation-Id

When it is handled

Then one is generated, used on every log line, and returned on the response

Scenario 3 — the MDC does not leak between requests

Given a request completes

Then the MDC is cleared, so a pooled thread cannot attribute the next request's lines to the previous correlation id

Scenario 4 — output is structured

Given the application is running

Then log output is JSON with the correlation id as a field, per .opencode/rules/observability.md

Notes

Take care with the SSE endpoint: an event stream is a long-lived request, so the correlation id covers the subscription rather than each event, and the heartbeat runs on a separate sse-heartbeat scheduler thread that has no request context at all. Decide deliberately what those lines are attributed to.

renderedFields.description:
Accepted non-blocking findings from the EOP-10 review (PR #36), grouped because each is small and none justifies its own ticket. Raised across @security-auditor, @code-reviewer and @architecture-guardian.

1. IdentityTokenHash javadoc claims a constant-time comparison that does not happen

The javadoc states: "Comparison happens as an indexed database lookup rather than in Java, so there is no meaningful timing side channel in this type." That is factually wrong. The real path is ResolvePlayerUseCase → GameSession.playerByTokenHash → players.stream().filter(p -> p.isIdentifiedBy(hash)) → String.equals — a short-circuiting byte-wise comparison, in Java, in memory, over at most six players. PlayerJpaRepository's own javadoc says the opposite of the claim: "There is no method that finds a player by credential digest." The uq_player_identity_token_hash index exists but is never used as a lookup path.

Not exploitable. The attacker controls the token, not the digest, so steering digest bytes requires SHA-256 preimage work vastly exceeding a direct 256-bit guess, and six sub-microsecond comparisons are invisible behind HTTP jitter.

The risk is documentary. The comment is a false safety certificate. A future lower-entropy credential — a rejoin PIN, a short reconnect code — routed through the same method would inherit a genuine timing oracle while the comment asserts one cannot exist.

Fix the comment, and preferably switch the comparison to MessageDigest.isEqual so the claim becomes true rather than merely retracted.

2. .env.example sample passwords do not read as placeholders

Secrets hygiene is otherwise clean — verified that every .env.example value differs from the corresponding live .env value, .env is gitignored, untracked and mode 0600, and DB_USERNAME=sa with an empty password is an H2 in-memory dev default rather than a secret. The residual point is that three sample passwords read as plausible real passwords, which invites copy-paste into a real deployment. CHANGE_ME is safer.

3. Redundant capacity re-check in GameSession.join()

join() checks players.size() >= MAXIMUM_PLAYERS and throws SessionFullException. nextSeatOrder(), called immediately before by the use case, already throws the same exception for the same condition, so the check in join() is unreachable by the normal call path. It is harmless as a safety net, but the rule is stated in two places and the javadoc does not explain why. Either document it as a deliberate belt-and-braces guard or remove it.

4. SessionRepositoryAdapter.mentions() matches constraint names on exception-message substrings

mentions(throwable, constraintName) walks the cause chain doing a lower-cased contains on the exception message to decide whether a violation was uq_player_session_seat or uq_game_session_join_code. Matching on constraint name rather than exception type is the right instinct — but the integration tests run on H2 while production is PostgreSQL, so a message-format change in either engine would silently turn a retryable seat collision into a 500. Worth asserting the matching against the production engine.

5. The Graphify index is stale

163 nodes, 559 edges, top hub StrideCategoryTest, and none of the session-lifecycle classes are present. ADR-011 adopts Graphify so reviewers can reason about blast radius; on this branch it contributed nothing and the architecture review was done by direct file reads. Either re-index, or record the limitation and the re-index trigger in ADR-011.

6. ADR-014 rests on an unreproducible manual verification

docs/adr/README.md claims ADR-014 was "verified on a real socket through Caddy". SessionStreamIntegrationTest exercises the stream, but the through-Caddy observation is a one-off with no way for a future reader to re-run it. Either capture it as a scripted check or mark it explicitly as a dated manual observation.

7. Root AGENTS.md claims ui/ is not scaffolded

AGENTS.md states the front end is "not scaffolded yet" and that no ui/ directory exists. ui/ does exist, with a Caddyfile, Vite config and five source files. The accurate statement is that ui/ holds a health-check shell only, and that the sessionStorage per-tab credential custody described by ADR-015 is not built — the string sessionStorage appears nowhere in it. EOP-11 delivers that half.

Acceptance criteria

Each of the seven items is either fixed or explicitly closed with a recorded reason. None is silently dropped.

comments.body:
Item 1 is resolved by EOP-120 — the inaccurate IdentityTokenHash Javadoc is gone, and the claim it made is now true rather than merely retracted.

The comment asserted that "comparison happens as an indexed database lookup rather than in Java, so there is no meaningful timing side channel in this type". That named a mechanism the code does not contain. The real path is ResolvePlayerUseCase → GameSession.playerByTokenHash → Player.isIdentifiedBy → the record's generated equals → String.equals on hex text: a short-circuiting byte-wise comparison, in memory, over at most six players. uq_player_identity_token_hash enforces uniqueness and is never a lookup path — PlayerJpaRepository declares exactly one query method, by session id.

Rather than delete the claim, EOP-120 made it true: IdentityTokenHash now overrides equals to compare through MessageDigest.isEqual over the US-ASCII bytes of the hex value, with a matching hashCode. Verified against this JDK's own MessageDigest source that there is no early return on a length mismatch, and that the one short-circuit (lenB == 0) is unreachable given the 64-character constructor check.

Nothing exploitable was closed, and the record says so. An attacker supplies a plaintext token, not a digest, so steering the compared bytes needs SHA-256 preimage work; the token is 256 bits of SecureRandom. The defect was documentary — a future lower-entropy credential (a rejoin PIN, a short reconnect code) added to this seam would have inherited a written guarantee that was never true.

The same false claim turned out to exist at three further sites, each found by a review gate rather than by the original sweep, and all three are now corrected: PlayerJpaEntity's column Javadoc, an XML comment sitting directly above the addUniqueConstraint in 003-session-lifecycle.xml, and a residual @return the digest to store and to look up by in IdentityTokenHash itself. Liquibase Golden Rule 1 did not block the migration edit — ChangeSet.generateCheckSum() digests only changes and SQL visitors, never comments, confirmed by bytecode.

Also recorded durably, because a prohibition in a Javadoc comment is not enough (per ADR-020 and ADR-027): ADR-015 now carries an amendment stating that comparison is constant-time in memory, that no lookup path resolves a digest, and that no hash-based collection may be keyed on IdentityTokenHash or Player — a HashMap compares the cached int before calling equals, which would quietly bypass the constant-time comparison.

The other six items on this ticket are untouched and remain open.

Item 1 closed by EOP-120 — items 2–7 remain open

Item 1 (IdentityTokenHash false safety certificate) is resolved by EOP-120, merged via PR #103, merge commit c1ef080. EOP-120 is now Done.

What was actually wrong, and what changed:

  • The Javadoc claimed identity comparison was an indexed database lookup. It was not — the real path is GameSession.java:251, players.stream().filter(player -> player.isIdentifiedBy(tokenHash)).findFirst(), i.e. in Java, in memory. The comment now says so explicitly.
  • The comparison itself was String.equals, which short-circuits on the first differing byte, so the timing-safety the comment asserted was not actually being honoured. IdentityTokenHash.java:135 is now MessageDigest.isEqual(asciiBytes(), candidate.asciiBytes()) — which makes the claim true rather than merely retracting it.
  • The false claim existed at four sites, not the one this item recorded. Three were Java Javadoc; the fourth was an XML comment directly above the addUniqueConstraint in db/changelog/changes/003-session-lifecycle.xml, stating it in a stronger form than the original. The third and fourth were both found by EOP-120's review round rather than by its original implementation.
  • Locked against silent regression by IdentityTokenHashTest.java:168, which asserts the source text contains the MessageDigest.isEqual(...) call, so a revert to the generated equals fails the build.
  • Rationale recorded in ADR-015, together with a standing prohibition on keying a hash-based collection on IdentityTokenHash or Player.

This ticket stays in To Do. Per its own acceptance criterion — "Each of the seven items is either fixed or explicitly closed with a recorded reason. None is silently dropped." — the remaining six are untouched by EOP-120 and still need a disposition:

  • Item 2 — .env.example placeholder passwords
  • Item 3 — redundant capacity re-check in GameSession.join()
  • Item 4 — SessionRepositoryAdapter.mentions() matching constraint names against H2 vs PostgreSQL exception-message substrings
  • Item 5 — stale Graphify index
  • Item 6 — ADR-014's unreproducible manual verification
  • Item 7 — root AGENTS.md claiming ui/ is not scaffolded

Note on item 7: this one appears to have been overtaken by events, since the root AGENTS.md now carries a detailed ui/ section describing the shipped React + TypeScript + Vite front end. That should be confirmed against the file and closed as already-fixed with a recorded reason, rather than assumed from this comment — the acceptance criterion requires a disposition, not silence.

Closing EOP-31. All seven findings are disposed of: three fixed, four explicitly closed with a recorded reason. None silently dropped, which was this ticket's acceptance criterion.

Delivered on branch EOP-31-hygiene-sweep, commit 5330a19, parent d4deccf. Pull request 106. Five files, 43 insertions, 6 deletions: .env.example, SETUP.md, src/main/java/org/maglez/eop/entity/GameSession.java, docs/adr/README.md, CHANGELOG.md.

THE THREE FIXES

Item 2, sample passwords. Four keys now ship the literal placeholder CHANGE_ME — the Grafana admin password, the InfluxDB password, and the Postgres and datasource passwords. DB_PASSWORD is deliberately left empty and SETUP.md now says why: it pairs with the sa username against in-memory H2, and the DB_ variable set is consumed only by the default profile, which hard-pins the H2 driver. The container path uses a disjoint variable set and never receives DB_-prefixed values at all. SETUP.md also gained the instruction the template hazard actually needed, because it previously told the developer to copy the file and never to replace anything: grep the copied file for CHANGE_ME and replace every hit before starting the stack.

Item 3, the redundant capacity re-check in GameSession.join(). Kept, not removed, and documented as deliberate. The ground is the defence-in-depth rule in the repository's own security rules: an entity must hold its own invariant regardless of the sequence it happens to be called in, and a future caller that seats a player without first asking for a seat number would otherwise seat a seventh. The false half was in nextSeatOrder()'s Javadoc, whose closing sentence claimed "Keeping the capacity rule here means one place states it" — falsified by the duplicate thirty lines below it since both were written. That sentence is gone and its replacement forecloses the regression by name. No executable line changed; @security-auditor proved that by diffing comment-stripped source (identical, 165 lines each) and hashing the extracted guard lines (same SHA on both commits).

Item 6, the ADR-014 through-Caddy claim. The index row now dates the observation to 2026-08-05 under EOP-10, commit 87d8c49, and scopes it to the two events that existed then. It names what does and does not reproduce it: the stream integration test hits the application directly, ADR-035 records that no test goes through Caddy, and ADR-017's k6 smoke test does go through Caddy but not on the SSE path — verified by grepping the k6 directory for SSE, stream and event references, which returns nothing.

THE FOUR CLOSURES

Item 1 was already closed by EOP-120 and is recorded in an earlier comment here. @architecture-guardian re-verified it rather than taking it on trust: the comparison really is MessageDigest.isEqual, the corrected prose now says "that closes no known exploit" with a scoped reason, and it additionally discloses that hashCode is not constant time.

Item 4 is closed with the residual risk recorded and a follow-up filed as EOP-136. The honest fix is a real engine in the test path and there is no Testcontainers dependency anywhere — a repo-wide grep returns two hits, one of them this story's own changelog entry. The suite runs plain H2 with no PostgreSQL compatibility mode set, against PostgreSQL 17 in production, and eight test sites already mark PostgreSQL behaviour as unmeasured. Adopting a container in the test path collides with the accepted decision not to install Docker Desktop, so it needs its own ADR. EOP-136 has since been widened, on @architecture-guardian's MAJOR finding, to carry the durable record as well as the adoption.

Item 5 is closed as already resolved. The graph was re-indexed and the limitation and re-index trigger are recorded at ADR-011 line 45. One correction to my own closure, which @architecture-guardian was right to make: the graph directory is gitignored, so those node and edge counts are one machine's working directory rather than repository evidence, and the artefact's built-from commit is behind HEAD, which by line 45's own wording is the signal worth acting on rather than the documented steady state. The durable half of this disposition is the trigger at line 45; the re-index is not something a commit can carry.

Item 7 is closed as fixed by events. No "not yet scaffolded" string survives anywhere, and the root AGENTS.md now carries an accurate section describing the front end as shipped.

THREE SELF-CORRECTIONS, ALL THE SAME DEFECT CLASS THIS TICKET EXISTS TO REMOVE

First, this ticket said three sample passwords read as plausible. Measurement says two. @security-auditor independently confirmed it across all seventeen commits of the file's history: two keys held an identical opaque eighteen-character value with every character class and no placeholder marker, while the other two already held the readable phrase choose-a-strong-value. All four were normalised anyway so the must-supply set is enumerable by one token, and widening beyond the two offenders is disclosed rather than slipped in.

Second, item 6 understated its own finding. The claim had not merely gone undated — it had silently widened. Commit 43f0cbc, 2026-08-14, inserted three more events into the same sentence ahead of an unchanged Caddy clause, so a two-event observation came to read as covering five. Verified by pickaxe, which returns exactly two commits for that phrase.

Third, and worst, my own fix shipped a fresh over-attribution. The join() Javadoc claimed the check "is what makes the maximum true of every instance". EOP-136 widened to carry the H2-versus-PostgreSQL record as well as the Testcontainers adoption. EOP-138 for two measurably falsified figures in ADR-011 and its missing Amendments section. EOP-139 to qualify ADR-014's no-buffering claim, which infers a measurement from the absence of a directive, and to move the widening history out of the index row. Raised by @architecture-guardian as finding F1 during the EOP-27 review (PR #37), and called a required follow-up.

EOP-27 withdrew a false consequence from ADR-008: "H2 console available at /h2-console in dev profile for ad-hoc queries". It was wrong twice over — there was no console, and there has never been a dev profile. ADR-012 fixes the profile set at {{

{default, prod}}} and states that the container runs SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod "rather than a third local overlay profile, so local and AWS execute byte-identical configuration".

That fixed the place that repeated the error. It did not fix the places that generate it.

h2. 1. The rule files instruct the reader to use profiles that do not exist

* .opencode/rules/configuration.md:5 — "Profile convention: dev (local), test (CI), prod (production)". Two of those three have never existed. ls src/main/resources/ yields application.yml and application-prod.yml and nothing else; the test suite uses src/test/resources/application.properties, not an application-test.yml, so there is no test profile either.
* .opencode/rules/caching.md:7 — "Profile-based: disable caching in dev profile to avoid stale-data confusion during development". Unactionable for the same reason.

These are .opencode/rules/ files, injected into every agent's context on every session. configuration.md:5 is almost certainly the origin of ADR-008's false consequence in the first place. The repository now contradicts itself on a matter of fact: ADR-008 line 70 asserts "There has never been a dev profile" while a rule file three directories away teaches that dev is the convention. Left alone it will produce a third instance.

The fix is not merely to delete dev and test. State the real convention and why it is two profiles rather than three, citing ADR-012 — otherwise the next reader re-derives the three-profile habit from muscle memory.

h2. 2. SETUP.md:138 conflates the default profile with a dev profile

Inside the "Security Notes — Accepted Risks" register: "application-prod.yml disables springdoc (/v3/api-docs, /swagger-ui.html). They remain enabled in the default (dev) profile for local development." The statement about springdoc is correct; the parenthetical (dev) is the same fiction, and it is sitting in the one document that future audits are told not to re-flag findings against. Not found by the review — found while verifying F1.

h2. 3. .opencode/rules/feature-flags.md has drifted from the implemented flag convention

The rule prescribes flag names of the form ff_{feature}_v{n} under an eop.feature-flags. root. The only flag that exists is eop.features.session-lifecycle, which ADR-013 records and SessionControllerDisabledIntegrationTest pins. Either the rule or the code is wrong; since the code is shipped and reviewed, the rule should follow it. Note configuration.md:3 separately mandates the eop. root, so eop.features is compliant there.

h2. 4. The ADR index lags two rows behind the files it indexes (F4)

* docs/adr/README.md:12 shows ADR-002 as plain Accepted; the file's own status line reads Accepted (framework version superseded 2026-07-27 — see Amendments).
* docs/adr/README.md:22 shows ADR-012 as undated Accepted (amended); the file reads Accepted; *deployment target withdrawn 2026-08-10* — superseded in part by ….

The ADR-008 row updated by EOP-27 is the correct form (Accepted (amended 2026-08-10), matching the ADR-003 precedent). These two were already wrong before that change.

h2. Acceptance criteria

Scenario 1 — no document names a profile that does not exist

Given a repository-wide search for dev profile and test profile references

When the sweep is complete

Then every remaining reference is either to a profile that exists in src/main/resources/, or is an explicit historical note recording that the profile never existed.

Scenario 2 — the rule states the real convention with its reason

Given a developer or agent reading .opencode/rules/configuration.md

When they look up the profile convention

Then they read {{{default, prod}

}} and the reason it is not three profiles, with a pointer to ADR-012, so the correction survives without the ADR in hand.

Scenario 3 — the flag rule matches the shipped flag

Given .opencode/rules/feature-flags.md

When compared against eop.features.session-lifecycle and ADR-013

Then the naming convention documented is the one actually in use, or the divergence is deliberate and stated.

Scenario 4 — the ADR index agrees with every ADR status line

Given each row of docs/adr/README.md

When compared with the *Status:* line of the file it links to

Then they agree, and amendments carry a date.

Delivered and awaiting merge: PR #38 on branch EOP-32-profile-fiction-and-adr-index, commit c976c79 — 11 files, 328 insertions / 24 deletions off main = 24502a1.

What shipped

  • .opencode/rules/configuration.md now states the real profile set — exactly two, the default profile and prod, no dev and no test — and why it is two rather than three, citing the deployment-target ADR, plus what tests actually do (no profile at all; src/test/resources/application.properties overrides suite-wide).
  • .opencode/rules/caching.md and .opencode/rules/feature-flags.md no longer reference a dev profile or an application-test.yml, and SETUP.md's accepted-risk register drops its (dev) parenthetical.
  • The feature-flag rule follows the shipped code: eop.features.{kebab-case-feature} with eop.features.session-lifecycle as the worked example, replacing the ff_{feature}_v{n} form that no flag has ever used. The generator was fixed too — the Product Owner story template named ff_feature_name_v1 in its flag-strategy field and both Gherkin scenarios, so every future story would have carried a banned name.
  • docs/adr/README.md: the two stale index rows re-synced (ADR-002 with its 2026-07-27 date, ADR-012 with 2026-08-10), and step 5 narrowed so it describes what is actually enforced.
  • New AdrIndexConsistencyTest (plain JUnit, no Spring context, ~0.05s) makes the index a build-enforced invariant rather than a manual checklist step that had been drifted past twice.

Corrected in passing, all same-defect-class: two CHANGELOG inaccuracies ("H2 in dev"; "no flag exists yet"), a stale /opt/eop/.env deployment premise in an application.yml comment left over from the withdrawn EC2 target, and — found during review — .opencode/rules/database.md's Liquibase context guidance, which turned out to be actively dangerous rather than merely fictional.

Acceptance criteria

All four met. AC1: no document names a nonexistent profile except as an explicit historical note. AC2: configuration.md states the set with the reason and the ADR citation. AC3: the flag rule matches the shipped flag. AC4: every index row agrees with its file, amendments carrying dates — now machine-checked.

Sign-offs — all five obtained

  • @tester-unit-and-quality — APPROVE. Nothing at BLOCKER/MAJOR/MINOR/NIT.
  • @tester-api — APPROVE. Verified application.yml comment-only with no property value altered, and that the rewritten flag rules match SessionControllerDisabledIntegrationTest exactly.
  • @security-auditor — APPROVE. Proved application.yml semantically identical to main (comment-stripped diff, both 504 bytes, matching md5). Ran a 21-encoding runtime probe through real YAML binding to confirm the corrected Liquibase guidance closes the leak rather than narrowing it.
  • @code-reviewer — APPROVE. Verified both new database.md claims against bytecode in liquibase-core-5.0.3.jar and hibernate-core-7.4.1.Final.jar.
  • @architecture-guardian — APPROVE. Confirmed finding F1 is discharged at source rather than relocated, that the ADR corpus now agrees with itself, and that no ADR needed amending to close this story. Endorsed the test as "a textbook executable architectural fitness function".

./mvnw verify: BUILD SUCCESS, 308 tests / 0 failures / 0 errors, SpotBugs 0, JaCoCo coverage met. Two negative controls run and restored: a duplicated status line and an index row pointing at no file each failed the build with the intended message.

Worth recording honestly

This story earned three rejections before approval, all of them for the defect class it exists to remove — asserting something the repository contradicts. The replacement text for caching.md claimed "no cache dependency" when spring-boot-starter-cache sits at pom.xml:55; the Liquibase mechanism was first stated inverted (a context tag was said to suppress a changeset when in fact an unset spring.liquibase.contexts means no filtering, so it runs everywhere); and the remediation clause then failed open twice more before landing. The reviewers caught every one by probing the mechanism rather than reading the prose.

Follow-ups filed

EOP-35 (mandatory, per @architecture-guardian — move the Liquibase mechanics into an ADR, keeping the directive in the rule file), EOP-36, EOP-37, EOP-38, EOP-39, EOP-40, EOP-41, EOP-42. EOP-33 and EOP-34 remain open from the EOP-27 round.

Not transitioning to Done until PR #38 is merged.

renderedFields.description:
Raised by @architecture-guardian as question 3 during the EOP-27 review (PR #37), and by @security-auditor's independent confirmation of the same mechanism.

The trap

Spring Boot 4 modularised optional autoconfiguration out of spring-boot-autoconfigure into standalone spring-boot- modules. *A `spring.` property whose owning module is not a declared dependency is inert.* Nothing reads it, nothing binds it, nothing warns, and nothing fails. The property sits in application.yml looking authoritative and doing nothing.

This project has now been bitten twice:

  1. `LiquibaseAutoConfiguration` → `spring-boot-liquibase`. spring.liquibase.* was configured; migrations did not run. Fixed by adding the module.
  2. `H2ConsoleAutoConfiguration` → `spring-boot-h2console`. spring.h2.console.enabled: true sat in application.yml from the Walking Skeleton onward and read to two separate reviewers as a live unauthenticated SQL endpoint — including a CRITICAL finding on the EOP-10 review that @security-auditor later recanted. The property was never read by anything.

The second case cost a false CRITICAL, a story (EOP-27) to correct the record, and an ADR amendment. Both directions of the failure are expensive: a property that silently does nothing when you want it, and a property that silently promises something alarming when you do not.

Worth recording precisely because the diagnosis is not obvious from the symptom. The tell is that @ConditionalOnBooleanProperty-gated autoconfiguration is absent, not disabled, so there is nothing in the logs either way. Confirming it took a dependency:build-classpath dump, scanning every jar for the class, grepping every jar's META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports, and finally downloading spring-boot-h2console-4.1.0.jar from Maven Central and decompiling it to prove the class exists somewhere but not here.

Why the existing record is insufficient

Repository-wide, this trap currently appears in two CHANGELOG.md bullets, one ADR-008 amendment, and one comment in application.yml. All four are incident write-ups. None is reachable by somebody about to make the mistake a third time — nobody adding a spring.* property consults a changelog entry about Liquibase.

Requested

1. One line in `.opencode/rules/configuration.md` — the only location with genuine preventive leverage, because that file is loaded into every agent's context on every session. @architecture-guardian's suggested wording:

On Spring Boot 4, autoconfiguration for optional features lives in standalone spring-boot- modules. A spring. property whose owning module is not a declared dependency is inert — nothing reads it and nothing fails. Confirm the module is in pom.xml before trusting any property. Precedents: spring-boot-liquibase, spring-boot-h2console.

2. A "Framework module inventory" section in `docs/architecture/building-blocks.md` — which module autoconfigurations are present versus deliberately absent is genuinely static structure, not trivia, and it is the arc42 static view's job. It makes spring-boot-h2console a documented intentional absence rather than an oversight, and gives a reviewer somewhere to check before inferring behaviour from a property name.

Note `docs/architecture/building-blocks.md` does not exist (@architecture-guardian finding F3). docs/architecture/ currently holds only C4-Diagrams.md and runtime-view.md, though the documentation protocol mandates the arc42 static module breakdown at that path. Pre-existing debt, out of EOP-27's scope, and the reason the two follow-ups combine into one piece of work: creating the file is a prerequisite for the inventory that lives in it.

Acceptance criteria

Scenario 1 — the warning is where the mistake gets made

Given a developer or agent about to add or trust a spring.* property

When they read the configuration rules that are always in context

Then they are told that a property is inert unless its owning module is a declared dependency, and both precedents are named so the warning is credible rather than abstract.

Scenario 2 — the module inventory exists and is checkable

Given docs/architecture/building-blocks.md

When a reviewer needs to know whether a Spring Boot autoconfiguration module is on the classpath

Then the document lists the spring-boot-* modules this project declares, and separately the notable ones it deliberately does not, with the reason for each deliberate absence.

Scenario 3 — the inventory does not become the third instance of stale documentation

Given the inventory is a hand-maintained list that will drift

When it is written

Then it either records how to regenerate it (for example the dependency:build-classpath and AutoConfiguration.imports scan actually used during the EOP-27 investigation), or it is narrow enough that drift is obvious. A list that quietly goes stale reproduces the exact defect class this ticket exists to close.

renderedFields.description:
Raised by @security-auditor during the EOP-27 review (PR #37) as the one gap that story's controls do not cover, explicitly not a condition of that merge.

The residual gap EOP-27 does not close

EOP-27 pinned spring.h2.console.enabled: false in both application.yml and application-prod.yml, and added a classpath tripwire in H2ConsoleAbsentIntegrationTest that fails the build the day spring-boot-h2console appears. All three controls guard the autoconfiguration path.

None of them guards the hand-written path, and the auditor found that path is closer than the EOP-27 write-up implied. com.h2database:h2 is <scope>runtime</scope>, and h2-2.4.240.jar already ships org/h2/server/web/JakartaWebServlet.class, WebServlet.class, WebServer.class — 13 classes in org.h2.server.web — including inside the production artifact. So H2ConsoleAutoConfiguration's @ConditionalOnClass gate is already satisfied; only the autoconfig module is absent.

A console is therefore reachable today with zero dependency changes, via either:

  • new ServletRegistrationBean<>(new JakartaWebServlet(), "/h2-console") in a @Configuration class, or
  • org.h2.tools.Server.createWebServer(...).start().

The tripwire detects neither. The auditor grepped the repository for createWebServer|JakartaWebServlet|org.h2.server|org.h2.tools|ServletRegistrationBean and confirmed no such path exists, so this is future-proofing rather than a live defect — which is why it is a follow-up and not a blocker.

1. Move h2 to <scope>test</scope>

The durable control. It removes the servlet classes from the runtime artifact entirely, closing the hand-registration path rather than merely discouraging it, and it is the correct scope on the merits once production runs Postgres and H2 exists only to make the test suite hermetic.

Blocked until then. application.yml currently resolves spring.datasource.driver-class-name: org.h2.Driver on the default profile, which every local ./mvnw spring-boot:run uses, so narrowing the scope today breaks local startup. This ticket should be picked up when the datasource story lands, and it is worth confirming at that point whether the default profile also moves to Postgres or whether a runtime-scoped H2 is still genuinely needed for local development. If the latter, say so explicitly and close the scope half — an accepted risk with a recorded reason beats a ticket that lingers.

2. Optional: ban spring-boot-h2console via maven-enforcer, alongside the tripwire and not instead of it

The auditor deliberately declined to require this on EOP-27, and the reasoning constrains how it should be implemented if it is done at all:

An enforcer ban is a stronger prohibition but a weaker control. It fires at validate and cannot be argued with — but it also cannot be satisfied. The first developer who legitimately needs a console for a debugging session hits a hard wall with no path through it, and the predictable outcome is -Denforcer.skip=true, or the ban being deleted outright, or org.h2.tools.Server.createWebServer() hand-rolled in a main method to route around it. A ban with no sanctioned escape hatch trains people to disable bans.

So: bannedDependencies on org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-h2console with a documented `-D` escape hatch and a comment pointing at ADR-008, added as a second gate. The tripwire must stay — it is the control that fails legibly and points the reader at a file that explains itself, which is the property that makes the guard survive contact with someone in a hurry.

Weigh this against doing nothing: with item 1 done, the enforcer ban guards a module whose @ConditionalOnClass gate would no longer be satisfiable at runtime anyway. It may be redundant by then, and redundancy that costs a build plugin and an escape hatch to maintain is not automatically defense in depth.

Acceptance criteria

Scenario 1 — the runtime artifact carries no web console classes

Given production runs on Postgres and H2 is needed only by the test suite

When com.h2database:h2 is moved to <scope>test</scope> and the application is packaged

Then org/h2/server/web/JakartaWebServlet.class is absent from the repackaged jar, and ./mvnw verify remains green including the EOP-27 tripwire.

Scenario 2 — local development still starts, or the gap is recorded

Given a developer runs ./mvnw spring-boot:run on the default profile

When the scope has been narrowed

Then the application starts against whatever datasource the default profile now names; or, if a runtime-scoped H2 is still required for local development, the scope change is explicitly closed as won't-do with that reason recorded and this ticket's item 1 marked accordingly.

Scenario 3 — if the enforcer ban is added, it is escapable and explained

Given maven-enforcer bans spring-boot-h2console

When a developer has a legitimate reason to add it

Then the failure message names the sanctioned -D override and points at ADR-008, and the EOP-27 tripwire test is still present and still runs.

comments.body:
Delivered on branch EOP-34-h2-artifact-hardening, PR #110 (three commits: 0e28e0b, 0a744d7, 57c1974), cut from main at f1baad6. Recorded as [ADR-047|docs/adr/ADR-047-h2-excluded-from-deployable-artifact.md].

Disposition against the acceptance criteria

Scenario 1 — satisfied, but by a different mechanism than item 1 proposed. org/h2/server/web/JakartaWebServlet.class is absent from the repackaged jar, and ./mvnw verify is green including the EOP-27 tripwire. The mechanism is <excludes> on the spring-boot-maven-plugin repackage execution, not <scope>test</scope>. The criterion was written about the artifact, and the artifact is what changed.

Scenario 2 — satisfied. ./mvnw spring-boot:run on the default profile still starts against in-memory H2: /health returned 200 after 5s with Database dialect: H2Dialect and Started Main in 3.696 seconds, no errors. So the second limb of Scenario 2 — closing the scope half as won't-do — was not needed, because local development was never disturbed.

Scenario 3 — not applicable. Item 2 is declined; see below.

Item 1 — delivered in substance, not in letter

The scope stays runtime. Moving it to test would break every local ./mvnw spring-boot:run, a path pinned by README.md, SETUP.md, docs/devops/local-development.md, ADR-008, ADR-021, ADR-035 and — decisively — by ADR-012, which states the default profile path "is a decision, not a defect, and should not be 'fixed' later". Moving the default profile to PostgreSQL instead was also rejected: it destroys clone-and-run, needs an ADR-012 amendment plus four document changes, and buys hardening of a path that does not compile today (see the correction below).

Excluding H2 from the artifact instead gets the durable property the ticket wanted — the 13 org.h2.server.web classes are gone from the jar that runs on EC2, and every deployed configuration runs the prod profile against PostgreSQL, so the artifact never needed H2 — while leaving local development and all H2-dependent tests untouched. It is also independent of scope: if someone later widens the dependency to compile, the classes still cannot reach the artifact.

A correction to the ticket's premise

The ticket states a console is reachable today "with zero dependency changes" via new ServletRegistrationBean<>(new JakartaWebServlet(), "/h2-console") or org.h2.tools.Server.createWebServer(...).start(). Neither compiles. runtime scope already keeps H2 off the compile classpath — settled by writing a probe class referencing org.h2.tools.Server and compiling it, which failed with package org.h2.tools does not exist. The residual reachable path is reflection, or a second reviewed change widening the scope first. The gap was real and worth closing; it was narrower than stated, and both the ADR and the changelog say so.

Note for anyone verifying this: dependency:build-classpath -Dmdep.includeScope=compile is misleading here — it lists h2-2.4.240.jar anyway. A real compile is the only reliable check.

Item 2 — declined, with reason

No maven-enforcer ban on org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-h2console, on @security-auditor's own EOP-27 reasoning: "a ban with no sanctioned escape hatch trains people to disable bans." H2ConsoleAbsentIntegrationTest is the better control because it is satisfiable — it fires at review time and a reviewer is its escape hatch. The two controls are complementary rather than redundant: the tripwire guards the autoconfiguration path, the new gate guards the artifact. Declining also keeps the declared Maven plugin count at six. @security-auditor re-reviewed this decision on the PR and ruled it defensible.

The gate, and its honest limits

tools/artifact/assert-no-h2-in-jar.sh runs in CI's build job — the only required check on main — between ./mvnw verify and Upload artifact, so nothing unverified is published. Four checks: exactly one jar; PostgreSQL driver present as a positive control; no BOOT-INF/lib/h2-.jar; no org/h2/* entries anywhere, which catches H2 arriving flattened or under other coordinates.

Proven to fail in both directions, not just to pass: restoring main's pom.xml and repackaging makes it exit 1 with FAIL: H2 is back inside the artifact, and pointing it at an empty directory also exits 1 rather than passing vacuously.

Two accepted residuals are recorded rather than glossed:

  1. On a laptop, ./mvnw spring-boot:run still has H2 on the runtime classpath, so a reflectively-registered console remains possible locally against a scratch in-memory database. This gates the artifact, not the workstation.
  2. ./mvnw spring-boot:run and java -jar now have different classpaths. ADR-012's thesis is byte-identical configuration, which is untouched; @architecture-guardian ruled ADR-047's recording sufficient and ADR-012 not in need of amendment. The divergence is bounded to one dependency the prod profile never loads, and fails loudly rather than silently. ADR-047 carries a revisit trigger if the default profile ever gains a deployed role.

Definition of Done — all five gates approved

Gate Verdict
@security-auditor APPROVE
@code-reviewer APPROVE (re-review after remediation: 0 blockers, 0 majors, 0 mediums, 0 lows)
@architecture-guardian APPROVE
@tester-unit-and-quality APPROVE
@tester-api APPROVE

./mvnw clean verify green throughout: 1256 tests, 0 failures, 0 errors, SpotBugs 0, coverage met (96% instruction, 88% branch over 141 classes). @tester-unit-and-quality independently confirmed the suite is unaffected — runtime scope still puts H2 on the test classpath, so all the jdbc:h2:mem: migration tests and their pinned H2 SQL states are untouched — and that the EOP-27 tripwire still runs, with none of its four assertions made newly vacuous.

Two defects found during the gate round and fixed rather than accepted

@code-reviewer found the claim "no test could gate this" overstated: maven-failsafe-plugin is already available at 3.5.6 from the Boot parent and binds after package, so a failsafe IT genuinely could do it. Only surefire is blocked. Narrowed at all four sites — one of which nobody had spotted in the first round — and the failsafe alternative is now recorded with its single rejection ground (it would be a seventh declared plugin) and a revisit trigger.

Separately, an exact jar-size delta was withdrawn rather than corrected. pom.xml is embedded in the artifact under BOOT-INF/classes/META-INF/maven/, so editing a comment in it grows the jar — which falsified a figure a reviewer had already verified arithmetically. The delta was fragile by construction, since it compares jars built from different poms. Replaced with durable facts, and each site says why no exact delta is given so a future author does not restore one.

Merged and verified on `main`.

Correction to the SHAs in my previous comment. PR #109 (EOP-86) landed first, so this branch was rebased before merging and all three commits carry new SHAs. The ones I cited earlier are no longer reachable from main — not lost, just rewritten:

Cited earlier Actual on main
0e28e0b a485979
0a744d7 2dd5d00
57c1974 0279e33

Merge commit `dd4f6b6`; main moved f1baad6..dd4f6b6. Topic branch deleted.

The rebase changed nothing that was authored here. git diff 57c1974 origin/main over pom.xml, tools/artifact/, .github/workflows/ci.yml and ADR-047 is empty. Individually confirmed on main: the <excludes> is still on <execution><id>repackage</id> and was not hoisted to the plugin; tools/artifact/assert-no-h2-in-jar.sh retains mode 100755; the CI step sits immediately before Upload artifact; ADR-047 carries exactly one *Status:* line and exactly one index row; and the deliberately withdrawn fragile jar-size delta (2,685,796) appears nowhere. Both this story's and EOP-86/87's changelog entries survived the rebase.

Green on the merged tree. ./mvnw clean verify locally at dd4f6b6: 1266 tests, 0 failures, 0 errors, SpotBugs 0, coverage met. The count is 1266 rather than the 1256 quoted earlier because EOP-86/87 merged alongside and added tests; no test of this story's was lost. Gate script exits 0 with PASS.

CI on `main` green — run 32529954334, all four jobs pass (build, ui, image, supply-chain). Two things worth having on the record:

  1. The new gate step provably executed on the runner rather than being skipped. From the build job log: ok: PostgreSQL driver present (positive control) / ok: no BOOT-INF/lib/h2-.jar / ok: no org/h2/* entries. So the protection is live inside the only required check on main, and mapfile behaves on ubuntu as expected.
  2. The image job's smoke test boots the packaged, H2-free artifact against real PostgreSQL and gets OK from /health. That is the end-to-end proof that removing H2 did not break the thing that actually ships — stronger evidence than the artifact inspection alone.

Closing as Done. Item 1 is delivered in substance (H2 absent from the artifact) but not in letter (scope stays runtime); item 2 is declined with reason. Both dispositions are recorded in [ADR-047|docs/adr/ADR-047-h2-excluded-from-deployable-artifact.md], which also carries the revisit trigger should the default profile ever gain a deployed role.
