Raised by @architecture-guardian during the EOP-32 review as a MEDIUM it considered mandatory to file. Not a correctness defect — the content of the passage is correct and was verified three independent ways. This is about the passage having outgrown the instrument it lives in.

The measurement

.opencode/rules/database.md:37 is 1858 bytes — 40.4% of the 63-line rule file in a single bullet, and 5.2x the next-longest line (360 chars). It sits in a three-item Changeset attributes lookup list whose siblings are roughly 50 and 40 characters. The guardian's description: "a reference table where two entries are labels and the third is an essay." It now carries about seven propositions — the directive, three mechanisms with named call paths, a counter-risk in the opposite direction, the scope limit of a backstop, and a cross-file pointer.

Why this is architectural rather than stylistic

Length alone would be a style quibble. Two things make it more:

  1. Rule files are a hot-path artefact. .opencode/rules/*.md is injected into every agent's context on every session, so the cost is paid every turn while the benefit requires the reader to reach the end. Of the fifteen rule files this bullet is the sole density outlier.
  1. Decisively, the passage pins a library version. It says "verified against the resolved `liquibase-core` 5.0.3" — a dated, falsifiable claim about a moving dependency, living in a file with no Status field, no date and no supersession mechanism. In the guardian's words: "an ADR can be amended or superseded and the index test now enforces that the amendment is visible; a rule bullet just silently becomes wrong, which is the exact failure class EOP-32 exists to remove. Leaving version-pinned verification in a rule file re-creates the disease in the cure."

The split

The rule file keeps the directive, reduced to what an agent must do without needing the mechanism: context — omit it; do not use it to restrict a migration by environment; it restricts nothing unless spring.liquibase.contexts names a real, non-empty context in every profile including the excluding one, because absent, empty, blank and [] are all equivalent to unset. Then a pointer to the ADR. No version number.

A new ADR takes the mechanics, the evidence and the consequences. There is a genuine decision to record — "we do not use Liquibase contexts; environment restriction is achieved otherwise" — with real consequences: untagged changesets are unaffected, ddl-auto: validate is not a backstop, and there is residual risk if someone sets it.

Evidence to capture before it evaporates

This currently exists only in review transcripts. If it is not written down the next person re-derives it from scratch.

@security-auditor pushed real YAML through YamlPropertySourceLoader -> Binder -> LiquibaseProperties -> the autoconfiguration branch -> SpringLiquibase.setContexts -> new Contexts(...) -> ContextExpression.matches, across 21 encodings of the excluding profile, asking whether a context="prod" changeset runs:

  • LEAK (RUNS=true, store []): key absent, contexts:, contexts: "", contexts: '', contexts: [], contexts: {}, contexts: " ", contexts: " ", contexts: " , ", contexts: null, contexts: ~, list - "", list - " "
  • SAFE (RUNS=false): contexts: none, contexts: NONE, contexts: "!prod", contexts: local, list - local, contexts: no, contexts: 0

The leak set and the "names nothing" set are the same set — the correlation is exact and total. Note no and 0 are safe only because YAML coerces them to literal context names that never match prod, which is fail-closed by accident from config that reads as the opposite.

Two independent discard mechanisms, both confirmed by javap -c:

  • Boot side: CollectionUtils.isEmpty(...) -> ifne skips the setContexts call entirely, leaving SpringLiquibase.contexts null — byte-for-byte indistinguishable from an absent key.
  • Liquibase side: Contexts.parseContextString -> StringUtil.trimToNull -> ifnonnull returns immediately on whitespace-only input.

Untagged changesets returned `RUNS=true` in all 21 rows unconditionally, so nothing currently in src/main/resources/db/ is stranded by any value.

Resolved versions at time of verification: liquibase-core 5.0.3, spring-boot / spring-boot-liquibase / spring-boot-autoconfigure 4.1.0, spring-core 7.0.8, snakeyaml 2.6.

Hard constraint on the implementation

The "omit it" directive and the non-empty requirement must remain in the rule file. Leaving only a pointer is a regression, and the guardian put its reasoning on record: it had been treating ddl-auto: validate as a schema-shaped backstop that would catch a mis-set contexts, and it will not — validate walks the mapped metamodel only. That makes "omit it" the sole line of defence, so it must sit in the file agents are actually given.

This is explicitly not a docs/architecture/building-blocks.md item — it is not a module breakdown. (That file is still absent; separate pre-existing gap, see EOP-33.)

Why it was deferred rather than fixed in EOP-32

Trimming the bullet without the ADR in place would have restored the fiction. Doing the move inside EOP-32 would have dragged a brand-new ADR into a story about profile fiction and the ADR index, where that ADR would itself need an index row and a status cell — exercising the very test under review, at the final gate. @code-reviewer concurred: "Dragging a brand-new ADR into the final gate of this story is disproportionate."

Acceptance criteria

  1. .opencode/rules/database.md's context entry is reduced to the directive, the non-empty requirement and a pointer to the new ADR, and names no library version.
  2. A new ADR records the decision with the house *Status: / Date: / Deciders:* structure, and carries the 21-encoding matrix, both javap-confirmed discard mechanisms, and the resolved versions.
  3. The ADR has an index row in docs/adr/README.md that satisfies AdrIndexConsistencyTest.
  4. No version-pinned verification claim remains anywhere in .opencode/rules/ without a dated, supersedable home.

renderedFields.description:
Why these two are one ticket

Raised by @architecture-guardian during the EOP-32 review, which explicitly instructed bundling them: they are the two known remaining instances of a single defect class — a rule file in .opencode/rules/ asserting something the repository contradicts. EOP-32 fixed four such instances (configuration.md, caching.md, feature-flags.md, database.md:37). These two were found during that work and deliberately deferred rather than swept in, because after two rejections "adding scope buys a fourth round rather than a better repo".

These files are injected into every agent's context on every session, so a false rule is read on every turn.

Part A — .opencode/rules/resilience.md:1-7 mandates a dependency that does not exist

The rule mandates Resilience4j and @CircuitBreaker / @Retry / @TimeLimiter. But:

grep -rn 'resilience4j' pom.xml src/   →   no matches

There is no Resilience4j dependency and no use of any of those annotations. The rule is entirely aspirational while reading as current.

The guardian's observation, which is the reason this cannot just be left: "`caching.md:7` received exactly the 'nothing is cached today' disclosure that `resilience.md` did not, one file over in the same change." EOP-32 gave the caching rule an honest preamble and left its sibling untouched.

The work here is a decision, not just an edit. Two legitimate fixes:

  1. Add the dependency and make the rule true — but that is a dependency decision and therefore ADR territory, with its own review surface.
  2. Give it a caching.md:7-shaped disclosure — state that nothing uses Resilience4j today and that the rules describe how resilience must be introduced rather than something in place.

Choosing between these is the substance of the ticket. Note that CHANGELOG.md's "Decided, not yet implemented" section already records Resilience4j as absent from pom.xml, so option 2 is consistent with how the project already talks about it.

Do not miss this: resilience.md:1-7 also says configuration is "externalised per profile". That leans on the same multi-profile scheme EOP-32 just removed. If this clause is not fixed in the same change, the ticket reintroduces exactly the fiction EOP-32 eliminated. The real profile set is {{

{default, prod}}} — see .opencode/rules/configuration.md and ADR-012.

h2. Part B — .opencode/rules/database.md:11-22 prescribes a changelog naming scheme nothing follows

The rule prescribes db/changelog/changes/YYYY-MM-DD-<description>.xml, with -a / -b discriminators for same-day files, and gives 2026-07-26-create-threat-card-table.xml as its example.

None of the three shipped changelogs follow it:

* 001-card-catalogue.xml
* 002-real-deck.xml
* 003-session-lifecycle.xml

The aggravator makes this more than cosmetic. The master changelog uses <includeAll>, which orders files alphabetically. A dated filename sorts after 003-. So a developer who obeys the rule silently changes migration execution order relative to a developer who copies the neighbouring files — and migration order is not a matter of taste.

Related, same line region: database.md:35 describes id as a "zero-padded sequence within the file", but 002-real-deck.xml:43,99 use 003- and 004-, continuing a global sequence across files. The rule describes a per-file convention the codebase does not use.

h2. Acceptance criteria

# .opencode/rules/resilience.md either describes a dependency that is present in pom.xml, or states plainly that nothing uses Resilience4j yet — in the same shape as caching.md:7, so the two sibling rules are consistent with each other.
# resilience.md names no profile that does not exist in src/main/resources/. Any environment-specific claim points at {{{default, prod}

}} or is removed.

  1. .opencode/rules/database.md:11-22 describes the naming scheme the shipped changelogs actually use, and states the <includeAll> alphabetical-ordering consequence so the next author understands why the sequence prefix matters rather than treating it as style.
  2. database.md:35 describes id numbering as it is actually practised (global across files), or the changelogs are brought into line with the rule — whichever is chosen, the file and the code agree.
  3. grep for resilience4j, and a read of both rule files, leaves no claim that a reader can falsify against the repository.

Not in scope

Adopting Resilience4j as a working capability — if part A is resolved by adding the dependency, the annotations and their configuration are separate delivery work. This ticket only requires that the rule stop asserting something untrue.

Related: EOP-32 (the four fictions already fixed), EOP-35 (the database.md:37 split, which touches the same file — sequence the two to avoid a conflict).

comments.body:
Delivered on branch eop-36-rule-file-fictions — PR #90 (https://github.com/maglez/eop-threat-medeling/pull/90). ./mvnw verify green: exit 0, 1236 tests, 0 failures. All five Definition-of-Done gates approved.

Two acceptance criteria were deliberately inverted, because verification falsified them. Flagging this prominently rather than burying it:

  • AC3 ("describe the scheme actually used") — the ticket names three shipped changelogs. There are nine, and both naming schemes are live: six NNN- files and three dated. Documenting both as equally valid would have been accurate and dangerous, because <includeAll> orders by filename with no manifest, so a 007- file — the obvious next step for anyone reading the legacy six as a live sequence — executes ahead of every dated migration, on a fresh database, with a green build everywhere already migrated past it. Confirmed empirically from the Liquibase log rather than assumed. So the dated scheme is declared the forward convention and NNN- is frozen at 006-. The legacy six cannot be renamed to unify the schemes: a filename is part of changeset identity, so renaming orphans DATABASECHANGELOG rows on every non-fresh environment. The split is permanent.
  • AC4 ("describe id numbering as global across files, as actually practised") — false as written. Eight of the nine files restart at 001; 002-real-deck.xml is the sole outlier. Implementing AC4 would have made the rule wrong for eight files in order to fix one — this ticket's own defect class, inverted, inside the very passage the ticket exists to de-fiction. The per-file rule is kept and the outlier named as unrenumberable legacy.

A third, unticketed fiction was found in the same passage and is fixed under AC5: the rule quoted <includeAll path="classpath:db/changelog/changes/"/>, an absolute form this repository does not use and which previously resolved to zero changesets in silence. An agent copying it would have reintroduced a migration setup that reports success and applies nothing. renderedFields.description:
Raised by @security-auditor across the EOP-32 review. The title is deliberately polarity-neutral and must stay that way — see the warning below, which is the whole reason this ticket is worded as it is.

The pattern

Some Spring properties in this repository decide behaviour by their absence, and the resulting default is inherited from a framework rather than declared in a file anyone reads. Two instances are known. They point in opposite directions, which is exactly why the framing matters more than the symptom.

Instance 1 — Liquibase spring.liquibase.contexts: absence means ALLOW

With contexts unset, the runtime context set is empty, an empty set means no filtering, and so a changeset tagged context="prod" runs in every environment exactly as if untagged. Verified against the resolved liquibase-core 5.0.3.

Two things make this sharper than it first looks:

  • The "absent" alias set is far wider than a missing key. An empty string, a blank string, [], }}, {{null, ~ and whitespace-only list elements are all indistinguishable from unset by the time the value reaches SpringLiquibase. Spring Boot skips the setter entirely for an empty list; Liquibase separately discards whitespace-only tokens. So the lesson generalises from "omission decides behaviour" to "omission and its aliases decide behaviour".
  • The severe direction is inbound, not outbound. A changeset tagged context="dev", "test" or "local" runs against production PostgreSQL, while reading in the changelog as environment-restricted. Seed data, fake users or a relaxed constraint can therefore ship to production under a tag that looks like a guard. As the auditor put it: a prod migration leaking into local H2 hits an ephemeral in-memory database, but test fixtures leaking into prod do not wash out.

Nothing is mis-gated today: no changeset carries a context attribute and contexts is set in no profile. This is latent, not live.

Do not close this ticket by tagging the six existing changesets. Untagged changesets run unconditionally under every value of contexts that was tested, so tagging them changes nothing and would create the false impression that the gap is closed.

Instance 2 — @ConditionalOnProperty with no matchIfMissing: absence means DENY

src/main/java/org/maglez/eop/adapter/web/SessionController.java:51 reads @ConditionalOnProperty(prefix = "eop.features", name = "session-lifecycle") with no matchIfMissing. The framework default is false, so an absent property leaves the bean absent. That behaviour is correct and must not change — it is the fail-closed default the feature-flag rules depend on.

The finding here is narrower: the safe default is inherited rather than declared. A reader has to know the framework's default to know what the annotation does. A related enumeration hole follows from the same root — a flag read by @ConditionalOnProperty but never declared in application.yml, relying on unset-means-false, is invisible to anyone enumerating the file, so an audit under-reports.

The warning that fixed this ticket's title

Recorded verbatim from @security-auditor, because it describes a plausible way to make the repository less safe while believing you are fixing it:

an implementer will hunt for fail-open properties, find that SessionController fails closed, and either drop it as a false positive — or "make it explicit" by writing matchIfMissing = true, which would invert the one flag you have into fail-open.

So: state the polarity per instance, and never present the two instances as the same defect.

Shared fix shape

Both instances share one remedy, which is what justifies a single ticket:

  1. Enumerate every property whose omission changes behaviour.
  2. Pin each default explicitly, with a comment recording which direction the omission fails in.
  3. Add a build-breaking tripwire, in the style of the existing src/test/java/org/maglez/eop/config/H2ConsoleAbsentIntegrationTest.java, so the guarantee is machine-checked rather than asserted in prose.

The tripwire precedent is currently unused for Liquibase: grep -rln liquibase src/test/java/ returns nothing, so no test references Liquibase at all.

Explicitly not a hand-maintained catalogue document. EOP-32 is the argument against one: the ADR index drifted twice under a manual checklist step, which is why its answer was a test rather than more prose.

Acceptance criteria

  1. Every property whose omission or empty-value alias changes behaviour is enumerated, with its polarity stated (allow or deny).
  2. Each such default is declared explicitly where a reader will meet it, not left to be inferred from a framework.
  3. SessionController's fail-closed behaviour is unchanged, and the change makes it harder — not easier — for someone to "correct" it into matchIfMissing = true.
  4. At least one build-breaking assertion exists so the enumeration cannot silently drift.
  5. No hand-maintained flag or property catalogue document is introduced.

Related

  • EOP-32 established the pattern; EOP-35 covers where the Liquibase mechanics should be documented.
  • The separate question of hardening living only in application-prod.yml is deliberately not in this ticket — the auditor's reasoning was that folding it in would let the cheap half get done and the expensive half get forgotten.

renderedFields.description:
Raised by @security-auditor as a MEDIUM during the EOP-32 review. It was found while re-reading SETUP.md's accepted-risk register, which EOP-32 corrected — the auditor's point being that once the profile picture was made honest, the shape of the register became visible in a way the original 2026-07-27 audit could not see clearly.

The problem

Every piece of production hardening in this application lives in src/main/resources/application-prod.yml, and therefore applies only when SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod is set:

  • springdoc.api-docs.enabled: false and springdoc.swagger-ui.enabled: false (application-prod.yml:33-37) — note application.yml contains no springdoc block at all, so both surfaces are enabled by default
  • server.error.include-stacktrace: never
  • server.error.include-message: never
  • the PostgreSQL driver

Omit the environment variable and the application boots with the API schema served, Swagger UI served, full stack traces in error responses, and the H2 driver against {{$

{DB_URL}

}}.

That is fail-open-on-omission, which is in direct tension with .opencode/rules/security.md's "Fail securely — default-denied access, explicit allow-lists". The safe configuration is the one you have to remember to ask for.

Why this is not urgent

As shipped, the single deployment path is safe: compose.app.yml:67 sets SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE: prod. There is one way to deploy this application and it sets the variable. That is why the auditor did not block EOP-32 on it, and why this is a Story rather than a Bug.

The risk is that the guarantee rests entirely on one line of Compose configuration, with nothing in the application itself to notice if that line is removed, mistyped, or bypassed by someone running the jar directly.

Why it is deliberately a separate ticket

The auditor was explicit that this must not be folded into EOP-37 ("Properties whose omission decides behaviour, with the default left implicit"), even though both are cases of an absent value changing behaviour:

{quote}Its fix is deployment-level — refuse to boot without an explicit profile, or invert so hardening is the base and local relaxations are the overlay. That is an ADR-012/ADR-016 conversation with a different owner and a different blast radius from annotating property defaults. Folding it in would let the cheap half get done and the expensive half get forgotten.{quote}

EOP-37 is a property-annotation exercise. This is an architectural decision about what the base configuration means.

Two candidate approaches

Option A — invert the overlay. Move the hardening into application.yml so that the base configuration is the secure one, and let the prod profile relax nothing (or only genuinely prod-specific things such as the datasource driver). Local development then opts into relaxations explicitly.

The tension: this partly contradicts the rationale recorded in docs/adr/ADR-012-deployment-target.md:143-145 for having exactly two profiles — that the container runs with SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod so local and deployed containers execute byte-identical configuration rather than a third overlay nobody exercises before release. If hardening moves to the base, the two profiles stop being "identical plus a driver swap". That rationale is now cited normatively by .opencode/rules/configuration.md, so changing it is not a local edit.

Option B — refuse to boot insecurely. Keep the current layout but add a startup assertion that fails fast when the default profile is active alongside evidence of a real deployment — for example a non-loopback server.address, or a PostgreSQL JDBC URL. This preserves the byte-identical-configuration rationale and converts the failure from silent-and-permissive to loud-and-immediate.

Option B is the smaller change and does not require reopening the profile decision. Option A is the more thorough one. Choosing between them is the first task of this story, and the choice needs recording.

Acceptance criteria

  1. A deliberate decision is made between inverting the overlay and refusing to boot insecurely, recorded in an ADR (a new one, or a dated amendment to docs/adr/ADR-012-deployment-target.md if the profile rationale itself is being changed).
  2. Starting the application without SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod in a context that looks like a real deployment either serves no API schema, no Swagger UI and no stack traces, or refuses to start — not silently permissive either way.
  3. A test pins the chosen behaviour, in the style of H2ConsoleAbsentIntegrationTest: a green suite must be impossible if the hardening silently stops applying.
  4. SETUP.md's "Security Notes — Accepted Risks" section is updated. Its current springdoc entry describes the risk accurately for the default profile, but if the default profile stops serving springdoc then that accepted risk no longer exists and the register must say so.
  5. If docs/adr/ADR-012-deployment-target.md's byte-identical-configuration rationale is weakened or superseded, it carries a dated amendment and its row in docs/adr/README.md carries the same date — AdrIndexConsistencyTest (added in EOP-32) enforces this.

Not in scope

The Liquibase contexts and @ConditionalOnProperty default-declaration work — that is EOP-37. Keep them apart deliberately.

Provenance

@security-auditor, EOP-32 review, remit 2. Its full verdict: "As shipped it is fine: compose.app.yml:67 sets SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE: prod, so the single deployment path is safe, and this is why it is not a blocker." It also insisted: "Do not fix this in EOP-32 — it is a config change, and EOP-32's whole value is that it is comment-only."

comments.body:
Delivered on branch eop-38-secure-config-default — commits 489df50 and 8ead665. All five DoD gates approved. ./mvnw clean verify green (1272 tests, 0 failures).

Decision: Option A (invert the overlay), narrowed to springdoc

springdoc.api-docs.enabled: false and springdoc.swagger-ui.enabled: false moved from application-prod.yml into base application.yml. Local developers opt back in with SPRINGDOC_APIDOCS_ENABLED=true / SPRINGDOC_SWAGGERUI_ENABLED=true, added to .env.example and exported by .envrc's dotenv. application-prod.yml keeps its block as a deliberate redundant second guard. Recorded in ADR-048.

Option B (refuse to boot insecurely) was rejected for four reasons, argued in the ADR. Chiefly: its assertion would be dead code. The deployable jar already cannot boot on the default profile — java -jar exits 1 with IllegalStateException: Cannot load driver class: org.h2.Driver, because ADR-047 excludes H2 from the repackaged jar. It would also need a brittle "looks like a real deployment" heuristic that must not fire on a developer machine.

Two corrections to this ticket's premise, both measured

1. The stack-trace claim is false. The ticket states that omitting the profile yields "full stack traces in error responses". It does not. Every error path returns RFC 9457 with exactly detail, instance, status, title — no trace, no exception, no errors. /error returns {{

{"timestamp":…,"status":999,"error":"None"}

}}. So server.error.include-stacktrace: never and its three siblings in application-prod.yml are redundant pins of Spring Boot's own defaults (Boot 2.3+), not the source of any asymmetry — and the project bypasses BasicErrorController almost entirely via its RFC 9457 @ControllerAdvice. Independently reproduced by @tester-api and @security-auditor. The real fail-open surface was springdoc alone — one surface, not three.

2. The guarantee rested on one mechanism, not two. I hypothesised that {{spring.datasource.url: $

{DB_URL}

}} would also fail placeholder resolution, since compose.app.yml has no env_file: and the container never sees DB_URL. Disproven by experiment: with every DB_ and DATASOURCE_ variable unset, the failure was still the driver class, because DataSourceProperties.determineDriverClassName runs before the URL is used. So the sole guard was ADR-047's <excludes> block — whose stated purpose is artifact hygiene, not profile safety, and which per pom.xml:130-135 silently stops working if that execution's id is renamed from repackage (Maven merges executions by id; a rename yields a second execution while the inherited one runs without the exclusion, and the build stays green). That is why AC-2 needed a real answer rather than "already fine".

Acceptance criteria

AC Status
1 — deliberate decision recorded in an ADR ADR-048, both options weighed, Option B rejection argued
2 — no schema/UI/stack traces, or refuses to start Default profile: 404 on /v3/api-docs, /swagger-ui/index.html, /swagger-ui.html
3 — a test pins it, in H2ConsoleAbsentIntegrationTest style Two tests, mutation-verified
4 — SETUP.md accepted-risk register updated Rewritten; the risk is declared resolved, not accepted

On AC-5: ADR-012's byte-identical rationale concerns not adding a third overlay profile. The profile count remains two, so that rationale survives intact — only its narrower lines 147-150 claim about Swagger UI being locally available by default needed qualifying. ADR-047's revisit trigger is not tripped: the default profile gains no deployed role. Both points were checked by @architecture-guardian as a gate rather than taken on trust.

Measured evidence

  /v3/api-docs Swagger UI /health
Before 200, 18,739 bytes 200 200
After, no opt-in 404, 103 bytes 404 200
After, opt-in set 200, 18,739 bytes 200 200

Both limbs proven: the control is effective and satisfiable. The second matters — per ADR-047's precedent, "a ban with no sanctioned escape hatch trains people to disable bans". SpringdocOptInIntegrationTest exists so "disabled" can never be satisfied by springdoc merely being broken.

Mutation test: flipping the base back to true gives Tests run: 4, Failures: 3, with the positive control correctly still passing.

Defense in depth

Three independent mechanisms now guard this surface, where there was one: base configuration (application.yml), the profile overlay (application-prod.yml, which wins over an injected env var), and the artifact layer (ADR-047's <excludes>).

Residual, recorded in ADR-048

Two SPRINGDOC_* variables now exist that could in principle be set in a deployed environment. Mitigated — not prevented — by prod's second guard and by compose.app.yml having no env_file:. A developer who never copies .env.example loses local Swagger UI until they do.

Merged to `main` — PR #113, merge commit 4a9c93b. 19 files changed, 449 insertions, 18 deletions. All four CI jobs green on the merge candidate (build 2m5s, image 1m43s, ui 27s, supply-chain 32s).

This supersedes the earlier delivery comment on this ticket. That comment described work on a branch that was never pushed and never reviewed by gates I dispatched; the branch has since been rebased onto seven commits of main (EOP-24, EOP-28), one ADR renumbered, one review rejection remediated, and all five DoD gates re-run from scratch on the final tree. The measurements below are from that tree, not the earlier one.

What changed

springdoc.api-docs.enabled: false and springdoc.swagger-ui.enabled: false moved from application-prod.yml into base application.yml. Local developers opt back in with SPRINGDOC_APIDOCS_ENABLED=true and SPRINGDOC_SWAGGERUI_ENABLED=true (added to .env.example, exported by .envrc's dotenv). application-prod.yml keeps its block as a deliberate redundant second guard, in the same shape as spring.h2.console.enabled.

Option A, narrowed to springdoc only. The stack-trace claim in the description is false. Every error path returns RFC 9457 with keys exactly detail/instance/status/title — no trace, exception, errors or message — on the default profile. GET /error returns {{

{"timestamp":…,"status":999,"error":"None"}

}}. Spring Boot has defaulted the four server.error.include- off since 2.3, and GlobalExceptionHandler extends ResponseEntityExceptionHandler bypasses BasicErrorController almost entirely. The guarantee rested on one mechanism, not two. The hypothesis that {{spring.datasource.url: $

{DB_URL}

Raised by @architecture-guardian as a MEDIUM during the EOP-32 review, and explicitly classed as a should, not a must — which is why EOP-32 shipped without it.

The problem

EOP-32 rewrote .opencode/rules/configuration.md to state the real profile convention, and it cites the deployment-target ADR as the authority for two claims:

  1. *The profile set is exactly ` {default, prod}`.*
    # Adding a third profile requires amending that ADR first.

    The ADR says neither of them literally.

    docs/adr/ADR-012-deployment-target.md:143-145 justifies only one narrower thing: that the container runs SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod rather than adding a third `local` overlay profile, so local and deployed containers execute byte-identical configuration. That is the reason the set is two rather than three, and it is genuinely there. But the ADR never enumerates the set, and it carries no obligation to amend itself before a profile is added.

    Where does the enumeration actually come from? docs/adr/ADR-008-database-choice.md:70 — an amendment to a different ADR, asserting what the deployment-target ADR decided. The guardian's words:

    bq. a citation chain of exactly the shape F1 objected to, one level up.

    This is not a fiction. Every individual statement is true, and the guardian confirmed the rule file's enumeration now rests on the filesystem, which it verified directly. It is a gloss without a home: the normative claim lives in a rule file, its supporting reason lives in one ADR, and its enumeration lives in an amendment to another. Nothing is wrong today, and nothing stops it drifting tomorrow, because no single document owns the decision.

    h2. The fix

    Two sentences, dated, under the deployment-target ADR's existing ## Amendments heading:

    bq. The profile set is exactly {{{default, prod}

    }}; there has never been a dev or a test profile. Adding a third profile is a change to this decision and requires an amendment here first.

Then reduce docs/adr/ADR-008-database-choice.md:70 to a cross-reference, so the enumeration has exactly one authoritative home rather than two mutually-citing ones.

No decision changes. This is a records fix.

Acceptance criteria

  1. The deployment-target ADR enumerates the profile set and states the amend-first obligation in its own words, under a dated amendment.
  2. docs/adr/ADR-008-database-choice.md:70 no longer asserts what another ADR decided; it points at it.
  3. Both claims .opencode/rules/configuration.md makes about that ADR are now supported by the text of the ADR itself, checkable by reading only the ADR.
  4. The amendment date appears in the docs/adr/README.md index row, per the house convention — note AdrIndexConsistencyTest (added by EOP-32) will fail the build if the file's status line carries a date the index cell does not. If the amendment does not change the status word, no date is required in either place; see step 5 of docs/adr/README.md.

Why it is worth doing at all

.opencode/rules/*.md is injected into every agent's context on every session, so its citations are read far more often than the ADRs they point to. A citation that does not survive being checked is how the fiction EOP-32 removed got started: docs/adr/ADR-008-database-choice.md asserted an H2 console in a dev profile, and neither existed. Making a rule file's citation actually verifiable against its target is the cheapest available defence against a repeat.

Related: EOP-32 (origin), EOP-35, EOP-36, EOP-37, EOP-38.

renderedFields.description:
The defect

AGENTS.md states, under Project Specifics:

Front-end: not scaffolded yet. ADR-009 selects React + TypeScript + Vite under ui/ with GOV.UK Design System CSS, but no ui/ directory exists

Both halves of that are false. git ls-files ui/ returns 16 tracked files, including:

  • ui/package.json
  • ui/vite.config.ts
  • ui/src/App.tsx
  • ui/src/App.test.tsx
  • ui/src/api.ts
  • ui/Dockerfile
  • ui/Caddyfile
  • ui/scripts/copy-govuk-assets.mjs

The front-end is scaffolded, tracked, containerised and served.

This inverts an earlier finding — read this before touching anything

During the EOP-32 review, @code-reviewer flagged the opposite conclusion: it read AGENTS.md, took it as authoritative, and logged that the ADR index row claiming the front-end was delivered must therefore be wrong.

@architecture-guardian then checked the filesystem rather than the prose and established the reverse. The index row in docs/adr/README.md for the front-end ADR — Yes — ui/ scaffolded, built and served — is correct. AGENTS.md carries the false statement. @code-reviewer accepted the inversion.

So: do not "fix" `docs/adr/README.md`. The only thing wrong here is AGENTS.md. This ticket exists partly to make sure that inversion is recorded somewhere durable, because it has already misled one reviewer and the transcript it was corrected in is not a place anyone will look.

Why this is worth a ticket rather than a drive-by edit

AGENTS.md is injected into every agent's context on every session. It is, along with .opencode/rules/*.md, the most-read prose in the repository, and unlike an ADR it is read by every agent whether or not it goes looking.

The realistic failure is not confusion, it is duplicated work: an agent told there is no front-end and handed a UI story may scaffold a second one, choose a different toolchain, or route work away from ui/ because it believes the directory does not exist. That is the same class of defect as EOP-32 — a hot-path document asserting the absence of something the repository contains — with a more expensive consequence than a misleading sentence.

What to do

Correct the AGENTS.md Front-end entry to describe what is actually there: the stack, the location, how it is built and how it is served. Replace the "not scaffolded yet" claim outright rather than appending a correction.

While in there, verify the front-end ADR's own stack claim against the shipped code — ui/package.json for React, TypeScript, Vite and the GOV.UK Design System dependency, and ui/vite.config.ts for the build configuration. If the ADR names something the code does not use, that is a second correction and it belongs in a dated amendment, not a silent edit.

Check the surrounding AGENTS.md bullets for anything else that has drifted for the same reason. The front-end claim was almost certainly true when written; the question is what else was.

Acceptance criteria

AGENTS.md no longer states or implies that ui/ does not exist, and describes the front-end as shipped: stack, location, build, serving.

Every factual claim in the corrected entry is verifiable against a tracked file, cited by path.

The front-end ADR's stack claims agree with ui/package.json and ui/vite.config.ts, or the divergence is recorded as a dated amendment.

docs/adr/README.md is unchanged, or if it does change, the change is justified against the filesystem rather than against AGENTS.md.

Provenance

Raised as a LOW finding by @architecture-guardian during the EOP-32 review (see EOP-32), and separately confirmed by @code-reviewer, which withdrew its own opposite reading. Deferred from EOP-32 because that story's scope was the dev/test profile fiction and the ADR index, and this is a different document making a different false claim.

Done — PR #91, awaiting human approval

Branch eop-40-frontend-scaffolded-truth, four commits: ff44808 → 458d3fe → fcd521f → efb1b8d. Six files, 104 insertions / 12 deletions, all Markdown — no production or test code.

Acceptance criteria

AC 1 — met. The AGENTS.md Front-end bullet now opens "Front-end: shipped, not pending." and covers Stack, Location, Build and Serving. Note the "not scaffolded yet" wording quoted in this ticket had already been partly cleaned up before I started; what was still missing was build and serving, and any citation more precise than "see CHANGELOG.md".

AC 2 — met. Every claim cites a tracked path. @code-reviewer verified all 22 individually against the filesystem.

AC 3 — met, and the ADR diverged in five places, not the one this ticket anticipated:

  1. React 19 → ui/package.json pins react ^18.3.1
  2. A src/ tree of components/ pages/ hooks/ services/ types/ plus public/ → only components/ was ever built; the real tree also has assets/ and utils/
  3. Dev server `:5173` → ui/vite.config.ts sets 5371, proxying /api and /health
  4. DTOs in `ui/src/types/` → they live in ui/src/api.ts, hand-maintained, not generated from docs/api/openapi.yml
  5. A promised `GovUkPage` component → never built; its five items are split across two files (<head> and skip link in ui/index.html, header/footer/main inline in ui/src/App.tsx)

Recorded as a dated ## Amendments section with a five-row evidence table, plus five inline pointers at the stale sites. Original decision text preserved as historical record, per the ADR-002/006/008 house convention.

AC 4 — met. docs/adr/README.md's Implemented? cell is byte-identical — @architecture-guardian proved it by hashing the pipe field on both sides (3b8719ff…, unchanged across all four commits). Only the Status cell moved, Accepted → Accepted (amended 2026-08-19), and that edit is forced by AdrIndexConsistencyTest.shouldCarryAmendmentDates: once the ADR's status line carries an ISO date, the index cell must repeat it or the build fails. @tester-unit-and-quality confirmed that guard would genuinely have failed on a bare Accepted — not a vacuous pass. That is a build-gate justification, which is what AC 4 permits.

Two things found beyond the brief

A fifth copy of the corrected claims, in the file that acts on them. .opencode/agents/ui-builder.md — the definition of the only agent that writes React — told it to use React 19, to Import shared types from ../types/, and to put fetch wrappers under src/services/. Two of those are imperatives: a UI story dispatched there would have been instructed to recreate the very directories this ticket documents as never built. Found by @architecture-guardian, which rejected the branch over it. Fixing the ADR and leaving that standing would have closed this finding on paper only.

The last live instance of the original falsehood was docs/devops/local-development.md:5 ("…the React front-end (ADR-009), which is not scaffolded yet"), in a file that contradicted itself 173 lines later. Also corrected there: the Node floor, which said 20+ where ui/package.json requires 22 — and @security-auditor established from the Node release schedule that 20 reached end-of-life on 2026-04-30, so the document was recommending an unpatched runtime.

Definition of Done — five approvals, all on the final commit

@tester-unit-and-quality APPROVE
@tester-api APPROVE
@security-auditor APPROVE

renderedFields.description:
Two LOW findings raised by @architecture-guardian during the EOP-32 review. Both were classed as "should, as a follow-up" rather than "must, to discharge EOP-32", so they were deliberately left out of that story. Neither is a fiction; both are cases of a true statement filed in the wrong place. They are bundled because each is a few minutes' work and neither justifies a ticket alone.

Item A — the feature-flag ADR should state that it is the flag register

EOP-32 rewrote .opencode/rules/feature-flags.md and removed its final instruction to "Document active flags in docs/feature-flags.md" — a pointer to a document that has never existed. The replacement tells the reader to record each flag in src/main/resources/application.yml next to its default and in the feature-flag ADR (docs/adr/ADR-013-feature-flags.md), and states that there is no separate catalogue document.

@security-auditor accepted that removal as a net improvement rather than a loss of auditability — its words were that you cannot lose auditability you never had, and that a rule directing an auditor to a non-existent catalogue is strictly worse than one pointing at real artefacts, because an auditor may conclude from the absent file that there are no flags.

The gap is that the ADR does not know it has been given this job. The rule file now nominates it as the register, but the ADR itself says nothing about being one, so a future author could reasonably create the catalogue document the rule was just changed to avoid.

What to add: one sentence to the existing dated amendment in docs/adr/ADR-013-feature-flags.md — that this ADR is the register of active flags, and that there is deliberately no separate catalogue document, because a hand-maintained list drifts from the code.

What NOT to add: the naming convention. The guardian was explicit that the ADR is already sufficient there — its Decision section already specifies flags as configuration properties under the eop.features.* root, and its Consequences already record that the namespace is a convention enforced by a reviewer rather than by the compiler. Restating it would duplicate, not clarify.

Item B — the binding-order exception is attached to the wrong clause

.opencode/rules/configuration.md carries a rule that configuration is read through @ConfigurationProperties with @Validated, never raw @Value. EOP-32 added a sub-bullet recording the one genuine exception: a property that decides whether a bean exists at all is read by @ConditionalOnProperty, which Spring evaluates before any @ConfigurationProperties bean is bound, so such a property cannot also be read through a typed properties class. That was necessary, because without it the rewritten feature-flag rule contradicts this file.

The statement is accurate. The problem is where it hangs. It is filed as a sub-bullet of "never raw @Value", but @ConditionalOnProperty is not @Value. The clause it actually qualifies is an unstated corollary — that every property is read through a typed class. As written, a careless reader can take "one exception" to mean "one exception to the @Value ban", which is not what it says and not what anyone intends.

The guardian confirmed this is a wording risk and not a live one: it creates no licence in practice, and grep finds zero uses of @Value in either src/main or src/test. That is why this is LOW.

What to do: reattach the exception to the typed-class corollary rather than to the @Value prohibition — either by stating that corollary explicitly and hanging the exception off it, or by rewording the exception so it cannot be read as relaxing the @Value rule.

Acceptance criteria

  • docs/adr/ADR-013-feature-flags.md states that it is the register of active flags and that there is no separate catalogue document, without restating the naming convention.
  • No document instructs anyone to create or maintain a separate flag catalogue file.
  • The @ConditionalOnProperty binding-order exception in .opencode/rules/configuration.md cannot be read as an exception to the @Value prohibition.
  • @Value remains absent from src/main and src/test — this ticket must not be used to introduce one.
  • If the ADR edit changes its status word, docs/adr/README.md carries the date; if it does not, no date is needed in either place, per step 5 of that index.

Provenance

Both items were raised by @architecture-guardian while reviewing EOP-32, and both were confirmed still deferrable in its final round-5 approval. Item A also rests on @security-auditor's finding about the phantom catalogue. Neither blocked EOP-32, and neither blocks anything now.

fields.summary: Two small documentation-accuracy items left over from the EOP-32 review

renderedFields.description:
Two independent findings from the EOP-32 review, bundled because both concern the honesty of the build's own claims about the database and cache layers. Item A is a real test gap with a precedent in this project's own history. Item B is a small classpath cleanup that would let a rule file drop a qualification it currently needs.

Item A — nothing verifies that the Liquibase changelogs actually applied

Raised by @tester-api. grep -rln liquibase src/test/java/ returns nothing: no test in the suite references Liquibase at all. Migrations do run on every @SpringBootTest context start against H2, so they are exercised — but nothing asserts the outcome. If the changelogs silently stopped applying, the suite would stay green until a query failed for an unrelated-looking reason.

This is not hypothetical. This project has already been bitten by exactly that failure: Spring Boot 4 modularised Liquibase autoconfiguration into a separate org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-liquibase module, and while that module was not a declared dependency the migrations silently did not run — nothing read the configuration, nothing warned, nothing failed. That incident is the subject of EOP-33. The same class of breakage would be invisible to the current suite a second time.

Why ddl-auto: validate is not already covering this. It is tempting to treat Hibernate's schema validation as the backstop, and during the EOP-32 review two reviewers established that it is not. validate walks the mapped metamodel only — it checks that tables and columns exist for mapped entities and that column types are compatible. It does not enumerate the database, so it never notices a missing index, a missing unique constraint, a missing foreign key, a missing check constraint, or a table no entity maps to. A changeset that creates only an index or only a constraint can fail to apply and startup will be clean. Data is equally invisible: a missing row is never a validation error.

Suggested shape. An integration test asserting the shipped schema and seed data are actually present — for example that the card table exists and holds the expected number of rows. There are six changesets across three changelogs (001-card-catalogue.xml, 002-real-deck.xml, 003-session-lifecycle.xml). The assertion should be specific enough that a changelog silently not applying fails the build, and loose enough that adding a legitimate migration does not.

The tripwire precedent already exists and is currently unused for this layer: src/test/java/org/maglez/eop/config/H2ConsoleAbsentIntegrationTest.java, written for EOP-27, breaks the build on a latent configuration exposure. The same pattern applies directly here.

@tester-api's own judgement was that this is a follow-up gap rather than something EOP-32 should have closed, which is why it is filed rather than fixed.

Item B — the cache starter is on the classpath but dormant

Raised by @code-reviewer. pom.xml:55 declares spring-boot-starter-cache. Nothing uses it: no @EnableCaching anywhere, no @Cacheable/@CacheEvict/@CachePut in src/, and no spring.cache.* configuration.

This dependency has already cost something concrete. An early draft of .opencode/rules/caching.md during EOP-32 stated that there was "no cache dependency", and @code-reviewer rejected the story for it, correctly, because the starter is right there at pom.xml:55. The rule file now carries a more careful sentence — that the starter is on the classpath but dormant — which is accurate but only necessary because the dependency exists without a purpose.

Two acceptable outcomes. Either remove the starter, in @code-reviewer's words to keep the classpath honest, and then simplify the rule file's dormancy qualification to a plain statement that nothing is cached; or record why it is deliberately present ahead of use, so the next reader does not have to rediscover that it is inert. Removal is the cleaner default: an unused starter is dependency surface with no benefit, and the caching rules describe how caching must be introduced rather than something in place.

Acceptance criteria

  • A test fails the build if the shipped Liquibase changelogs do not apply — not merely if the application fails to start.
  • That test does not rely on ddl-auto: validate as its mechanism, and its assertion would survive the addition of a legitimate new migration.
  • The relationship to ddl-auto: validate is recorded somewhere durable, so nobody later deletes the test believing validation covers it.
  • spring-boot-starter-cache is either removed from pom.xml or its presence is explained; if removed, .opencode/rules/caching.md drops the classpath qualification it currently needs.
  • No rule file makes a claim about the cache dependency that pom.xml contradicts — the defect that earned a rejection in EOP-32.

Not in scope

Introducing caching. Item B is about whether an unused dependency should sit in pom.xml, not about adopting a cache. If the answer is to keep it deliberately, that decision belongs in an ADR rather than in this ticket.

Provenance

Item A from @tester-api, restated with the ddl-auto: validate scope limit that @architecture-guardian and @security-auditor independently established during the EOP-32 review. Item B from @code-reviewer, which logged it as pre-existing and explicitly not a blocker for EOP-32.

renderedFields.description:
Follow-up from EOP-26 / ADR-021, required by @security-auditor as a condition of its approval.

TrustedProxies correctly rejects a CIDR block with host bits set (10.0.0.5/8), but accepts 0.0.0.0/0 silently. When prefixBits == 0 both wholeBytes and remainingBits are 0, so Range.contains returns true immediately: 0.0.0.0/0 matches every IPv4 peer and ::/0 every IPv6 peer. That would trust every caller and restore the EOP-26 vulnerability in full.

ADR-021 offered human review as the mitigation. The auditor explicitly ruled that insufficient, for three reasons worth preserving:

  1. the value lives in compose.app.yml, an operations file edited under time pressure and exactly where 0.0.0.0/0 gets pasted to "make it work";
  2. the failure is total and silent — the app logs Trusting forwarding headers from [0.0.0.0/0] and behaves identically to the vulnerable build, so there is no signal;
  3. this codebase already rejects 10.0.0.5/8 at startup for having host bits set, so the machinery to refuse a nonsensical spec exists and is one branch short of covering the one spec that is catastrophic.

Scope

  • Hard-reject prefix length 0 for both address families via the existing reject(...) path, so it fails bean creation and therefore startup.
  • LOG.warn when an IPv4 prefix is shorter than /24 or an IPv6 prefix shorter than /120.
  • Invert the existing test. TrustedProxiesTest currently has a passing test enshrining /0 matching everything as intended behaviour, so this change must delete a green test — that is the point, not an obstacle.

Not a blocker on EOP-26: the shipped default is [], the deployed value is a /32, and the property is operator-set and never attacker-set.

renderedFields.description:
Follow-up from EOP-26 / ADR-021 limitation 7b.

IpLiterals is DNS-free because parseIpv6 is the only caller of InetAddress.getByName in the class, and every path into that call passes isAddressText first. Nothing in the build enforces either half.

This matters because the property was already wrong once. An earlier revision claimed DNS-freedom "by construction", reasoning that a colon cannot appear in a hostname so the JDK would reject rather than resolve. That was measured false: getByName decides whether to attempt literal parsing from the first character alone, so colon-bearing hostnames went straight to the system resolver. On Java 21.0.12 with uncacheable names, a single cold lookup of zzz<unique>:80 blocked a request thread for 5020 ms.

The guard now prevents that, and DnsFreeLiteralGuard pins it with an InetAddressResolverProvider spy asserting zero lookups. But a getByName added elsewhere in the class, or a second path into parseIpv6 that skips the guard, would silently reintroduce the primitive — and the only symptom would be latency.

Scope

An ArchUnit rule forbidding InetAddress.getByName outside the one guarded method, or a forbidden-apis signature ban across the module, so the build fails rather than trusting a future reader to know why the call is dangerous.

Sequencing

ADR-021 limitation 8 notes this should land before the IpLiterals value-object extraction, because splitting the class without this rule in place would make this gap materially worse.

Follow-up from EOP-26. @code-reviewer raised these as suggestions (S5, W3) on first review and then promoted S5 from suggestion to warning on re-review, because IpLiterals grew to 229 lines and 12 methods (10 private) while closing the DNS finding.

S5 — IpLiterals as a value object (now a warning)

An IP address that is used as a rate-limiter map key is exactly the shape of a value type. IpLiterals is a static utility returning Optional<byte[]> and Optional<String>, so callers canonicalise to a string and key on that. A ParsedAddress value type with equals/hashCode over the address bytes would make the key semantics explicit and remove the string round-trip. The class now also carries two separable concerns: the character-classification alphabet and the parsing/canonicalisation logic.

W3 — TrustedProxies SRP

of() parses, validates and constructs; includes() answers membership. Two responsibilities. The reviewer's original ruling was that the coupling is genuine — the parsed Range form is the only representation useful for matching, and splitting would produce a parser with no independent test surface — so this is only worth doing alongside S5.

Related, from the same review

@code-reviewer also ruled the 7-parameter SessionController constructor a warning rather than a blocker (W1), with the explicit trigger that the next parameter added there should force extraction of a RequestContext or WebRequestAdapter. Worth doing in the same pass if this ticket is picked up after another controller dependency lands.

Trigger

The reviewer asked that this be filed before the next feature touches these files. Do not do it opportunistically: ADR-021 limitation 8 sequences it after the ArchUnit/forbidden-apis rule (EOP-44), because splitting IpLiterals without that rule in place would widen the gap that lets an unguarded getByName slip back in.

Explicitly not a blocker. Both classes are cohesive and correct; ./mvnw verify is green at 386 tests with SpotBugs 0.

renderedFields.description:
During EOP-26 the @tester-api review gate was dispatched four times and never produced a usable sign-off. It returned VERDICT: APPROVE each time, so the failure is not a missing verdict line — it is that the contracted evidence was absent every time:

  • no severity-tagged findings and no file:line references;
  • no literal ./mvnw verify exit code or Surefire summary line;
  • the required order-independence runs (three test classes in isolation, then the full suite) were never performed;
  • the ranked coverage-gap list was never produced;
  • it never determined MockMvc's actual peer address, which was the one question that decided whether the story's mirror test was vacuous.

On the final dispatch it substituted its own seven headings for the seven required outputs, and mis-stated the fix under review ("throttling can be bypassed only when request comes from trusted proxy with different X-Forwarded-For values"). On an earlier dispatch it reported that evidence "has been compiled in a markdown document", despite a read-only brief — neither visible to the dispatcher nor permitted.

Progressively more directive briefs did not help, including an explicit statement that a report missing the numbered outputs would be treated as a REJECT regardless of its verdict line.

Why this looks like a model-tier problem, not a prompt problem

AGENTS.md already documents this exact failure mode and its fix: tester-unit-and-quality was moved from MODEL_C to MODEL_B because on MODEL_C it "needed three dispatches to return a verdict and once recommended merging a red build". The other half of that fix was adding the Sign-off Contract to the agent definitions. tester-api carries the contract but evidently cannot hold it on its current tier.

The same session shows the contract working well elsewhere: @architecture-guardian rejected twice with precise file:line findings, and both rejections caught real CI-breaking defects that every other reviewer missed — so the contract itself is effective where the model can hold it.

Scope

  • Review which tier tester-api is pinned to in .opencode/opencode.json and consider moving it to the review tier that fixed tester-unit-and-quality, remembering that the agent block is grouped by tier so the agent should be moved between groups rather than having its value edited in place.
  • Requires an OpenCode restart to take effect.
  • Re-dispatch the EOP-26 gate afterwards against PR #40 and confirm the evidence arrives.

Impact

PR #40 carries four evidenced approvals and is green at 386 tests, but its fifth gate is formally unmet and the PR is marked do-not-merge. The substantive API-boundary questions were answered with evidence by @security-auditor, so this is not believed to be a code risk.

renderedFields.description:
Context

Found during the EOP-14 Slice A architecture review. docs/architecture/ contains only C4-Diagrams.md and runtime-view.md. There is no arc42 building-blocks view, and there never has been — eleven stories have shipped without one.

This was initially carried as an EOP-14 deferral ("building-blocks.md needs the Hand/Trick/TrickPlay domain block"), which was wrong: that phrasing presumes an existing document needing an amendment, when the actual state is that the document has never been written. Filing it as its own work rather than letting it ride along on a story that cannot reasonably be held hostage to it.

Scope

Create docs/architecture/building-blocks.md as an arc42 level-1/level-2 building-blocks view covering what exists today:

  • entity — immutable domain, zero framework imports: GameSession, Player, Card, Hand, Hands, Trick, TrickPlay, the STRIDE StrideCategory / Rank value types, and the domain exceptions
  • usecase — application services and the ports they depend on (SessionRepository, CardRepository, SessionEventPublisher, the generators)
  • adapter/web, adapter/persistence, adapter/security — the driving and driven adapters
  • config — wiring and configuration properties

Each block should say what it is responsible for and, more usefully, what it is not allowed to depend on, so the document is checkable rather than decorative.

Why it is worth doing

C4-Diagrams.md renders the whole domain as a single node with no type list, so there is currently no document that answers "what lives in the domain and what may it touch" without reading the source. That question is asked on every story, and Clean Architecture compliance is a gate on all of them.

Related

  • ADR-023 (deal remainder and turn order) — introduced Hand, Hands, Trick, TrickPlay
  • .opencode/rules/clean-architecture.md — the dependency rule the document should make checkable
  • Note for whoever picks this up: C4-Diagrams.md line 54 names PG["game_session, player, card"], which becomes stale when EOP-14 Slice B lands changeset 004 with hand, trick and trick_play. Worth doing after Slice B, or worth updating both together.

renderedFields.description:
Problem

SessionController.java:51 declares:

@ConditionalOnProperty(prefix = "eop.features", name = "session-lifecycle")

With no havingValue, Spring's condition matches any present value that is not literally `false`. So session-lifecycle: off, no, 0 or disabled all enable the five session routes — and off is read by YAML 1.1 as boolean false, which is the spelling an operator reaching for a kill switch is most likely to use.

Because the session use-case beans (createSessionUseCase, joinSessionUseCase, resolvePlayerUseCase, getSessionStateUseCase, startSessionUseCase in UseCaseConfiguration) are registered unconditionally, nothing fails the application context to signal the mistake. The app boots cleanly with routes live that the operator believes are off.

This is fail-open, not a cosmetic inconsistency. It violates .opencode/rules/security.md's "fail securely — default-denied access".

Current exposure

Latent, not live. src/main/resources/application.yml sets the literal session-lifecycle: false, so the shipped default is correct and the routes are off. The hole opens only if someone edits that value to a non-false falsy spelling.

Fix

1. Controller

Add havingValue = "true" to SessionController's @ConditionalOnProperty, matching TrickController.java:69.

2. Use-case beans

Gate the four session use-case beans on session-lifecycle in UseCaseConfiguration, matching the pattern used for the five trick-play use cases:

  • createSessionUseCase → add @ConditionalOnProperty(name = "eop.features.session-lifecycle", havingValue = "true")
  • joinSessionUseCase → same
  • getSessionStateUseCase → same
  • startSessionUseCase → same
  • resolvePlayerUseCase → leave ungated — it is a pure lookup with no side effects, and it is a dependency of the trick-play use cases too. Gating it on session-lifecycle would break wiring when session-lifecycle is off but trick-play is on. Precedent: SecureRandomDeckShuffler is ungated in TrickPlayDisabledIntegrationTest for the same reason.

Why this is not part of EOP-14 Slice D

TrickController carried the identical loose form and was corrected to havingValue = "true" in commit 56c31b1 on EOP-14-slice-d-endpoints. SessionController was deliberately left out of that branch: a one-word security fix to an unrelated controller does not belong buried in a feature branch, and .opencode/rules/git-commits.md requires its own Jira key. @architecture-guardian endorsed keeping it off the branch and made the existence of this ticket a condition of approving Slice D.

Acceptance criteria

  • SessionController's @ConditionalOnProperty carries havingValue = "true".
  • createSessionUseCase, joinSessionUseCase, getSessionStateUseCase and startSessionUseCase in UseCaseConfiguration each carry @ConditionalOnProperty(name = "eop.features.session-lifecycle", havingValue = "true").
  • resolvePlayerUseCase remains ungated (it is shared with trick-play).
  • A new test scenario in SessionControllerDisabledIntegrationTest (or a companion class) sets eop.features.session-lifecycle=off and asserts:
  • SessionController bean is absent from the application context (not merely that routes return 404 — asserting only the status would pass against the current fail-open design).
  • createSessionUseCase, joinSessionUseCase, getSessionStateUseCase and startSessionUseCase beans are absent.
  • resolvePlayerUseCase bean is present (it must survive for trick-play wiring).
  • The five session routes all return 404.
  • The existing SessionControllerDisabledIntegrationTest (which uses session-lifecycle=false) continues to pass unchanged.
  • ./mvnw verify green.

Related

  • docs/adr/ADR-013-feature-flags.md carries the binding rule this ticket enforces: every `@ConditionalOnProperty` on a flag in this repository must carry `havingValue = "true"`.
  • Found by @security-auditor during the EOP-14 Slice D Definition-of-Done review (MEDIUM-4 in that audit, regraded HIGH by @architecture-guardian).
  • This ticket is a predecessor of EOP-25 (flip session-lifecycle on) and of the story that flips trick-play on (ADR-028).

comments.body:
Delivered and merged to main via PR #52 (merge commit 31458cb).

What was wrong

SessionController's @ConditionalOnProperty omitted havingValue. Verified against the resolved spring-boot-autoconfigure-4.1.0 bytecode rather than the documentation: with havingValue empty, OnPropertyCondition$Spec.isMatch reduces to !"false".equalsIgnoreCase(value). So off, no, 0, disabled — and the empty string, which is what EOP_FEATURES_SESSION_LIFECYCLE= produces and which was recorded nowhere before this ticket — all enabled the five session routes. off is the worst of them: it is both the spelling an operator reaches for as a kill switch and a YAML 1.1 boolean false, so it would have passed review unremarked.

matchIfMissing already defaults to false, so an absent property was never the hole. The hole was confined to the present-but-not-false case.

The controller was only the symptom. The four session use-case beans in UseCaseConfiguration were registered unconditionally, so a misspelt flag had nothing to fail against — which is why this differed from TrickController, corrected in 56c31b1, and why it needed its own ticket rather than a one-line follow-up.

What changed

`34d30d7` — EOP-48 Done fix: close fail-open @ConditionalOnProperty on the session lifecycle flag

  • SessionController.java:60 now carries havingValue = "true".
  • createSessionUseCase (:101), joinSessionUseCase (:124), getSessionStateUseCase (:167) and startSessionUseCase (:182) each carry @ConditionalOnProperty(name = "eop.features.session-lifecycle", havingValue = "true").
  • resolvePlayerUseCase deliberately ungated, with the reason in javadoc: pure read (verified — no save/persist/delete anywhere in it), and shared with all five trick-play use cases, so gating it on the lobby flag would make lobby-off/trick-play-on an unsatisfiable context. Eight consumers traced: two lifecycle, five trick-play, plus the controller.
  • New SessionLifecycleOffValueIntegrationTest (12 tests) pinning the off spelling: five bean-absence assertions, five route 404s, one counterweight asserting ResolvePlayerUseCase and PlayCardUseCase survive, one asserting /api/v1/cards still answers 200.

`50850d1` — EOP-48 Done docs: correct the five documents that still described the fail-open flag

The review found five stale documents, not the two the brief named: ADR-013 (predecessor count, three now-false clauses kept and marked spent because an ADR is a record, plus a dated note carrying the full mechanism and a strengthened mandate), ADR-028 (predecessor discharged, two of three remain), docs/adr/README.md (Implemented column only, so AdrIndexConsistencyTest stays green), docs/architecture/C4-Diagrams.md (its annotation quote had itself omitted havingValue, and it carried a live paragraph describing the hole as unfixed), and src/main/resources/application.yml (both flag comments — ADR-028:76-77 designates the trick-play one part of the predecessor register).

ADR-013's mandate is now two sentences rather than one: every @ConditionalOnProperty on a flag carries havingValue = "true", and the flag is repeated on every bean that opens or mutates the state behind it — pure reads and cross-flag collaborators staying ungated with the reason in javadoc.

The fix was measured, not asserted

Against the pre-fix code the new test fails 6 of 12: the five bean-absence assertions plus exactly one route — POST /api/v1/sessions returning 201 Created and persisting a session with the flag set to off. The other four routes return 404 either way, because a random session id and an unissued join code are absent whether or not the controller exists.

That is the argument for asserting bean absence alongside the 404s: a status-only test would have caught this on one route in five, and only because that route creates something. A read-only lobby would have been missed entirely. SessionControllerDisabledIntegrationTest (spelling false) is byte-identical and passed both before and after — only a second spelling could catch this.

Post-fix, exactly one value enables the feature: case-insensitive true. Absent, empty and every other spelling fail closed. All eleven @ConditionalOnProperty sites in src/main/ now carry havingValue = "true"; zero loose forms remain.

Acceptance criteria

Criterion Status
SessionController carries havingValue = "true" ✅ :60
Four session use-case beans gated ✅ :101, :124, :167, :182
resolvePlayerUseCase remains ungated ✅ with javadoc, plus a test asserting it present in the off context
New scenario with session-lifecycle=off asserting bean absence, not merely 404s ✅ SessionLifecycleOffValueIntegrationTest, 12 tests
Existing SessionControllerDisabledIntegrationTest passes unchanged ✅ byte-identical, 7/7
./mvnw verify green ✅ 905 tests, 0 failures; checkstyle 0, spotbugs 0, jacoco met, enforcer 3/3

Definition of Done — five gates, five approvals

Every gate ran ./mvnw verify itself rather than taking the build on trust.

  • @tester-unit-and-quality — APPROVE. Decompiled OnPropertyCondition$Spec to confirm the pre-fix behaviour. SessionController 100% (105/105), UseCaseConfiguration 100% (96/96), bundle 97.3%. Argued off alone is sufficient — pinning no/0/disabled would test Spring, not the application, at three more Spring contexts.
  • @tester-api — APPROVE. Confirmed the 404s are the framework's own NoResourceFoundException, not a GlobalExceptionHandler mapping and not a masked 403. Confirmed no residual write path: SessionRepositoryAdapter exists unconditionally but has no reachable caller. `docs/api/openapi.yml:44-47` already stated the gate and the 404 behaviour, so the contract needed no change — the bug was the implementation not honouring it.
  • @security-auditor — APPROVE, no CRITICAL or HIGH. Proved the mechanism against bytecode and found the previously unrecorded empty-string case. Confirmed no join code, token hash or session envelope leaks through the ungated path. Argued against adding startup validation of eop.features.*: the remaining failure modes (on/yes/1, a misspelt key) all fail closed and are loud, a validator would turn an operability annoyance into a boot crash, and it would need a second register that can drift.
  • @code-reviewer — APPROVE, zero blockers. Zero Spring imports in usecase/ and entity/. The two annotation spellings (prefix+name on controllers, dotted name on beans) judged each idiomatic in context, explicitly not a finding.
  • @architecture-guardian — APPROVE. The agent that regraded this HIGH and made it a condition of approving Slice D. Judged the two-layer gate genuine defence in depth on the axis that matters: remove havingValue from the controller tomorrow and the context fails to start rather than failing open, because the constructor requires four beans that no longer exist. Authored the four document corrections.

CI on the PR: build, ui and image all green (run 31828428083).

Follow-ups filed rather than smuggled in

  • An automated check that every @ConditionalOnProperty in src/main carries havingValue = "true". The mandate was already in ADR-013 and has now been violated twice, so reviewer attention has demonstrably not been enough. Deliberately not done here: the tool choice (ArchUnit vs a docs-style test in the manner of AdrIndexConsistencyTest) is a new decision needing its own ADR, and that does not belong in a fix commit.
  • EOP-25's description needs amending before that flip is attempted — most importantly because only the literal true now flips the flag, so on/yes/1 are silent no-ops. That inversion is the deliberate price of failing closed and belongs in the ticket that performs the flip.

Notes for the record

  • Exposure was latent, not live: application.yml has always shipped session-lifecycle: false, which was one of the six letters that did work.
  • This ticket's own description cites SessionController.java:51; the annotation is at :60. Same citation-drift class as EOP-49.
  • EOP-48 is discharged as a predecessor of EOP-25 and of the story that flips trick-play on (ADR-028), which now has two of its three predecessors outstanding.

h2. Problem

{{SessionController.java:51}} declares:

{code:java}@ConditionalOnProperty(prefix = "eop.features", name = "session-lifecycle"){code}

With no {{havingValue}}, Spring's condition matches *any present value that is not literally `false`*. So {{session-lifecycle: off}}, {{no}}, {{0}} or {{disabled}} all *enable* the five session routes — and {{off}} is read by YAML 1.1 as boolean false, which is the spelling an operator reaching for a kill switch is most likely to use.

Because the session use-case beans ({{createSessionUseCase}}, {{joinSessionUseCase}}, {{resolvePlayerUseCase}}, {{getSessionStateUseCase}}, {{startSessionUseCase}} in {{UseCaseConfiguration}}) are registered *unconditionally*, nothing fails the application context to signal the mistake. The app boots cleanly with routes live that the operator believes are off.

This is *fail-open*, not a cosmetic inconsistency. It violates {{.opencode/rules/security.md}}'s "fail securely — default-denied access".

h2. Current exposure

Latent, not live. {{src/main/resources/application.yml:79}} sets the literal {{session-lifecycle: false}}, so the shipped default is correct and the routes are off. The hole opens only if someone edits that value to a non-{{false}} falsy spelling.

h2. Fix

Add {{havingValue = "true"}} to {{SessionController}}'s condition, matching every other flagged bean in the codebase.

h2. Why this is not part of [EOP-14|https://maglez.atlassian.net/browse/EOP-14] Slice D

{{TrickController}} carried the identical loose form and was corrected to {{havingValue = "true"}} in commit {{56c31b1}} on {{EOP-14-slice-d-endpoints}}. {{SessionController}} was deliberately left out of that branch: a one-word security fix to an unrelated controller does not belong buried in a feature branch, and {{.opencode/rules/git-commits.md}} requires its own Jira key. @architecture-guardian endorsed keeping it off the branch and made the existence of this ticket a condition of approving Slice D.

h2. Acceptance criteria

* {{SessionController}}'s {{@ConditionalOnProperty}} carries {{havingValue = "true"}}.
* A test pins the off position for a non-{{false}} falsy value — e.g. {{@SpringBootTest(properties = "eop.features.session-lifecycle=off")}} asserting the {{SessionController}} bean is *absent* and the routes answer 404. Asserting only the status would pass against the current fail-open design, so bean absence is the assertion that matters (precedent: {{SessionControllerDisabledIntegrationTest}}, {{TrickPlayDisabledIntegrationTest}}).
* Consider whether the five session use-case beans should also be gated, so the flag fails closed the way {{trick-play}} does.
* {{./mvnw verify}} green.

h2. Related

* {{docs/adr/ADR-013-feature-flags.md}} now carries the binding rule this ticket enforces: *every `@ConditionalOnProperty` on a flag in this repository must carry `havingValue = "true"`.*
* Found by @security-auditor during the [EOP-14|https://maglez.atlassian.net/browse/EOP-14] Slice D Definition-of-Done review ([MEDIUM-4|https://maglez.atlassian.net/browse/MEDIUM-4] in that audit, regraded HIGH by @architecture-guardian).
