renderedFields.description:
Symptom

When a game finished, every client was returned to the initial home page and no leaderboard was ever displayed. Session storage was cleared, so players could not recover the session.

Root cause

Two independent faults compounded.

1. `eop.features.game-over` was `false` (primary).

With the flag off, GameOverController is never registered as a bean, so {{GET /api/v1/sessions/

{sessionId}

/leaderboard}} fell through to Spring's static-resource handler and returned a framework 404:

{"detail":"No static resource api/v1/sessions/.../leaderboard.","title":"Not Found"}

PersistGameResultUseCase is gated on the same flag, so PlayCardUseCase never persisted a GameResult row either — meaning even after enabling the flag, games played under the old build have no result to show.

2. `GameOverScreen` treated a leaderboard 404 as a dead session (secondary).

if (err instanceof ApiError && (err.status === 403 || err.status === 404)) {
  onSessionEnd();   // clears sessionStorage, navigates to home
}

A 404 from the leaderboard means "no result persisted yet", not "your session is gone". Conflating the two turned a recoverable, transient condition into an unrecoverable ejection for every connected client.

Fix

  • src/main/resources/application.yml — set eop.features.game-over: true
  • ui/src/components/GameOverScreen.tsx — eject only on 403; on 404 render the error message plus a Retry loading results button so the screen degrades gracefully instead of destroying the session

Verification

Full three-player game driven end-to-end against the running stack via the real API:

Step Result
Create session, join two players 201 / 200, seats 0–2
Start + deal 200 / 204, 22 cards each
Play to completion 66 plays, tricks auto-resolve server-side
Session status COMPLETED
GET /leaderboard HTTP 200, all three players ranked with capturedBySuit across six STRIDE suits

Served UI bundle confirmed to carry the guard (status === 403 only) and the retry button.

Note on recurrence

This is the third incident in this class: EOP-76 and EOP-78 were both stale/misconfigured local-image faults. The initial diagnosis here was also delayed by rebuilding only eop-ui:local — ./scripts/update-local.sh rebuilds both images and is the only supported path.

Acceptance criteria

  • Leaderboard renders for a completed game in the local Docker stack
  • A leaderboard 404 does not clear session storage or navigate home
  • Automated regression coverage exists for the flag-on leaderboard path, so a green ./mvnw verify would have caught this

PR opened: https://github.com/maglez/eop-threat-medeling/pull/85 — branch eop-82-fix-leaderboard-ejection, 4 commits off main.

All three CI checks green: build pass (1m30s), ui pass (28s), image pass (1m27s). Locally ./mvnw verify → 1215 tests / 0 failures / SpotBugs 0 / all coverage checks met; ui/ → tsc --noEmit clean, eslint clean, 168 tests across 9 files.

All five Definition-of-Done gates approved:

Gate Verdict
@tester-unit-and-quality APPROVE
@tester-api APPROVE
@security-auditor APPROVE
@code-reviewer APPROVE
@architecture-guardian REJECT → APPROVE (two documentation BLOCKERs, both discharged in 21b4bc1)

Acceptance criteria:

  1. Leaderboard shown after a game completes — verified end-to-end against the local Docker stack: three players, 66 plays to status = COMPLETED, GET /leaderboard → HTTP 200 with all three players ranked and capturedBySuit across all six STRIDE suits.
  2. Clients are not ejected to home — ejection narrowed to 403 only; a 404 or 409 now renders the error with a Retry loading results button. Confirmed in the served production bundle, not just the source.
  3. Automated regression coverage such that a green `./mvnw verify` would have caught this — three guards, two of them mutation-verified. ShippedFeatureFlagDefaultsTest reads application.yml off the classpath rather than through the Spring Environment (the Environment resolves the test-resource override, so an Environment lookup would have passed against the broken YAML); flipping the flag back to false fails exactly that test. GameOverScreen.test.tsx is new: the component was the only one in ui/src/components/ without a test file, which is why fault 2 shipped.

Follow-up tickets filed and linked *Relates:* EOP-83 through EOP-91. None of them is a downgraded rejection — every gate finding was either fixed on this branch or is a pre-existing issue this branch does not touch.

Awaiting human review on the PR.

renderedFields.description:
Context

Found while verifying [EOP-82|https://maglez.atlassian.net/browse/EOP-82] end-to-end against the running stack. Neither divergence blocked that fix, but both mean docs/api/openapi.yml currently misdescribes the implementation. Per the contract-first rule in .opencode/rules/api-design.md the spec is authoritative, so either the spec or the code must move.

Divergence 1 — deal distributes 66 of 68 cards

openapi.yml documents {{POST /sessions/

{sessionId}

/deal}} as dealing the entire 68-card deck, distributing the remainder to the lowest seats — for three players that is 23 / 23 / 22.

Observed at runtime with three players: 22 / 22 / 22 = 66 cards. Two cards are unaccounted for.

Needs a decision on which is correct:

  • If the spec is right, the dealing logic drops two cards and that is a domain bug affecting scoring completeness.
  • If even distribution is intended, the spec and the dealing rules in the domain docs need correcting.

Divergence 2 — leaderboard availability contradicts the use case

openapi.yml states the leaderboard "is available in any session state, not only COMPLETED".

GetLeaderboardUseCase throws GameNotCompletedException → 409 Conflict for any session that is not COMPLETED.

The frontend already handles 409 as a non-fatal error, so nothing is broken today — but a client written against the spec would reasonably expect 200 for an in-progress session and has no documented reason to expect 409. The 409 is also absent from the documented response codes for that operation.

Suggested resolution

Confirm intended behaviour for both, then update whichever side is wrong in a single change so the contract and the implementation agree. Add the missing 409 to the leaderboard operation's documented responses either way.

Acceptance criteria

  • Deal card-count behaviour agreed and spec/implementation reconciled
  • Leaderboard availability agreed and spec/implementation reconciled
  • All response codes the leaderboard endpoint can actually return are documented, including 409
  • A test asserts the agreed deal distribution so the count cannot drift again

comments.body:
Delivered in PR #109 (commit 001f654), but both premises in this ticket turned out to be stale, so the outcome is not what the ticket describes. Recording that here because the first one alleges a domain bug that does not exist.

Divergence 1 — "the dealing logic drops two cards" is disproved

The spec's 23/23/22 for three players is correct, and so is the code. Four independent facts agree:

  • Hands.deal runs for (index = 0; index < orderedDeck.size(); index++) — the whole deck, round-robin, nothing truncated. Its javadoc is titled "Deals every card in the deck, so that nothing is discarded" and already asserts 23/23/22.
  • The migrations leave exactly 68 rows: 78 seeded in 002-real-deck.xml, minus 4 in 2026-08-17-trim-deck-to-74-printed-cards.xml, minus 6 in 2026-08-18-remove-ace-cards.xml.
  • DeckTrimMigrationRoundTripTest pins 68 after the full chain (and 74/78 on rollback); CardRepositoryAdapterIntegrationTest pins 68 read through the real repository plus the per-suit distribution, so a wrong mix cannot hide behind a right total.
  • HandsTest pins 23/23/22, 17×4, 14/14/14/13/13 and 12/12/11/11/11/11 with every card dealt exactly once at every supported table size; DealHandsUseCaseTest pins totalCards() == 68 and 23 at the first seat.

The observed 22/22/22 = 66 is exactly `68 − (68 mod 3)` — the arithmetic signature of the equal-hands truncation EOP-72 introduced and EOP-92 reverted. The observation predates that revert.

Consequently the acceptance criterion "a test asserts the agreed deal distribution so the count cannot drift again" was already satisfied four times over, and no fifth pin was added. Adding one would have been duplicate coverage presented as a fix.

Divergence 2 — real, but mislocated, and its second half is false

The leaderboard operation and GetLeaderboardUseCase never disagreed. What was wrong sat in the `Leaderboard` schema description, which claimed the leaderboard is "available in any session state, not only COMPLETED" — contradicting the operation description directly above it and the 409 guard. So the spec contradicted itself, not the code. The schema description was rewritten; the code was not touched.

The claim that "the 409 is absent from that operation's documented responses" is false, and was already false when the ticket was written. git show b6e8447:docs/api/openapi.yml shows a full inline '409' block with an application/problem+json body on that operation at the merge base. The one place the stale claim had propagated — a javadoc sentence in GameOverControllerIntegrationTest.Rfc9457ContractGuards saying the reconciliation "is tracked as EOP-83" — is corrected.

Net change

Documentation only — no production Java touched (CHANGELOG.md, docs/api/openapi.yml, and one test javadoc). ./mvnw clean verify green at 1266 tests.

One limit stated plainly: this does not decide whether the leaderboard should become available before completion. It records that today it is not, in both halves of the spec. If that behaviour is wanted, it is a two-sided change — LeaderboardDto.sessionStatus is one of EnumMirrorParityTest's four client-checked unions, so an ABANDONED value would raise ContractViolationError in the browser (ADR-045) — and it deserves its own ticket rather than being smuggled in here.

renderedFields.description:
Context

EOP-82 shipped a feature dark for two stories: eop.features.game-over was false in src/main/resources/application.yml while the whole slice was complete, and nothing flipped it. No test could catch it, because src/test/resources/application.properties pins all three flags true (as .opencode/rules/feature-flags.md requires), so the Spring Environment in every @SpringBootTest resolves the override, never the shipped YAML.

The interim mitigation is src/test/java/org/maglez/eop/config/ShippedFeatureFlagDefaultsTest.java, which reads application.yml off the classpath via YamlPropertiesFactoryBean. @architecture-guardian ruled this a workaround, not the architectural answer, and ADR-042 records that ruling.

The problem with the interim guard

It asserts three hand-named values. Compare EOP-27's fix for the same class of trap (spring.h2.console.enabled), recorded in the Amendment, 2026-08-10 (EOP-27) block of docs/adr/ADR-008-database-migration-liquibase.md: that put the load-bearing assertion as a tripwire on the autoconfiguration class, so the build fails the day the module lands.

Consequence: flag #4 is invisible to it. A fifth feature added next month, shipped dark per the rules, and never flipped, reproduces EOP-82 exactly and this test stays green. It detects the recurrence of this instance, not the class of fault. It must also be hand-edited whenever a flag's intended state legitimately changes — under exactly the pressure that makes people edit tests to pass.

Proposed fix

Invert the direction of the assertion so it is derived from the set of flags that exist rather than a list someone remembered to write:

  1. Enumerate every key under eop.features in the shipped application.yml, or every @ConditionalOnProperty(prefix = "eop.features") on the classpath.
  2. Require each to appear in a single registry declaring an intended state, an owning story and an expiry.
  3. Fail the build on: any flag present in code but absent from the registry; any shipped value disagreeing with its declared intent; any flag past its expiry.

As ADR-042 puts it, this inverts the default from silent unless someone remembers to fails until someone declares intent.

Acceptance criteria

  • A flag added under eop.features with no registry entry fails ./mvnw verify, demonstrated by a deliberate mutation.
  • A flag whose shipped value disagrees with its declared intent fails the build.
  • A flag past its expiry fails the build.
  • ShippedFeatureFlagDefaultsTest's hand-written key list is replaced by the derived check (the file may be deleted or rewritten; the YAML-off-the-classpath parsing technique is sound and may be kept).
  • ADR-013 and ADR-042 amended to record the mechanism now in place.

References

  • ADR-042 (game-over flag on) — records this as future work
  • ADR-013 (feature flags), ADR-008 EOP-27 amendment (the tripwire precedent)
  • .opencode/rules/feature-flags.md

comments.body:
Implemented — PR 119(https://github.com/maglez/eop-threat-medeling/pull/119), branch `eop-84-derived-feature-flag-registry`, 8 commits, awaiting human review and merge.

./mvnw verify → Tests run: 1347, Failures: 0, Errors: 0, Skipped: 0, BUILD SUCCESS, zero [ERROR] lines.

What changed

ShippedFeatureFlagDefaultsTest is deleted. FeatureFlagRegistryTest derives the flag set three independent ways and requires all three equal:

Source Mechanism
Shipped config keys under eop.features in application.yml, read as a ClassPathResource through YamlPropertiesFactoryBean, no Spring context
Compiled code every @ConditionalOnProperty in target/classes resolving into that namespace, via SimpleMetadataReaderFactory as ADR-052's scanner does
Declared intent entries in the new src/test/resources/feature-flag-registry.yml

Each pairing catches a different fault. A YAML key with no registry entry is an undeclared flag whose intended state nobody wrote down. An annotation key in neither the YAML nor the registry is the fail-closed trap itself — no declared default, so the flag ships OFF silently. An entry with neither is a stale or misspelled declaration describing protection that is not there.

The direction of the assertion is what changed. The old guard was silent unless someone remembered to add a line; this one fails until someone declares intent — the tripwire EOP-27 built, rather than a snapshot of today's three positions.

The registry declares key, shipped-default, owner-story and expiry, all four mandatory in both directions so shipped-defualt fails as a surplus field rather than reading as an absent shipped-default plus a harmless extra key. expiry may be null but may not be omitted — that is what stops a new flag inheriting no-expiry by silence. game-over carries the 2026-09-18 date ADR-042 wrote in prose, now enforced; the other two carry null, because ADR-042 condemned inventing dates no decision authorised.

Zero new dependencies — SnakeYAML was already compile-scope. git diff --stat e88b2c2..HEAD – src/main/java/ src/main/resources/ docs/api/openapi.yml is empty: no production code, shipped config or API contract changed.

Acceptance criteria — each demonstrated by deliberate mutation

Mutation Test that failed
new YAML key, no registry entry shouldAgreeBetweenShippedYamlAndRegistry
that key plus an entry, but no @ConditionalOnProperty shouldAgreeBetweenBytecodeAndRegistry
registry shipped-default: false while YAML says true shouldMatchShippedValueToDeclaredIntent
game-over expiry moved one day into the past shouldFailOnceAFlagPassesItsExpiry
expiry field omitted shouldRequireEveryFieldOnEveryEntry

Documentation: new ADR-053 + index row; ADR-042 amended (§3 superseded, both weakness bullets closed); ADR-013 amended; .opencode/rules/feature-flags.md reworded to except a machine-read build-gating registry from its "no separate flag catalogue document" prohibition; CHANGELOG.md.

Definition of Done — five of five approved on final HEAD

Gate Verdict
@tester-unit-and-quality APPROVE
@tester-api APPROVE (one REJECT raised and cleared)
@security-auditor APPROVE
@code-reviewer APPROVE
@architecture-guardian APPROVE

Four rounds, not one. Five substantive faults were found by reviewers and fixed rather than shipped as caveats:

  1. A `shipped-default` typo read as a deliberate declaration. Boolean.TRUE.equals(raw) answered false for anything that was not the boolean true, so shipped-default: flase arrived as a String and read back as "this flag ships dark". Worse, the same typo in application.yml would have agreed with it, since Spring treats every value but the literal true as disabled — the pair would have passed the guard while the flag shipped OFF. The EOP-82 fault reintroduced through the mechanism built to catch it. Field values are now type-asserted, not coerced.
  2. The ADR-053 index row was inserted out of sequence (051, 053, 052), and AdrIndexConsistencyTest does not check row order — silent drift of exactly the kind this story exists to remove.
  3. `registryKeys()`'s javadoc promised declaration order while the code sorted. The sort was dropped rather than the javadoc amended, because declaration order points a reader at the line to edit and the other two derivations sort for a reason this one does not have.
  4. ADR-042 carried a false claim — that a suite staying green after an incomplete flag removal is the evidence of it. It goes red: the OFF-position test asserts bean absence, not merely that the routes 404. This mattered because it is the paragraph whoever removes game-over on 2026-09-19 reads first, and a reader expecting green who meets red may revert a correct change.
  5. That claim existed in three places, in three file types, and correcting it took three commits one round apart — the ADR, the expiry assertion message, and the registry comment (the last found by @tester-api, which rejected the commit before it). Each was found by a reviewer; none by the build.

One of my own claims was false and is corrected in the record: I repeated a round-1 assertion that the consistent-removal gap was already documented in ADR-053. It was not. It is now, in §5 and in Consequences.

Recorded as bounds, not glossed

  • owner-story and shipped-default are checked for shape and agreement, never for truth — nothing verifies EOP-25 is a real issue.
  • A consistent removal across all three sources is undetected. The vacuity floor is "at least one", not "exactly the three that exist today"; pinning the count would make the guard a snapshot again, and the count cannot be derived because all three sources are what is under suspicion.
  • `game-over`'s expiry will turn `main` red on 2026-09-19 in a project that deploys every passing commit — accepted as the intended signal, on the accepted-advisories.json precedent.
  • ADR-037's front-end VITE_ flags remain *entirely uncovered; a front-end feature can still ship dark.
  • The masking trap itself is untouched — flags stay pinned ON in test resources. ADR-053 routes around it rather than removing it.

@architecture-guardian ruled EOP-84 architecturally complete with no follow-up tickets required.

Merged and closed.

  • PR #119 merged to main at 2026-08-23T09:11:37Z by miguel-gonzalez-gca-gov-uk, merge commit bd21c37. All eight commits are ancestors of origin/main (verified with git merge-base --is-ancestor ba80ca5 origin/main).
  • Post-merge trunk CI run 32630322934 for bd21c37: completed / success. All five jobs green — build, dependency-cve, supply-chain, ui, image. Checked rather than assumed: the run before last on this trunk (c75af72, PR #117) failed, so a green post-merge CI here is a fact and not a default.
  • Status moved To Do to In Progress to Done. Ticket remains unassigned.

One correction to an earlier note in this ticket. I reported that the previous comment's markdown tables and bold markers had been stripped by Jira. Reading the stored body back, that was overstated: the tables survive as intact rows and top-level bold is preserved. The actual damage is five malformed emphasis markers in the nested list under "Recorded as bounds", where the closing asterisks were lost (never for truth*, is undetected*, and three more). The content of that comment is accurate; only that nested list renders untidily. Left in place rather than edited, so the record shows what was posted.

Nothing outstanding on this ticket. The one dated obligation it creates lives in the registry rather than here: eop.features.game-over carries expiry: "2026-09-18", so ./mvnw verify turns red on 2026-09-19 until the flag is removed or the date is extended under review. The removal procedure is in the comment on that entry in src/test/resources/feature-flag-registry.yml, and it is worth reading before starting: the leftover OFF-position test asserts the beans are absent, so leaving it behind turns the build red rather than quietly green, and the correct response is to delete it, not to relax its assertions.

Context

As of EOP-82 there are three feature flags in src/main/resources/application.yml and all three are permanently `true`:

Flag   Turned on by   Date
eop.features.session-lifecycle EOP-25 2026-08-16
eop.features.trick-play EOP-70 (ADR-040) 2026-08-17
eop.features.game-over EOP-82 (ADR-042) 2026-08-18

No flag has ever been removed. .opencode/rules/feature-flags.md says a flag is removed "one release after full rollout" and ADR-013's Decision says "A flag is deleted once its feature is released". That commitment has been restated in prose three times — ADR-013's EOP-25 amendment, ADR-040, and the application.yml comment added by EOP-82 — and acted on zero times. A promise with no date, no owner and no failing build is not a lifecycle step.

Why it matters, and why the cost compounds

.opencode/rules/feature-flags.md identifies the specific consequence: because the flag key is unversioned and never retired, an override set months ago for one meaning silently governs whatever that flag later comes to mean, with no audit trail beyond the shell history of whoever exported it. The rule explicitly names flag removal as the only thing bounding that consequence. With three live keys, three such time bombs are armed. Every un-deleted flag also carries permanent dead weight: its OFF-position test and its conditional branches.

Second-order trap — do not miss this

When a flag is deleted, its OFF-position test must be deleted in the same commit, not left asserting an unreachable condition. For game-over that is GameOverControllerDisabledIntegrationTest, whose @SpringBootTest(properties = "eop.features.game-over=false") override is now the only place the OFF position is exercised. After removal the property is inert, the beans unconditional, and the test asserts nothing. As ADR-042 states: a green suite after removal, without having touched that test, is evidence the removal was incomplete — not that it was safe.

Scope

Remove all three flags and everything that exists only to support them:

  • the eop.features keys and their comment blocks in application.yml
  • all @ConditionalOnProperty(prefix = "eop.features", ...) guards (GameOverController:33 and the bean guards in UseCaseConfiguration)
  • the Optional<...> injection points that exist only because a flag can remove a bean (e.g. Optional<PersistGameResultUseCase> in PlayCardUseCase and ResolveTrickUseCase)
  • the OFF-position tests (GameOverControllerDisabledIntegrationTest, SessionLifecycleOffValueIntegrationTest and equivalents)
  • the flag lines in src/test/resources/application.properties
  • the corresponding assertions in ShippedFeatureFlagDefaultsTest

Acceptance criteria

  • grep -rn "eop.features" src/ ui/ returns nothing, or only what is deliberately retained with a documented reason.
  • No test asserts an unreachable OFF condition.
  • ./mvnw verify green; the removal of each OFF-position test is a deliberate, reviewed deletion rather than an oversight.
  • ADR-013, ADR-040 and ADR-042 amended to record the removals and to close out their expiry commitments.

ADR-042 sets a dated expiry for `game-over`: the story closing EOP-83, or 2026-09-18, whichever is first — and states the date does not move silently.

renderedFields.description:
Context

src/main/java/org/maglez/eop/usecase/GetLeaderboardUseCase.java:71-72:

{code:java}

gameResultRepository.findBySessionId(sessionId)

.orElseThrow(() -> new SessionNotFoundException(sessionId));

{code}

This makes a recoverable timing condition (the game_result row has not been written yet) indistinguishable from a missing aggregate (no such session). The use case's own javadoc already confesses the ambiguity: @throws SessionNotFoundException if no session has that identifier, or the session is completed but no result has been persisted yet. A documented ambiguity is still an ambiguity — the type system carries one meaning and the prose carries two.

The enumeration-defence argument does not survive the call order

The usual justification for collapsing "not found" and "not yours" into one 404 is enumeration defence. It has no work to do at this line. Membership is resolved at `:67` via resolvePlayerUseCase.execute(sessionId, playerToken), three lines before the throw. Anyone who reaches :72 has already proven they are seated in that session; a stranger guessing an identifier is stopped at :67 with PlayerNotRecognisedException to 403 and never reaches the result lookup. Splitting the two meanings at :72 therefore discloses nothing to anyone not already inside the session. The argument would be valid at :67. It is not valid at :72.

The user-visible consequence

A seated player is told "No session found with identifier ..." about the session they are sitting in. EOP-82 stopped that lie from destroying their credential (the frontend now ejects only on 403), which was the important half — but the wrong message is still rendered next to a Retry loading results button, which reads as a contradiction.

Proposed fix — deliberately narrow

Introduce a distinct domain exception at :72 (e.g. GameResultNotYetPersistedException) and keep the HTTP status at 404. This preserves the client contract EOP-82 just established — 404 means retry, do not eject — while separating the identity and the message, so the retry path gets an honest label. Splitting the status as well would invalidate the front-end logic and is not wanted.

The new exception must live in org.maglez.eop.* with zero Spring imports, and GlobalExceptionHandler must map it to 404 with its own title and detail, per .opencode/rules/error-handling.md.

Acceptance criteria

  • A distinct exception is thrown at GetLeaderboardUseCase:72; SessionNotFoundException there is reserved for a genuinely absent session.
  • GlobalExceptionHandler maps it to 404 with an accurate title and detail that does not claim the session is missing.
  • A unit test asserts the HTTP status mapping (mandatory per error-handling.md) and an integration test asserts the RFC 9457 body on the completed-but-unpersisted path — a gap @tester-api already noted as uncovered.
  • The @throws javadoc no longer documents two meanings for one type.
  • docs/architecture/runtime-view.md Sequence 11 currently shows a single GameResult (else 404) edge; split it so the diagram distinguishes the two conditions.

renderedFields.description:
Two defects at one line

src/main/java/org/maglez/eop/adapter/web/GameOverController.java:79:

{code:java}

return LeaderboardDto.from(leaderboard.scoreSheet(), "COMPLETED");

{code}

1. The status literal is only accidentally right

It is correct today solely because GetLeaderboardUseCase:68 already throws GameNotCompletedException to 409 for any other status. The controller restates an invariant proved elsewhere instead of reading the value it already has. That is temporal coupling to another class's guard clause: not wrong, accidentally right, and silently wrong the day the 409 is relaxed.

That day is foreseeable: docs/api/openapi.yml already claims the leaderboard "is available in any session state, not only COMPLETED" — one of the two divergences tracked in EOP-83. Whichever way EOP-83 resolves, if it resolves toward the spec, this literal starts lying.

2. leaderboard.gameResult() is discarded entirely

LeaderboardDto.from is from(final ScoreSheet, final String) (LeaderboardDto.java:42) — it never receives the GameResult. So LeaderboardResult (:17, with Objects.requireNonNull(gameResult) at :26) requires and carries an aggregate no consumer reads: it is loaded at GetLeaderboardUseCase:71 purely as an existence gate, then dropped.

Worse, LeaderboardResult's javadoc claims it bundles the result "so the controller can build the full leaderboard DTO". That claim is untrue of the current code. Harmless at runtime, but it is a misleading contract sitting immediately next to the field whose absence produces the 404 discussed in the sibling ticket.

Proposed fix

Carry the resolved session status through LeaderboardResult and pass it to LeaderboardDto.from, at which point the literal and the misleading javadoc both go. One line of honesty, not a refactor. Either make LeaderboardResult.gameResult() genuinely used or drop it from the record and correct the javadoc — do not leave a required field that nothing reads while its documentation says otherwise.

Acceptance criteria

  • sessionStatus in the response is derived from the resolved session, not a string literal.
  • LeaderboardResult's javadoc matches what the code does; any field it requires is either consumed or removed.
  • An integration test asserts $.sessionStatus reflects the actual session status rather than passing because the literal happens to match.
  • No behaviour change for a COMPLETED session — the existing shouldReturnLeaderboardForCompletedSession test still passes unmodified.

renderedFields.description:
Finding

Raised as MEDIUM by @security-auditor and MINOR by @architecture-guardian during the EOP-82 DoD review. Not introduced by EOP-82; EOP-82 made one more route reachable and added a client-side retry that can drive it.

*There is no rate limit on `GET /api/v1/sessions/

{id}

/leaderboard` at any layer.* Verified during review:

  • A grep for addInterceptors, HandlerInterceptor, OncePerRequestFilter and FilterRegistrationBean across src/main/java returns no output at all — there is no servlet filter and no MVC interceptor anywhere in the application, so no cross-cutting throttle exists.
  • ui/Caddyfile contains no `rate_limit` directive; handle /api/* applies only {{request_body { max_size 16KB }

    }} and reverse_proxy. Caddy's rate limiter is a non-standard plugin and is not present.

  • eop.web.session-creation-limit and the join-attempt limiter guard creation only. The SSE subscriber cap guards the event stream only. Nothing covers reads.

Amplification introduced by EOP-82

ui/src/components/GameOverScreen.tsx renders a Retry loading results button whenever the leaderboard failed to load. Each click issues one GET /leaderboard, which performs findById + findBySessionId + findTricks (up to ~66 trick plays for a three-player game) + a full ScoreSheet recomputation. EOP-82 added a pending/disabled state so a double-click cannot issue two concurrent fetches, but there is still no attempt cap and no backoff — a determined click storm is a self-inflicted DoS on a comparatively expensive route.

Mitigating factors (why this was not a blocker on EOP-82)

  • The route requires a valid seated-player token — 403 without one, so it is not an unauthenticated amplifier.
  • Retry is human-click-driven; there is no automatic retry loop.
  • The gap is a pre-existing property of every authenticated read route, not something EOP-82 created.

Scope

Design and implement rate limiting for authenticated read routes as a cross-cutting concern rather than per-route:

  • Decide the layer (servlet filter / MVC interceptor / Caddy plugin) and record it in an ADR — this is an architectural decision, not a local change.
  • Key on the resolved player or session, never on a client-supplied header. ADR-021 / EOP-26 is the precedent to read first: the integration suite previously got its throttle isolation from X-Forwarded-For, which was itself the vulnerability. Do not repeat that.
  • Return 429 with an RFC 9457 application/problem+json body, per .opencode/rules/error-handling.md.
  • Make the limit configurable under the eop.* root via @ConfigurationProperties with @Validated, per .opencode/rules/configuration.md.
  • Consider a bounded attempt cap or backoff on the GameOverScreen retry button as defence in depth.

Acceptance criteria

  • A documented, configurable limit applies to authenticated read routes including GET /leaderboard.
  • Exceeding it returns 429 with a problem+json body; a unit test asserts the status mapping and an integration test asserts the body.
  • The limiter key cannot be influenced by any request header (explicit test).
  • Test isolation does not depend on forging the limiter key — use @DirtiesContext or an equivalent, per the EOP-26 precedent.
  • An ADR records the layer chosen and the alternatives rejected.

comments.body:
Implemented on branch eop-88-read-route-rate-limiting. PR open for human review and merge: https://github.com/maglez/eop-threat-medeling/pull/117

Acceptance criteria

AC Status Evidence
1. Documented configurable limit on read routes incl. GET /leaderboard Met ReadRateLimitProperties binds eop.web.read-rate-limit (limit: 300, max-tracked-keys: 10000); ReadRateLimitInterceptor registered by WebInterceptorConfiguration on GET/HEAD under /api/v1/**
2. 429 + RFC 9457 problem+json, unit-tested mapping and integration-tested body Met Mapping was already covered by GlobalExceptionHandlerTest before this story — verified, not rewritten. Body asserted by ReadRateLimitIntegrationTest incl. a Retry-After value matched against ^[1-9][0-9]*$
3. Limiter key cannot be influenced by any request header, explicit test Met Key is ClientAddressResolver.of(request). ReadRateLimitInterceptorTest has a 15-case nested class over twelve headers — X-Forwarded-For (including rotated per request), Forwarded, X-Real-IP, X-Client-IP, Client-IP, True-Client-IP, CF-Connecting-IP, X-Cluster-Client-IP, X-Originating-IP, X-Remote-Addr, X-Forwarded, and X-EoP-Player-Token. server.forward-headers-strategy: none is the second independent guard
4. Test isolation does not forge the limiter key Met Suite-wide raised limit in src/test/resources/application.properties, plus @SpringBootTest(properties = "eop.web.read-rate-limit.limit=3") and @DirtiesContext per class. No test sends a forwarding header
5. ADR records the layer and the rejected alternatives Met [ADR-051|docs/adr/ADR-051-read-route-rate-limit.md] — interceptor chosen; servlet filter, Caddy plugin and per-controller checks each rejected with reasons, plus ten accepted limitations

Terminology correction

The ticket says "authenticated read routes". ADR-015 records that there is no authentication in this application — the routes carry an X-EoP-Player-Token capability and answer 403 without one. The ADR and the code say token-bearing instead.

Why the key is an address and not the player token

The counter must fail closed when its key table saturates (ADR-033). A token is client-supplied and unvalidated at the interceptor layer, so keying on it would let one caller mint 10,000 bogus tokens, fill the table, and have the limiter refuse everybody. A spoofable identifier must not select the bucket a fail-closed control counts in.

Definition of Done — all five gates approved

@tester-unit-and-quality, @tester-api, @security-auditor, @code-reviewer and @architecture-guardian all returned VERDICT: APPROVE. The first two rejected initially; commit a1072f6 closed their findings and both re-approved.

Two findings were substantive and are worth recording here:

  • `ProblemDetail.type` was documented as required but is never sent. RFC 9457 §3.1 makes the member optional with a default of about:blank, and Spring omits it while it holds that default. docs/api/openapi.yml listed it in required — a claim no response in this API has ever satisfied. Corrected to required: [title, status]. Pre-existing and affecting every 4xx/5xx response, in scope here only because this story added seven new references to TooManyRequests.
  • *`GET /api/v1/sessions/ {id}

    /events` answers 404, not 403, for an unknown session* — it checks session existence before resolving the player, unlike /leaderboard. The integration test now pins that status.

Known limitations, recorded rather than hidden

SSE reconnection is not rate limited — preHandle runs again on the ASYNC dispatch, so a naive counter would double-count every stream; its cost is bounded by the ADR-034 subscriber cap instead. Counters are in memory and per-instance (ADR-012). NAT'd players share one bucket and address rotation remains a deterrent rather than an absolute cap. The public card catalogue shares one budget with the token-bearing reads. The sliding-window algorithm now exists in three places — EOP-152 filed to migrate the join and creation limiters onto SlidingWindowCounter, deliberately not done here because ADR-019 makes the join throttle a primary security control.

Evidence

./mvnw clean verify BUILD SUCCESS — 1336 tests, 0 failures, 0 errors, 0 skipped; SpotBugs 0 findings; JaCoCo all coverage checks met with SlidingWindowCounter at 100% instruction and 100% branch (18/18); Javadoc and Checkstyle clean. npm run verify green in ui/ (typecheck, ESLint, Vitest, production build).

renderedFields.description:
Finding

Raised as LOW/INFO by @security-auditor during the EOP-82 DoD review, and explicitly not run as an ad-hoc scan because it would have proved nothing about that branch (EOP-82 changes no dependency and no lockfile).

Verified absent — greps for dependency-check, owasp, trivy, snyk, ossindex, sonatype, cyclonedx and sbom against pom.xml, and for those plus npm audit, codeql and dependency-review across .github/, all return no match.

There is no OWASP dependency-check plugin, no Trivy, no Snyk, no `npm audit` step, no CodeQL, no dependency-review action and no SBOM generation anywhere in pom.xml or .github/workflows/ci.yml.

maven-enforcer-plugin covers dependency convergence and banned dependencies (.opencode/rules/build-quality.md), which is supply-chain hygiene — but it is not CVE detection. A transitive dependency with a published critical CVE would pass every gate the project currently has.

This is a gap on both sides of the stack: the Java dependency tree via Maven, and the front-end tree under ui/ via npm.

Scope

  • Add CVE scanning for the Maven dependency tree (OWASP dependency-check, or an equivalent chosen deliberately).
  • Add CVE scanning for the ui/ npm tree.
  • Decide and document the failure policy: which severities fail the build versus warn. build-quality.md's existing posture is that high/medium SpotBugs findings fail the build, which is the precedent to reason from.
  • Decide and document the suppression mechanism, because an unsuppressable scanner in a blocking gate gets disabled the first time it fires on an unfixable transitive.
  • Consider SBOM generation (CycloneDX) as a separate, non-blocking output.
  • Record the choice and the rejected alternatives in an ADR — which scanner, which layer, which severities block, and how suppressions are reviewed.

Acceptance criteria

  • ./mvnw verify (or a clearly-documented separate CI job) scans both dependency trees for known CVEs.
  • The failure policy is explicit, documented, and demonstrated — a deliberately-introduced vulnerable dependency fails the gate.
  • Suppressions live in a reviewed file with a reason and an expiry per entry, not as a blanket disable.
  • An ADR records the decision.
  • CI runtime impact measured and noted; if the scan needs a cache or a scheduled rather than per-commit run, that trade-off is recorded rather than discovered later.

comments.body:
Delivered — merged to main as 7d30fb2 (PR #115)

All five acceptance criteria met

AC-1 — both dependency trees scanned. A new dependency-cve job in .github/workflows/ci.yml runs tools/supply-chain/scan-dependencies.sh, which scans pom.xml (Maven, transitively — CVE-2026-49844 was found at depth 3 via log4j-to-slf4j, proving real resolution rather than a shallow read) and ui/package-lock.json (npm — the lockfile, because every version in ui/package.json is a caret range). A separate CI job rather than ./mvnw verify, which this AC explicitly permits and which ci.yml twice insists on by requiring the build job stay Java-only and fast.

AC-2 — failure policy explicit, documented and demonstrated. Gates on HIGH and CRITICAL only, matching audit-plugins.sh's existing gating set. The divergence from build-quality.md's SpotBugs high/medium posture is argued rather than glossed: a SpotBugs medium is in our own code and always actionable, whereas a third-party transitive medium is frequently unreachable, often has no in-range fix, and arrives at a volume set by other people's release cadence.

Demonstrated in six steps by reintroducing the real HIGH this ticket fixed, so the demonstration doubles as proof the version override is load-bearing:

Step Condition Result
1 branch as merged, empty allowlist exit 0
2 postgresql.version reverted to 42.7.11 exit 1 — HIGH CVE-2026-54291 with no entry
3 allowlist entry expiring 2027-02-22 added exit 0, suppression printed
4 same entry, expires set to 2026-08-01 exit 1 — "re-argued, not re-dated"
5 fix restored, entry left in place exit 1 — "DELETE the entry"
6 entry deleted exit 0

AC-3 — suppressions reviewed, with a reason and an expiry. tools/supply-chain/accepted-cves.json, modelled on accepted-advisories.json but with two deliberate divergences. Eleven mandatory fields including a prose reachability trace and the `expires` field the existing model lacks. Keyed ID@module rather than by bare ID, because CVE-2026-59889 was measured hitting com.fasterxml.jackson.core:jackson-databind and tools.jackson.core:jackson-databind in the same scan — a bare key would have suppressed both when only one was traced. The file ships empty, which is the correct steady state.

AC-4 — ADR. ADR-050, amended in place and dated after the incident below.

AC-5 — runtime measured. 4.75 s warm for both scan passes, plus 3 s for the Maven resolve step; ~6 s more on a cold Trivy DB (108.82 MiB). Two caches keyed differently on purpose: /.cache/trivy by UTC date, ~/.m2/repository by POM hash. Observed in CI at 17 s warm.

Six real vulnerabilities found and fixed, not just a scanner installed

The scanner found 1 HIGH and 5 MEDIUM on main. All six were closed by four patch-level overrides of Spring-Boot-parent-managed properties — postgresql 42.7.11→42.7.12 (CVE-2026-54291, MITM protection bypass via SCRAM-SHA-256, the only HIGH and the only directly-declared dependency), jackson-2-bom 2.21.4→2.21.5, jackson-bom 3.1.4→3.1.5, log4j2 2.25.4→2.25.5.

So the gate arrived green rather than red. A gate that is red the day it lands gets switched off rather than fixed.

The gate's exit contract earned its keep on day one

The job's first CI run failed — 429 Too Many Requests from Maven Central, Retry-After: 1800, on spring-data-bom. The script exited 2, not 0, refusing to report a clean tree from a scan that could not resolve the tree.

The root cause was a claim this change made about its own design: Trivy resolves the Maven tree with its own parser rather than invoking Maven, so the job originally carried no setup-java. True of the parser, false of the job — the parser keeps no cache and re-fetches every parent POM on every run, enough to trip Central's limiter from a shared CI address. Fixed with setup-java, an ~/.m2/repository cache sharing the build job's restore prefix, and a ./mvnw B dependency:resolve step. `-offline-scan` was refused: it would silently shrink the tree Trivy believes exists, an under-report presented as a clean scan — the one failure mode this design refuses.

The false claim had shipped in four documents. All four were corrected, and ADR-050's amendment is dated and states explicitly what is not amended, so the audit trail survives.

Sign-off

All five DoD gates returned VERDICT: APPROVE against the merged commit 3b3cb59 — @security-auditor, @code-reviewer, @architecture-guardian, @tester-unit-and-quality, @tester-api. Two findings they raised (an undated ADR amendment; -q suppressing the very output that diagnosed the incident) were remediated rather than deferred, and all five were then re-dispatched rather than carrying earlier approvals forward. ./mvnw verify green throughout: 1280 tests, 0 failures, all coverage checks met. All five CI jobs green.

Follow-ups filed

EOP-146 (unguarded heredoc vs the exit contract), EOP-147 (gating logic has no automated test), EOP-148 (nothing detects an override overtaken by the Boot parent), EOP-149 (promote to a required check), EOP-150 (no complete-field-set API test), EOP-151 (stale plugin count in ci.yml).

Costs accepted, not hidden

The four overrides are rot liabilities with no automated check (EOP-148). The scan reads the resolved tree, so ADR-047's H2 exclusion is not honoured and an H2 CVE would gate falsely — the safe direction of that error, but real. Fat-jar scanning was measured not to work (num=0, unchanged with --java-db-repository set explicitly), which is why CycloneDX is deferred rather than rejected. The gating tier is empty today, so the policy rests on demonstration rather than a standing log. The job is not yet a required status check.

Finding

Raised as NIT by @architecture-guardian during the EOP-82 DoD review, noted while reading the file for the EOP-27 masking-trap precedent. Pre-existing and out of scope for EOP-82.

docs/adr/ADR-008-database-migration-liquibase.md Consequences contains two statements that are no longer true:

  • `:47` — "H2 console available ... in dev profile". Withdrawn by this same ADR's own Amendment, 2026-08-10 (EOP-27) block, which records that spring.h2.console.enabled is pinned false and that H2ConsoleAbsentIntegrationTest puts a tripwire on the autoconfiguration class. The ADR now contradicts itself: an amendment later in the file retracts a Consequence that still stands earlier in it.
  • `:49` — "Staging environment runs against PostgreSQL". There is no staging environment. ADR-012 established exactly two profiles — the default profile and prod — and .opencode/rules/configuration.md states there is no dev profile and no test profile, and that config, code or docs referencing one must not be written.

Both lines therefore assert infrastructure that the project's own configuration ADR forbids. The dev profile reference is the more harmful of the two: it invites a reader to add one.

Scope

  • Correct or strike ADR-008:47 so it agrees with the EOP-27 amendment rather than contradicting it.
  • Correct or strike ADR-008:49 so it does not assert a staging environment.
  • Sweep the rest of docs/ for the same two claims — configuration.md is unambiguous that no dev or test profile exists, so any other occurrence is the same defect.

Acceptance criteria

  • No ADR Consequence contradicts a later amendment in the same file.
  • No document under docs/ asserts a dev profile, a test profile or a staging environment as existing.
  • AdrIndexConsistencyTest still green (it enforces one Status line per ADR and index/file agreement).

renderedFields.description:
Problem

onSessionEnd() clears sessionStorage and returns the client to the home screen. Because ADR-015 stores only a SHA-256 of the player token and SessionAdmission is the only response that ever carries the plaintext, calling `onSessionEnd()` destroys a credential that cannot be reissued. It is an irreversible, security-relevant client-side action.

After EOP-82 the rule for which HTTP statuses trigger that destruction is deliberately asymmetric across screens, and that asymmetry is recorded nowhere in a diagram:

Call site Triggering statuses Why
ui/src/components/LobbyScreen.tsx:57 (in refreshSession) `403   404` On the session resource a 404 means the session is genuinely gone
ui/src/components/LobbyScreen.tsx:87 (third positional arg of subscribeToSession, not a named onError) `403   404` Same reasoning
ui/src/components/GameScreen.tsx SSE error handler `403   404` Same reasoning
ui/src/components/GameScreen.tsx refreshGameState getSession 403/404; fetchHand/getTrickState 403 only Mixed
ui/src/components/GameOverScreen.tsx loadLeaderboard 403 only (since EOP-82) On the leaderboard sub-resource a 404 means the game_result row is not yet written — a race with a best-effort persist, not a missing session

Same code shape, opposite meaning depending on the resource. Copying the pattern from one screen to another without re-deriving the semantics is exactly the defect that produced EOP-82 fault 2: every client was ejected to home because a transient leaderboard 404 was read as "session gone".

Why this is a documentation gap and not just a code comment

@architecture-guardian raised this at both DoD review rounds on EOP-82 and it is the only one of its findings that no ticket owns:

  • grep -rn "GameOverScreen" docs/ returned zero matches before EOP-82; it now returns 3, all prose in docs/adr/ADR-042-game-over-flag-on.md and the ADR index row.
  • docs/architecture/runtime-view.md:170 documents onSessionEnd() only in the LobbyScreen context.
  • No sequenceDiagram anywhere depicts the client-side decision "which error statuses destroy the session credential".
  • docs/architecture/runtime-view.md:7-10 currently defers the leaderboard-404 client handling to ADR-042 rather than duplicating it. That is an acceptable interim state for a bug-fix branch, but it means the rule is reconstructable only by reading two ADR paragraphs and four TSX files.

The guardian's argument, recorded verbatim in the EOP-82 review: a rule that every call site of `onSessionEnd` appears in the runtime view with its triggering statuses enumerated would have made fault 2 visible on the page before it shipped.

Acceptance criteria

  1. docs/architecture/runtime-view.md gains a section (with a Mermaid sequenceDiagram or a table where a diagram would not add clarity) enumerating every onSessionEnd() call site in ui/src/, the resource each one is reacting to, and the exact set of statuses that trigger credential destruction at that site.
  2. The section states explicitly why the leaderboard sub-resource differs from the session resource, so the asymmetry reads as a decision rather than an inconsistency.
  3. The section notes that onSessionEnd() is irreversible under ADR-015 (server holds only the SHA-256; SessionAdmission is the only response carrying plaintext), so a wrong status in this table costs the user their seat.
  4. A short rule is added to the architecture documentation (and, if the team agrees, to .opencode/rules/) requiring any new onSessionEnd() call site to be added to that section in the same commit.
  5. docs/architecture/runtime-view.md Sequence 11 (the game-over leaderboard sequence, currently :1093-1122) gains a note on the client-side handling of its else 404 arm, so the diagram and the new section agree. EOP-82 deliberately left Sequence 11 untouched.
  6. runtime-view.md's currency marker is advanced, and ./mvnw verify stays green (AdrIndexConsistencyTest included if any ADR status line moves).

Notes

  • Raised by @architecture-guardian during the EOP-82 Definition-of-Done review (both the REJECT round and the follow-up APPROVE round). Documentation-only; no production code change is expected.
  • Related but separately ticketed: EOP-86 (GetLeaderboardUseCase overloads SessionNotFoundException for "result not yet persisted") will change what a leaderboard 404 means, so these two should be sequenced together — resolving EOP-86 first would let this section describe a distinct exception rather than an overloaded one.
  • docs/architecture/building-blocks.md is still absent project-wide (EOP-47); this ticket does not depend on it.

renderedFields.description:
Context

The product owner has withdrawn a requirement they set at EOP-72. Verbatim:

"One correction, at one point I said that no all cards need to be dealt, that all players should have the same number of cards and the rest should be discarded but this come with the risk of the 3 of Tampering being discarded and then the game not be possible to start because the player with the 3 of Tampering needs to start the game. Make sure that the code behaves in a way where all cards are dealt and none are discarded"

EOP-72 superseded ADR-023 Decision 1 with an equal-hands rule: deal floor(D / n) * n cards and discard the remainder. This story reverts that and reinstates the original rule — every card is dealt, nothing is discarded, with the remainder falling to the lowest seats through the existing round-robin.

Current behaviour

Hands.deal(List<Card>, List<Seat>) truncates the deck to an equal hand size and discards the rest. Against the 68-card printed deck (ADR-041, EOP-75) a three-player table is dealt 22/22/22 = 66 cards, discarding 2. Verified at runtime against the local Docker stack.

Two reasons to revert, not one

  1. The reason the product owner gives. The opening lead belongs to the holder of the lowest-ranked Tampering card. Discarding the remainder risks discarding that card and leaving the game unstartable.
  1. A fairness bias in the mitigation, which they have not seen. Hands.deal() already guards against (1): it scans for the lowest Tampering card and, if that card falls outside the kept range, swaps it to index keptSize - 1. That index is always dealt to (keptSize - 1) % playerCount — the last seat, every time. So whenever the swap fires, the opening lead is handed deterministically to the highest-seated player instead of being random. Dealing the whole deck deletes the special case and the bias with it.

Expected behaviour

All D cards dealt round-robin in the order given, seats ascending. Hand sizes differ by at most one, with the extra cards going to the lowest seats. For the 68-card deck:

  • 3 players — 23 / 23 / 22
  • 4 players — 17 each
  • 5 players — 14 / 14 / 14 / 13 / 13
  • 6 players — 12 / 12 / 11 / 11 / 11 / 11

This is already what docs/api/openapi.yml documents, so the change resolves divergence 1 of EOP-83 in favour of the specification. EOP-83's second divergence (the leaderboard 409) is unrelated and stays open.

Risk assessment: low

The unequal-hands machinery was never removed at EOP-72 — that story only made the rule trivially satisfied. Trick.isComplete(Collection<Integer> seatsHoldingCards) and Trick.seatToPlay(Collection) both take the set of seats still holding cards as a parameter, and PlayCardUseCase passes it. Short final tricks are still supported end to end.

Acceptance criteria

  1. Hands.deal() deals every card in the deck it is given. No card is discarded on any supported table size.
  2. The Tampering scan-and-swap block is deleted, because dealing everything makes it unreachable. NoTamperingCardDealtException stays as the guard for a deck holding no Tampering card at all.
  3. Automated tests assert, for 3, 4, 5 and 6 players over a 68-card deck, that the dealt hands sum to the deck size, that no card is lost or duplicated, and that hand sizes differ by at most one with the surplus on the lowest seats.
  4. A test asserts the opening leader is the holder of the lowest Tampering card, and a test asserts a short final trick resolves correctly.
  5. The reversal is recorded as an amendment to ADR-023 superseding the EOP-72 amendment, carrying a 68-card arithmetic table and the fairness-bias rationale above.
  6. ./mvnw verify passes, and the equal-hands truncation restored by hand fails the new tests (mutation-verified).

comments.body:
PR open and all CI checks green: https://github.com/maglez/eop-threat-medeling/pull/86 (build, ui, image all pass). Branch eop-92-deal-every-card, 4 commits. Awaiting human review and merge.

Acceptance criteria — evidence

1. Every card is dealt; nothing is discarded. Hands.deal() loses the handSize/keptSize truncation, the mutable workingDeck copy and the whole Tampering scan-and-swap block. The loop runs to orderedDeck.size().

2. Correct seat-order distribution. 3 players 23/23/22, 4 players 17/17/17/17, 5 players 14/14/14/13/13, 6 players 12/12/11/11/11/11 — all summing to 68 with nothing discarded. Independently re-derived by @tester-unit-and-quality and confirmed against HandsTest, the ADR-023 amendment and openapi.yml.

3. The opening-lead card can no longer be discarded. It is now total by construction rather than by a swap: the lowest Tampering card is in the deck, so it is in a hand. NoTamperingCardDealtException is deliberately kept and remains reachable for a deck containing no Tampering card at all — @security-auditor confirmed it still fails closed, throwing before any deal is persisted or any event published.

4. Regression coverage, mutation-verified. Restoring the truncation fails 10 HandsTest tests, with the new shouldDiscardNothingAtAnyTableSize conservation guard failing at 3, 5 and 6 players but not at 4 — because 68 ÷ 4 = 17 exactly, so four players lose nothing under truncation either. The guard discriminates rather than blanket-failing. Also added: shouldPlaceTheSurplusOnTheLowestSeats, shouldDealTheFinalCardOfTheDeck, and TrickTest.shouldCompleteAShortFinalTrick (whose third assertion, that the same trick reads incomplete when the exhausted seat is wrongly said to hold a card, is what makes it discriminating rather than tautological).

5. Build green. ./mvnw verify — 1226 tests, 0 failures, SpotBugs BugInstance size is 0, All coverage checks have been met., 0 checkstyle violations. Hands itself is at 99.1% instruction and 95.0% branch coverage; removing the branch-heavy swap improved it.

6. End-to-end against a rebuilt local stack. Three real players over https://localhost/api/v1 after ./scripts/update-local.sh: dealt 23/23/22, TOTAL DEALT = 68, zero duplicate cardIds, 68 plays (up from 66 — the 68th is the short final trick resolving with seat 2 empty), status COMPLETED, leaderboard 200.

A defect found that was not in the request

EOP-72's mitigation swapped the lowest Tampering card to index keptSize - 1. Since keptSize = floor(D / n) x n is a multiple of n by construction, (keptSize - 1) mod n is identically n - 1 — so the swap could only ever land on the last seat. Whenever it fired (~2.9% of three- and six-player games, ~4.4% of five-player, never at four) the opening lead was handed deterministically to the highest-seated player. It was invisible to a green build because every test asserted hand sizes, and a swap to a fixed index satisfies those by construction. This is the stronger justification for the revert and is recorded in the ADR-023 amendment.

Recorded honestly alongside it: removing the swap makes the lead shuffle-determined, not uniform — each seat's probability is proportional to its hand size (0.338/0.338/0.324 at three players), exactly uniform only at four. @security-auditor raised that over-claim before any document made it, and ADR-023 now forbids restating it as uniformity.

Five DoD gates — all approved, two after rejection

  • @tester-unit-and-quality — REJECT, then APPROVE. Rejected on two stale comments in TrickControllerIntegrationTest still describing the discarded-remainder rule, one sitting directly above the loop whose hand.isEmpty() guard exists precisely because seats do not all run out together. Remediated by fixing both and then sweeping the repository for the same defect class, which found three more.
  • @tester-api — APPROVE. Confirmed EOP-83 divergence 1 fully resolved and every asserted status code and JSON path verified against controller and GlobalExceptionHandler source.
  • @security-auditor — APPROVE. Verified the shuffle is unbiased Fisher-Yates over a self-seeded SecureRandom with no settable seed, that Hand/Hands remain deeply immutable so dropping the defensive copy is safe, and that no DTO exposes another player's card count or contents. Net assessment: a security improvement.
  • @code-reviewer — APPROVE. All four gates green including tsc --noEmit, eslint and 168 front-end tests.
  • @architecture-guardian — REJECT, then APPROVE. See below.

The architecture rejection, and why it mattered

Two Documentation Gate defects, both introduced by me, neither a code defect:

1. The ADR-023 index row had ~6.4 KB of its own prose pasted past the terminating pipe, giving a four-column table a five-cell row. GFM discards cells beyond the header count, so that text vanished from the rendered index while sitting in the source — and the row that vanished was the one this story exists to correct. Fixed, and then fixed at the level of the mechanism: AdrIndexConsistencyTest gains a fifth invariant, shouldGiveEveryRowTheDeclaredColumnCount, which counts cells the way a renderer counts them. The reviewer verified by mutation that it fires on a deficit cell as well as a surplus one, and that it survives a legitimate table widening without needing an edit — a tripwire on the world, not a snapshot of a value.

2. ADR-042 still asserted the runtime deals 66 cards, which would have left two ADRs disagreeing about the current code. It now carries a dated part-supersession recording that divergence 1 closed in favour of the spec.

EOP-83

Divergence 1 (deal card count) is resolved by this story — in favour of the spec, since openapi.yml had documented the full deal correctly all along and the implementation was what drifted. Only divergence 2 remains open: the leaderboard is documented as available in any session state but returns an undocumented 409 unless the session is COMPLETED.

Deferred with tickets, all linked Relates

  • EOP-93 — sweep the ~11 surviving 74-card references left by EOP-75, in src/ as well as docs/. Trick.java:489-492's worked example is now unreachable and should go first.
  • EOP-94 — no test asserts the opening leader is not a fixed seat.

EOP-75 trimmed the printed deck from 74 cards to 68 (aces removed, ADR-041) but left the deck size stated as 74 in roughly a dozen places. The EOP-92 review surfaced these because reinstating the full deal made several of them load-bearing again.

Two reviewers found them independently: @code-reviewer flagged the Hands javadoc, @architecture-guardian enumerated the rest.

Locations

Documentation:

  • docs/adr/ADR-023-deal-remainder-and-turn-order.md:673-674 - "At 74 cards, all four supported table sizes (3, 4, 5 and 6 players) produce unequal hands". This sits in ADR-023's original Consequences, the section EOP-92 explicitly reinstates, so EOP-92 makes it live again while it is false at 4 players. The deck size is covered by the EOP-75 amendment's blanket supersession of "all references to 74 cards"; the all four table sizes quantifier is not covered by anything.
  • docs/requirements/PRD-eop-card-game.md:124 - "At 74 cards no supported table size divides evenly". Doubly wrong now: 68, and 4 divides evenly.
  • docs/adr/ADR-019-session-lifecycle-and-join-codes.md:166-168
  • docs/adr/README.md:29 (ADR-019 row) - "74 cards do not divide evenly at 3, 4, 5 or 6 players"
  • docs/adr/ADR-030-scoring-is-derived-not-accumulated.md:179 - "a six-player game plays 74 cards in 13 tricks and a three-player game 74 in 25" (68 gives 12 and 23)
  • docs/adr/ADR-031-the-score-is-read-through-its-own-route.md:257 - "three players hold 25 or 24 cards each and a hand runs to 25 tricks" (68 gives 23/22 and 23 tricks)

Source comments:

  • src/main/java/org/maglez/eop/entity/Trick.java:20-21 and :489-492 - do this one first. The worked example at :489-492 justifies nextLeaderSeat's fallback and reads "At four players seats 0 and 1 hold nineteen cards and seats 2 and 3 hold eighteen", which is now impossible (4 players get 17/17/17/17). It is actively misleading about the property EOP-92 restores.
  • src/main/java/org/maglez/eop/entity/SeatOrder.java:15-16
  • src/main/java/org/maglez/eop/entity/NoTamperingCardDealtException.java:7-8 - "the printed 74-card deck", in the class whose whole purpose is deck composition
  • src/main/java/org/maglez/eop/entity/Hands.java:204 - openingLeaderSeat javadoc, "the 74-card deck this application seeds"
  • src/test/java/org/maglez/eop/adapter/web/TrickControllerIntegrationTest.java:481 - "74 cards over three seats leave a hand missing a named suit about three times in a thousand". The probability argument is still directionally right at 68.

Not in scope

Correct historical references inside dated amendment blocks must be left alone per the amend-don't-rewrite convention: ADR-039:16, ADR-023:1495-1534, ADR-041:14/25/58, and docs/EoP_Microsoft_Docs/LICENCE-eop-deck.md:60-73 all describe the printed deck's history and are correct as written.

Acceptance criteria

Every location above states 68 cards, or is confirmed as a correct historical reference and left alone with that judgement recorded in the PR.

The "all four supported table sizes produce unequal hands" and "no supported table size divides evenly" claims are corrected wherever they appear - 68 divides evenly by four, so hands are equal at that one table size.

Trick.java:489-492's worked example uses figures that are actually reachable.

./mvnw verify stays green. No production behaviour changes; this is comments and documentation only.

Consider whether a mechanical guard is feasible - the EOP-92 review noted that three documents were simultaneously stale with a green build, and this is the same class of failure.

renderedFields.description:
EOP-72 shipped a deterministic fairness defect that the entire test suite was blind to, and the blindness was structural rather than accidental.

What happened

EOP-72 truncated the deal and, to guarantee the opening-lead card was never discarded, swapped the lowest Tampering card to index keptSize - 1. Because keptSize = floor(D / n) x n is a multiple of n by construction, (keptSize - 1) mod n is identically n - 1 - so the swap could only ever land on the last seat. Whenever it fired, the opening lead was handed deterministically to the highest-seated player. It fired in roughly 2.9% of three- and six-player games and 4.4% of five-player games at 68 cards.

Every test asserted hand sizes. None asserted a distributional property of the opening lead. A swap that moves a named card to a fixed index passes size assertions by construction, so the defect was invisible to a green build for a whole story. It was found by reading the code during EOP-92, not by a failing test.

Why EOP-92 does not close this

EOP-92 removed the swap, which removed the bias - but it added no guard against reintroducing it. HandsTest.shouldDiscardNothingAtAnyTableSize pins conservation, which is the right property for the discard defect and was mutation-verified. It says nothing about who leads. A future change that re-biased the opening lead would pass the suite exactly as EOP-72 did.

Raised by @architecture-guardian as a structural lesson during the EOP-92 sign-off.

What the deal actually guarantees

Removing the swap makes the lead shuffle-determined, not uniform. The lead falls on whoever holds the lowest Tampering card, so each seat's probability is proportional to its hand size: 0.338/0.338/0.324 at three players, 0.176/0.176/0.162 at six, exactly uniform only at four where 68 divides evenly. Any test must assert the weaker, true property - no seat receives the lead by fiat - and must not assert uniformity. This is recorded in the EOP-92 amendment to ADR-023.

Acceptance criteria

A test drives Hands.deal over many independent shuffles (using the real SecureRandomDeckShuffler, or a seeded shuffler if determinism is needed - note ADR/EOP-14 deliberately refused a settable seed on SecureRandomDeckShuffler, so a separate test double is likely required) and asserts every seat wins the opening lead at least once.

The test does not assert uniformity. It asserts the lead is not constant, and ideally that each seat's share is consistent with being proportional to its hand size within a tolerance wide enough never to flake.

The test is deterministic or has a flake probability small enough to state explicitly in a comment, with the arithmetic shown.

Mutation-verified: reintroducing the EOP-72 swap (or any change pinning the lead to a fixed seat) fails it. Record the actual failure output in the PR.

./mvnw verify green.

renderedFields.description:
A behaviour change to a documented API surface went in without touching the contract that describes it, and nothing detected the drift for a whole story.

What happened

This project is contract-first by rule (.opencode/rules/api-design.md: "hand-author docs/api/openapi.yml before implementing new endpoints"). EOP-72 changed the observable dealing behaviour - from all 68 cards dealt to floor(D/n) x n with the remainder discarded - and did not amend docs/api/openapi.yml, which went on documenting the full deal correctly. So the spec was right and the implementation was the thing that drifted.

The drift was found by a manual audit (EOP-83 divergence 1), not by the build. EOP-92 then resolved it in favour of the spec by changing the code back.

Worse, three documents were simultaneously stale during that window and the build was green throughout:

  • docs/api/openapi.yml described a full deal the code no longer performed
  • docs/adr/README.md's ADR-023 row described the whole-deck deal for the whole EOP-72 period (this row now carries a note admitting so)
  • docs/architecture/C4-Diagrams.md's "POST /deal ... facilitator deals the whole deck" row was stale for the same period and nobody amended it

Raised by @architecture-guardian during the EOP-92 sign-off, which observed that the Documentation Gate has now been the only thing standing between a stale corpus and main on two consecutive stories (EOP-82 and EOP-92). That is a signal about where the process is thin, not about either branch.

Why AdrIndexConsistencyTest does not cover this

That test checks structural invariants of the index - file/row bijection, one Status line per ADR, status-word agreement, amendment dating, and now column count. By design it does not check agreement between a document and the code, and no test can do that in general.

Scope - this is a process and tooling ticket, not a bug

Investigate what is mechanically enforceable, and accept that some of it is not:

  • Whether a CI check can require that a commit touching a controller, a use case reachable from one, or a request/response DTO also touches docs/api/openapi.yml - and whether that is worth the false positives it will generate on pure refactors.
  • Whether the generated OpenAPI document (springdoc is already on the classpath) can be diffed against the hand-authored docs/api/openapi.yml in CI. Note this only catches signature and status drift, not prose drift, and the EOP-72 defect was prose - "all 68 cards are dealt" is a description, not a schema. Be honest in the ADR about that limit rather than overselling the check.
  • Whether the PR template should carry an explicit "does this change behaviour any document describes?" item, and whether a checklist item is worth anything given the three that were missed here.

Acceptance criteria

A decision is recorded as an ADR, including an explicit statement of what the chosen mechanism does not catch.

If a mechanical check is adopted, it fails the build on a deliberately introduced drift, with the failure output recorded in the PR.

If no mechanical check is adopted, the ADR says so and explains why the reviewer-only path is the accepted cost - do not leave this ticket resolved by a promise, which is the failure mode ADR-042 already documents for feature-flag removal.

comments.body:
Resolved by PR #120 on branch eop-95-openapi-contract-drift-gate, recorded as ADR-054.

Option (b) adopted as a JUnit build gate. OpenApiContractDriftTest fetches the springdoc-generated document from /v3/api-docs and compares it against docs/api/openapi.yml bidirectionally on two axes — path+method bijection and declared response status codes per operation. Reading the generated document means the gate cannot disagree with what Spring actually serves. No allow-list: the whole surface is covered, so GET /health is now authored into the contract rather than excluded.

Options (a) and (c) rejected with reasoning in the ADR. (a) fires on pure refactors and is trivially satisfied by a whitespace edit to the YAML, so it trains a token edit rather than a correct one. (c) is exactly the "resolved by a promise" outcome criterion 3 forbids as the sole remedy — three documents were missed on this very story while checklists existed.

Acceptance criteria

  1. ✅ ADR-054 carries a first-class "What the mechanism does NOT catch" section, stating outright that the gate would not have caught EOP-72, plus schema/property drift, reachability, proxy-layer contributions beyond one declared 413, and parameters/headers/security/tags.
  2. ✅ Four deliberate-drift experiments with verbatim failure output in the PR body. Notably experiment C — a dishonest PROXY_PRODUCED entry — produces two failures rather than none, so the declared-exception list is a required claim, not an escape hatch.
  3. n/a — a mechanical check was adopted.

What the gate forced. Making the annotated surface truthful was the bulk of the work and exposed a standing api-design rule violation: SessionController had @Operation on all five methods and @ApiResponse on none (springdoc reported a bare 200 each, including POST /api/v1/sessions which returns 201), and every GET across four controllers was missing ADR-051's 429. Each added status was traced to its emitter rather than added to go green.

Build: serial ./mvnw clean verify → Tests run: 1351, Failures: 0, Errors: 0, SpotBugs 0, JaCoCo all checks met (97.0% instructions, 88.9% branches).

DoD: all five gates returned VERDICT: APPROVE — @tester-unit-and-quality, @tester-api, @security-auditor, @code-reviewer, @architecture-guardian. One finding acted on: a stale count in the guard's own Javadoc, whose investigation surfaced a worse error both reviewers had missed (the sentence named the wrong test — the two comparison directions are not interchangeable).

CI green on PR #120 — all five jobs pass, PR is mergeable and awaiting human approval.

gh pr checks 120 (run 32633737594):

Job Result Duration
build pass 1m55s
ui pass 37s
image pass 1m32s
dependency-cve pass 24s
supply-chain pass 33s

mergeStateStatus: CLEAN, mergeable: MERGEABLE.

Note this is the first CI run in which OpenApiContractDriftTest executed on the cold path — a fresh runner with no target/ — so the gate booted its own Spring context, fetched /v3/api-docs and compared both axes against docs/api/openapi.yml without any warm-build shortcut. That matters for this story in particular, because the same cold/warm distinction is what forced a local ./mvnw clean verify: the Javadoc goal had reported "everything is up to date" despite src/main Javadoc having changed.

Ready for human review and merge.
